parts.problemMd:
***Note: For this question ensure you are working in degrees.***

The height, $h$ cm, of water in a wave tank, at time $t$ seconds after the tank is switched on, is measured according to the function

$h ( t ) = 20 \text{sin}  ( 15 t )$°

$t \geq 0$

The model is designed so that a height of 0 cm represents calm, still water.

(i) What is the maximum height the water will reach?

(ii) How long does it take the water to first reach its maximum height?

(iii) Find the height of the water after 8 seconds.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The greatest value of the sine function is 1, so the greatest height is 20 times that

**Final answer:** $\text{Maximum height} = 20$** cm**

**[B1]**

(ii)

The sine function first equals 1 when the angle is 90°

$15 t = 90$

Divide by 15 to reach the time

**Final answer:** $t = 6$** seconds**

**[B1]**

(iii)

To find the height after 8 seconds, substitute $t = 8$ into the model

$h ( 8 ) = 20 \text{sin}  ( 15 \times 8 )$*°*

Simplify the angle

$h ( 8 ) = 20 \text{sin}  120$*°*

Use the exact value of the sine of 120°

$h ( 8 ) = 20 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

Give the height in exact form and correct to 3 significant figures

**Final answer:** $h = 10 \sqrt{3}$** cm, which is **$17 . 3$** cm (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The maximum height of 20 cm. The value 20 on its own is enough, and no working is needed.
> 
> **B1**: The time of 6 seconds. Accept the answer with or without units. Working is not required, but $15 t = 90$ leading to $t = 6$ shows where the value comes from.
> 
> **B1**: The height after 8 seconds, given either as the exact value $10 \sqrt{3}$ or as an answer which rounds to 17.3. An answer of 11.6 comes from evaluating the sine in radians and earns nothing.

parts.problemMd:
A business owner invests 30 000 dollars at an interest rate of 1.14% per year.

The value, $V$ dollars, of the investment $t$ years after the initial investment is modelled by the formula

$V ( t ) = 30000 ( 1 + \frac{1.14}{100} )^{t}$

Find the value of the investment after 7 years.
parts.solutionMd:
To find the value after 7 years, substitute $t = 7$ into the model

$V ( 7 ) = 30000 ( 1 + \frac{1.14}{100} )^{7}$

Evaluate

**Final answer:** $V = 32477 . 45$** dollars, to the nearest cent**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The value of the investment after 7 years. Accept any answer of 3 significant figure accuracy or better, so 32500 and 32477.45 both score. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd: Find the least number of whole years it will take before the value of the investment has doubled.
parts.solutionMd:
The investment has doubled when it is worth 60 000 dollars, so set the model equal to that value

$30000 ( 1 + \frac{1.14}{100} )^{t} = 60000$

**[M1]**

Divide both sides by 30000

$1 . 0114^{t} = 2$

Take natural logarithms of both sides

$\text{ln}  ( 1 . 0114^{t} ) = \text{ln}  2$

Use the power law to bring the exponent down

$t  \text{ln}  1 . 0114 = \text{ln}  2$

**[M1]**

Divide to make $t$ the subject

$t = \frac{\text{ln}2}{\text{ln}1.0114} = 61 . 148 . . .$

Round up, since after 61 years the value has not yet doubled

**Final answer:** $t = 62$** years**

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The direction of the rounding is where this sort of question is most often lost. If you are unsure, put both whole years back into the model and see which one first passes 60 000. Here 61 years gives about 59 900 and 62 years gives about 60 600, which confirms that 62 is the answer.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of the model to set up the doubling condition, either as $30000 ( 1 . 0114 )^{t} = 60000$ or as $1 . 0114^{t} = 2$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of logarithms on both sides, with the power law used to bring $t$ down. Logarithms to any base are accepted.
> 
> **A1**: The integer conclusion of 62 years. An unrounded answer of 61.1, or a value rounded down to 61, does not earn this mark, because the question asks for the number of whole years before the value has doubled.

parts.problemMd:
The value, $W$ dollars, of a second investment $t$ years after the initial investment is modelled in the same way, with an initial investment of 25 000 dollars at an interest rate of 1.3% per year.

Write down a formula for $W$ in terms of $t$.
parts.solutionMd:
Keep the structure of the first model, replacing the initial investment and the interest rate

$W = 25000 ( 1 + \frac{1.3}{100} )^{t}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The correct formula. The simplified form $W = 25000 ( 1 . 013 )^{t}$ is equally acceptable, as is the use of $V$ in place of $W$.

parts.problemMd:
The flight of a hot air balloon ascending from the ground to its cruising altitude is modelled according to the function

$a ( t ) = 5 t^{3} + 5 t^{2}$

$0 \leq t \leq 10$

where $t$ is the time of ascent in minutes and $a$ is the altitude in feet.

Find the altitude of the hot air balloon after:

(i) 4 minutes,

(ii) 6 minutes.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

To find the altitude after 4 minutes, substitute $t = 4$ into the model

$a ( 4 ) = 5 ( 4 )^{3} + 5 ( 4 )^{2}$

Evaluate

**Final answer:** $a = 400$** feet**

**[B1]**

(ii)

Substitute $t = 6$ in the same way

$a ( 6 ) = 5 ( 6 )^{3} + 5 ( 6 )^{2}$

Evaluate

**Final answer:** $a = 1260$** feet**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The altitude of 400 feet after 4 minutes. Units are not required.
> 
> **B1**: The altitude of 1260 feet after 6 minutes. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd: Find the change in altitude of the hot air balloon between 5 minutes and 9 minutes.
parts.solutionMd:
The change in altitude is the altitude at 9 minutes minus the altitude at 5 minutes, so find each in turn

$a ( 5 ) = 5 ( 5 )^{3} + 5 ( 5 )^{2} = 750$

$a ( 9 ) = 5 ( 9 )^{3} + 5 ( 9 )^{2} = 4050$

Subtract to find the change

$4050 - 750$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $\text{Change in altitude} = 3300$** feet**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of the model at both 5 minutes and 9 minutes, with the two altitudes subtracted. Subtracting in the other order, giving $- 3300$, also earns this mark.
> 
> **A1**: The change in altitude of 3300 feet. A negative answer does not earn this mark, since the balloon is rising over this interval.

parts.problemMd: Explain why the model should not be used for larger values of $t$.
parts.solutionMd:
Consider what the model predicts once $t$ grows beyond the given interval

**Final answer:** **As **$t$** increases the altitude keeps increasing without limit, but a hot air balloon cannot rise forever, so the model is only valid up to its cruising altitude**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Any statement making clear that the altitude given by the model grows without limit while a real balloon cannot keep rising, or that the balloon levels off once it reaches its cruising altitude. A comment only that the model is valid for $0 \leq t \leq 10$, without saying why, does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd:
A gardener is modelling the number of hours of daylight his allotment receives at different times of the year using the function

$h ( t ) = 12 + 5  \text{sin}  ( \frac{2πt}{365} )$

$t \geq 0$

where $h$ is the number of hours of daylight on a given day, and $t$ is the time measured in whole days. Note that $t = 0$ corresponds to the first day of the model.

(i) Find the number of hours of daylight on the 100<sup>th</sup> day.

(ii) Write down the maximum and minimum number of daylight hours the model predicts.

(iii) Assuming the allotment is located in the UK, give a reason why the first day of the model most likely does ***not*** correspond to 1<sup>st</sup> January.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Since $t = 0$ is the first day, the 100<sup>th</sup> day is $t = 99$

$h ( 99 ) = 12 + 5  \text{sin}  ( \frac{2π\times99}{365} )$

**[M1]**

Evaluate, working in radians

$h ( 99 ) = 16 . 9555 . . .$

**Final answer:** $h = 16 . 96$** hours (2 d.p.)**

**[A1]**

(ii)

The sine function ranges between $- 1$ and 1, so the model ranges 5 either side of 12

**Final answer:** $\text{Maximum} = 12 + 5 = 17$** hours**

**[B1]**

**Final answer:** $\text{Minimum} = 12 - 5 = 7$** hours**

**[B1]**

(iii)

Find what the model predicts on its own first day

$h ( 0 ) = 12 + 5  \text{sin}  0 = 12$

Compare this with what the UK actually experiences in early January

**Final answer:** **The model gives 12 hours of daylight on its first day, but daylight in the UK on 1 January is close to the minimum of 7 hours, so the model must start at a different time of year**

**[B1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Read the definition of the variable before you substitute. Here $t = 0$ is the first day, so the 100<sup>th</sup> day is $t = 99$, and substituting 100 instead gives 16.94, which is close enough to look right but is not. Whenever a question defines a starting value explicitly, it is usually because the off-by-one matters.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct substitution of $t = 99$ into the model. Substituting $t = 100$ does not earn this mark, because the question states that $t = 0$ is the first day.
> 
> **A1**: Accept any answer of 3 significant figure accuracy or better, so both 17.0 and 16.96 score. An answer of 16.94 comes from using $t = 100$ and scores nothing here. Working in degrees rather than radians gives 12.1 and earns neither mark.
> 
> **B1**: The maximum of 17 hours, from $12 + 5$.
> 
> **B1**: The minimum of 7 hours, from $12 - 5$.
> 
> **B1**: Any reason making clear that the model predicts 12 hours on its first day while UK daylight on 1 January is near the yearly minimum. Stating only that the answer should be near the minimum, without linking it to what the model gives at $t = 0$, is not enough for this mark.

parts.problemMd:
In a simple model of an investment account, the function

$V ( t ) = I ( 1 + \frac{r}{100} )^{t}$

is used, where $I$ is the initial amount invested, $r$ % is the interest rate, and $V$ is the value of the investment $t$ years later.

For an initial investment of 1000 dollars, find the value after 12 years at an interest rate of 0.8%.
parts.solutionMd:
Substitute the initial amount, the rate and the time into the model

$V ( 12 ) = 1000 ( 1 + \frac{0.8}{100} )^{12}$

**[M1]**

Evaluate

$V ( 12 ) = 1000 \times 1 . 008^{12}$

**Final answer:** $V = 1100 . 34$** dollars, to the nearest cent**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct substitution of $I = 1000$, $r = 0 . 8$ and $t = 12$ into the model. The multiplier 1.008 seen raised to the power 12 also earns this mark.
> 
> **A1**: The value of the investment. Accept any answer of 3 significant figure accuracy or better, so 1100 and 1100.34 both score.

parts.problemMd:
After investing 400 dollars for 8 years the value of the investment is 448.82 dollars.

Find the interest rate, correct to three significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
Substitute the values that are known into the model, leaving $r$ as the unknown

$400 ( 1 + \frac{r}{100} )^{8} = 448 . 82$

**[M1]**

Divide both sides by 400 to isolate the bracket

$( 1 + \frac{r}{100} )^{8} = 1 . 12205$

Raise both sides to the power $\frac{1}{8}$ (taking the 8th root, `root index 8 of blank`)

$1 + \frac{r}{100} = 1 . 12205^{\frac{1}{8}} = 1 . 0144987 . . .$

**[M1]**

Subtract 1

$\frac{r}{100} = 0 . 0144987 . . .$

Multiply by 100 to reach the percentage rate

**Final answer:** $r = 1 . 45$** % (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct substitution of the initial amount, the final value and the time into the model, giving an equation in $r$ alone.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method to undo the power of 8, either by raising both sides to the power $\frac{1}{8}$ or by taking logarithms of both sides and dividing by 8. Both routes are equally acceptable.
> 
> **A1**: An answer which rounds to 1.45. The percentage sign is not required. An answer of 0.0145, left as a decimal rather than converted to a percentage, does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd: Find the least number of years 20 000 dollars would need to be invested at an interest rate of 3.4% in order for its value to have doubled.
parts.solutionMd:
The value has doubled when it reaches 40 000 dollars, so set the model equal to that value

$20000 ( 1 + \frac{3.4}{100} )^{t} = 40000$

**[M1]**

Divide both sides by 20000

$1 . 034^{t} = 2$

Take natural logarithms of both sides

$\text{ln}  ( 1 . 034^{t} ) = \text{ln}  2$

Use the power law to bring the exponent down

$t  \text{ln}  1 . 034 = \text{ln}  2$

**[M1]**

Divide to make $t$ the subject

$t = \frac{\text{ln}2}{\text{ln}1.034} = 20 . 7313 . . .$

**[A1]**

Round up, since after 20 years the value has not yet doubled

**Final answer:** $t = 21$** years**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of the model to set up the doubling condition, either as $20000 ( 1 . 034 )^{t} = 40000$ or as $1 . 034^{t} = 2$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of logarithms on both sides, with the power law used to bring $t$ down. Logarithms to any base are accepted.
> 
> **A1**: The unrounded value, which is any answer rounding to 20.7.
> 
> **A1**: The integer conclusion of 21 years. Rounding down to 20 does not earn this mark, because the value has not doubled by the end of the 20th year.

parts.problemMd: Describe a refinement to the model that would more realistically reflect the way savings and investment accounts work.
parts.solutionMd:
The model fixes the rate and assumes no money moves in or out, so relax one of those assumptions

**Final answer:** **Allow the interest rate to change over time, or allow money to be paid into or taken out of the account**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Either refinement is enough on its own. Accept allowing the interest rate to vary from year to year, or allowing deposits and withdrawals during the investment. Accept also interest being added more often than once a year. A comment only that the model is unrealistic, with no refinement described, does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd:
***Note: For this question ensure you are working in degrees.***

A wave tank is used to simulate the sea at high tide. At a certain point along the tank the height of water is measured relative to the calm water level, which has a height of 0 cm.

The height of water in the tank is modelled by the function

$h ( t ) = 12  \text{cos}  ( 20 t )$°

$t \geq 0$

where $h$ cm is the height of water and $t$ seconds is the time after the peak of the first wave passes the measuring point.

Sketch a graph of $h$ against $t$ for $0 \leq t \leq 54$.
parts.solutionMd:
The coefficient of the cosine is the amplitude, so the curve runs between $12$ and $- 12$

$\text{Maximum} = 12$

$\text{Minimum} = - 12$

A full cycle of the cosine takes 360° of the angle, so divide by the 20 inside the bracket to get the period in seconds

$\text{Period} = \frac{360}{20} = 18$

Since $54 = 3 \times 18$, the interval holds exactly three complete waves, and the cosine starts at its maximum

![Sketch of h against t from t = 0 to t = 54, showing a cosine curve starting at its maximum of 12 at t = 0, falling to a minimum of minus 12 at t = 9, and repeating for three complete waves with peaks at t = 0, 18, 36 and 54](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-maths-20-pure-3/algebra-and-functions/further-modelling-with-functions/assets/005-sketch-of-h-against-t-from-t-0-to-t-54-showing-a.png)

**[B1 B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A cosine shape starting at its maximum when $t = 0$. A sine shape, starting at zero, does not earn this mark.
> 
> **B1**: The maximum and minimum values shown as 12 and $- 12$.
> 
> **B1**: Three complete waves drawn across $0 \leq t \leq 54$, equivalent to a period of 18 seconds. The curve must finish at a peak at $t = 54$.

parts.problemMd:
(i) What is the maximum height the water reaches according to the model?

(ii) How frequent are the waves generated by the tank?

(iii) How often is the water at its calm level?

(iv) When will the peak of the 12<sup>th</sup> wave pass the measuring point?
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The amplitude is the coefficient of the cosine

**Final answer:** $\text{Maximum height} = 12$** cm**

**[B1]**

(ii)

One wave takes one full period, found above

**Final answer:** **One wave every 18 seconds**

**[B1]**

(iii)

The water is at its calm level when $h = 0$, so the cosine must be zero

$20 t = 90 ,  270 ,  450 ,  . . .$

$t = 4 . 5 ,  13 . 5 ,  22 . 5 ,  . . .$

These are 9 seconds apart, which is half a period

**Final answer:** **Every 9 seconds, starting at **$t = 4 . 5$** seconds**

**[B1]**

(iv)

The peak of the first wave is at $t = 0$, so the 12<sup>th</sup> peak comes 11 periods later

$t = 11 \times 18$

**Final answer:** $t = 198$** seconds**

**[B1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Count the gaps, not the peaks. The question tells you $t = 0$ is when the first peak passes, so by the 12<sup>th</sup> peak only 11 full waves have gone by, giving $11 \times 18$ rather than $12 \times 18$.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The maximum height of 12 cm.
> 
> **B1**: One wave every 18 seconds. Accept any equivalent statement of the period, such as a frequency of one wave per 18 seconds.
> 
> **B1**: Every 9 seconds. The starting time of 4.5 seconds is not required for the mark, but a bare 4.5 seconds without the interval does not earn it.
> 
> **B1**: The time of 198 seconds. An answer of 216, from counting 12 periods rather than 11, does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd: Comment on the suitability of using this model to simulate actual sea waves.
parts.solutionMd:
Compare what the model repeats with what real water does

**Final answer:** **Every wave the model produces is identical, whereas real sea waves vary in height and spacing, so the model is not entirely realistic**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Any comment making clear that the model gives identical, perfectly regular waves while real sea waves vary. Accept comments on varying height, varying period, or the waves continuing unchanged forever. A comment only that the model is unrealistic, with no reason, does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd:
A gardener wants to model the number of hours of daylight his allotment receives at different times of the year using a function of the form

$h ( t ) = a + b  \text{sin}  ( \frac{2π}{365} t )$

$t \geq 0$

where $h$ is the number of hours of daylight on a given day, $t$ is the time measured in whole days, and $a$ and $b$ are positive constants. Note that $t = 0$ corresponds to the first day of the model.

(i) Given that the model needs to predict a maximum of 17 hours daylight and a minimum of 7 hours daylight, find the values of $a$ and $b$.

(ii) Explain the significance of the value $\frac{2π}{365}$ in the model.

(iii) Suggest, with a reason, the date of the year that the model starts on.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Since $b$ is positive, the maximum occurs where the sine equals 1 and the minimum where it equals $- 1$

$a + b = 17$

$a - b = 7$

**[M1]**

Add the two equations to eliminate $b$

$2 a = 24$

$a = 12 ,  b = 5$

**[A1]**

(ii)

Consider what the angle does over a full year, as $t$ runs from 0 to 365

$\frac{2π}{365} t$* runs from *$0$* to *$2 π$

That is one complete cycle of the sine

**Final answer:** **It makes the model repeat once every 365 days, so the pattern of daylight repeats once a year**

**[B1]**

(iii)

Find what the model gives on its own first day, and which way it is then heading

$h ( 0 ) = 12 + 5  \text{sin}  0 = 12$

The model starts at the halfway value of 12 hours and increases from there towards its maximum

**Final answer:** **The model starts at the spring equinox, around 20 March, because that is when daylight passes through 12 hours while still increasing**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of the maximum and minimum to form two equations in $a$ and $b$. Accept the equivalent route of taking $a$ as the mean of 17 and 7 and $b$ as half their difference.
> 
> **A1**: Both values, $a = 12$ and $b = 5$. Both are needed.
> 
> **B1**: Any explanation making clear that this value sets the period to 365 days, so the model repeats once a year.
> 
> **B1**: The spring equinox, or any date around 20 or 21 March, supported by a reason. The reason must refer to the daylight being 12 hours and increasing, or to the model being at its mean value on the way up. A date with no reason does not earn this mark, and neither does the autumn equinox, where daylight is decreasing. Allow "middle of spring" or similar.

parts.problemMd:
A hot air balloon is modelled ascending from the ground to its cruising height according to the function

$a ( t ) = 8 t^{3} - 132 t^{2} + 726 t$

$0 \leq t \leq 11$

where $t$ is the time of ascent in minutes and $a$ is the altitude in feet.

(i) It takes 11 minutes for the hot air balloon to reach its cruising altitude. Find the cruising altitude.

(ii) Show that the hot air balloon rises by just 250 feet between 3 and 8 minutes. What does this suggest about how the pilot flew the hot air balloon during its ascent?
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The balloon reaches its cruising altitude at 11 minutes, so substitute $t = 11$

$a ( 11 ) = 8 ( 11 )^{3} - 132 ( 11 )^{2} + 726 ( 11 )$

Evaluate

**Final answer:** $\text{Cruising altitude} = 2662$** feet**

**[B1]**

(ii)

Find the altitude at each end of the interval, starting at 8 minutes

$a ( 8 ) = 8 ( 8 )^{3} - 132 ( 8 )^{2} + 726 ( 8 ) = 1456$

Now find the altitude at 3 minutes

$a ( 3 ) = 8 ( 3 )^{3} - 132 ( 3 )^{2} + 726 ( 3 ) = 1206$

**[M1]**

Subtract to find the rise over the interval

**Final answer:** $1456 - 1206 = 250$** feet, as required**

**[A1]**

To judge how the pilot flew, compare this with the rise over the two intervals either side

$a ( 3 ) - a ( 0 ) = 1206 - 0 = 1206$

$a ( 11 ) - a ( 8 ) = 2662 - 1456 = 1206$

The balloon gains 1206 feet in each of the outer intervals but only 250 feet in the middle one

**Final answer:** **The pilot ascended quickly at the start and at the end of the flight, but much more slowly between 3 and 8 minutes**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The cruising altitude of 2662 feet. Units are not required.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of the model at both 8 minutes and 3 minutes. Both altitudes must be seen, since the answer is given.
> 
> **A1**: The subtraction shown to give 250 feet. Because the result is printed in the question, the working must be visible; a bare statement that the rise is 250 feet does not earn this mark.
> 
> **B1**: Any comparison making clear that the balloon rose much more slowly between 3 and 8 minutes than it did before 3 minutes or after 8 minutes. Supporting figures are not required, but a comment only that the rise is small, with nothing to compare it against, does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd: Show that there is only one real solution to the equation $a ( t ) = 0$ and hence explain why the model cannot be used indefinitely for the altitude of the hot air balloon.
parts.solutionMd:
Set the model equal to zero

$8 t^{3} - 132 t^{2} + 726 t = 0$

Every term has a factor of $2 t$, so take it out

$2 t ( 4 t^{2} - 66 t + 363 ) = 0$

**[M1]**

One solution comes from the factor outside the bracket

$2 t = 0$

Divide by 2

$t = 0$

Test the quadratic factor with the discriminant $b^{2} - 4 a c$, where $a = 4$, $b = - 66$ and $c = 363$

$( - 66 )^{2} - 4 ( 4 ) ( 363 ) = 4356 - 5808$

**[M1]**

$b^{2} - 4 a c = - 1452 < 0$

A negative discriminant means the quadratic has no real roots, so nothing else can make the product zero

**Final answer:** **The only real solution is **$t = 0$**, as required**

**[A1]**

Interpret that in the context of the flight

**Final answer:** **The model gives an altitude of zero only at take off, so it predicts the balloon never returns to the ground and therefore cannot describe the flight indefinitely**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct factorisation of the cubic, taking out a factor of $t$ or $2 t$ to leave a quadratic. Accept $t ( 8 t^{2} - 132 t + 726 )$ as an equivalent factorisation.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of the discriminant on the quadratic factor. If the factorisation was $t ( 8 t^{2} - 132 t + 726 )$, the discriminant is $( - 132 )^{2} - 4 ( 8 ) ( 726 ) = - 5808$, which is equally acceptable.
> 
> **A1**: A negative discriminant stated, the conclusion that the quadratic has no real roots, and hence that $t = 0$ is the only real solution. All three are needed, since the result is given.
> 
> **B1**: Any explanation making clear that the model has the balloon at ground level only at the start, so it never predicts a landing. Accept also that the altitude increases without limit beyond the given interval.

parts.problemMd:
A gardener is modelling the number of hours of daylight his allotment receives at different times of the year using the function

$h ( t ) = 12 - a  \text{sin}  ( \frac{2πt}{365} )$

$t \geq 0$

where $h$ is the number of hours of daylight on a given day, $t$ is the time measured in whole days, and $a$ is a positive constant.

(i) Given that the maximum amount of daylight predicted by the model is 16 hours, write down the value of $a$.

(ii) The gardener is also a keen golfer.

In order to have enough daylight to play golf after working in the garden there needs to be at least 9 hours daylight in the day.

On approximately how many days of the year can the gardener ***not*** play golf?
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The sine term is subtracted, so $h$ is greatest when the sine takes its least value of $- 1$

$16 = 12 - a ( - 1 ) = 12 + a$

$a = 4$

**[B1]**

(ii)

The gardener cannot play golf when there are fewer than 9 hours of daylight, so start from the boundary case $h = 9$

$9 = 12 - 4  \text{sin}  ( \frac{2πt}{365} )$

Rearrange to isolate the sine

$4  \text{sin}  ( \frac{2πt}{365} ) = 3$

$\text{sin}  ( \frac{2πt}{365} ) = \frac{3}{4}$

**[M1]**

Take the inverse sine to find the first angle, working in radians

$\frac{2πt}{365} = \text{sin}^{-1}  ( \frac{3}{4} ) = 0 . 848062 . . .$

Multiply by $\frac{365}{2π}$ to convert the angle back to a day

$t = 49 . 3$

**[A1]**

The sine curve is symmetrical about its peak, so the second angle is $π$ minus the first

$\frac{2πt}{365} = π - 0 . 848062 . . . = 2 . 293530 . . .$

$t = 133 . 2$

**[M1]**

A sketch shows which stretch of the year falls below the 9 hour line

![Sketch of h against t for one year, showing the curve h(t) dipping below the horizontal line h = 9 between t = 49.3 and t = 133.2, with those two crossing points marked](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-maths-20-pure-3/algebra-and-functions/further-modelling-with-functions/assets/004-sketch-of-h-against-t-for-one-year-showing-the-c.png)

Test the whole days at each end, since the days must be counted inclusively

$h ( 49 ) = 9 . 01$* and *$h ( 50 ) = 8 . 97$

$h ( 133 ) = 8 . 99$* and *$h ( 134 ) = 9 . 04$

So the short days run from day 50 to day 133 inclusive, which is $133 - 50 + 1$ days

**Final answer:** **The gardener cannot play golf on approximately 84 days**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The value $a = 4$. No working is required, since the question says to write it down.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $h = 9$ and rearrangement to $\text{sin}  ( \frac{2πt}{365} ) = \frac{3}{4}$, or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: The first value, which is any answer rounding to 49.3. The angle 0.848 on its own is enough for this mark. Working in degrees gives 48.6 for the angle and does not lead to a correct day, so it earns nothing here.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of the symmetry of the sine curve to obtain the second angle as $π - 0 . 848$, leading to a value which rounds to 133.2.
> 
> **A1**: The count of 84 days. Accept 83 or 84, since the question asks only for an approximate figure, and accept the count reached either by the inclusive day count from 50 to 133 or by the difference $133 . 2 - 49 . 3 = 83 . 9$ rounded to the nearest day.

parts.problemMd:
***Note: For this question ensure you are working in degrees.***

A wave tank is used to simulate the sea at high tide.

At a certain point along the tank the height of water is measured relative to the calm water level, which has a height of 0 cm.

The graph of the height of water, $h$ cm, against the time after the simulation is started, $t$ seconds, is shown below.

![Graph of h in centimetres against t in seconds showing a sine curve through the origin, rising to a peak of 20, with the curve crossing the horizontal axis at t equals 0, 12, 24, 36, 48 and 60](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-maths-20-pure-3/algebra-and-functions/further-modelling-with-functions/assets/002-graph-of-h-in-centimetres-against-t-in-seconds-s.png)

(i) According to the graph what is the maximum height the water will reach?

(ii) How frequent are the waves generated by the tank?

(iii) Use the graph to write down a function for the model in the form

$h ( t ) = A  \text{sin}  ( B t )$°

$t \geq 0$
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Read the height of the peak from the graph

**Final answer:** $\text{Maximum height} = 20$** cm**

**[B1]**

(ii)

One complete wave runs from one crossing of the axis to the second one after it, so the curve repeats every 24 seconds

**Final answer:** **One wave every 24 seconds**

**[B1]**

(iii)

The amplitude is the maximum height, so $A$ is the value found in part (i)

$A = 20$

**[B1]**

A full cycle of the sine takes 360° of the angle, so divide that by the period to find $B$

$B = \frac{360}{24} = 15$

**Final answer:** $h ( t ) = 20  \text{sin}  ( 15 t )$**°**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The maximum height of 20 cm, read from the graph.
> 
> **B1**: One wave every 24 seconds. Accept any equivalent statement of the period, such as 2.5 waves per minute.
> 
> **B1**: The value $A = 20$.
> 
> **B1**: The value $B = 15$, or the complete function. A value of $B = \frac{2π}{24}$, from working in radians, does not earn this mark, since the question specifies degrees.

parts.problemMd: Write down a model of the form $h ( t ) = A  \text{sin}  ( B t )$° that could be used to generate waves of double the amplitude and at a frequency of 15 waves per minute.
parts.solutionMd:
Doubling the amplitude doubles $A$

$A = 2 \times 20 = 40$

**[B1]**

At 15 waves per minute, each wave takes a minute divided by 15, and a minute is 60 seconds, so find the new period in seconds

$\text{Period} = \frac{60}{15} = 4$

Divide 360° by the new period to find $B$

$B = \frac{360}{4} = 90$

**Final answer:** $h ( t ) = 40  \text{sin}  ( 90 t )$**°**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The amplitude $A = 40$.
> 
> **B1**: The value $B = 90$, or the complete function. The period of 4 seconds seen on its own is not enough without $B$.

parts.problemMd: Suggest a way the model can be improved for simulating actual sea waves.
parts.solutionMd:
The model repeats one identical wave forever, whereas real waves differ from one another

**Final answer:** **Allow the height to vary from wave to wave, so that the waves are not all identical**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Any improvement which introduces variation between waves. Accept varying the amplitude, varying the period, or adding a random element. Accept also allowing the tide level to change over time.

parts.problemMd:
In a simple model of an investment account, the function

$V ( t ) = I ( 1 + \frac{r}{100} )^{t}$

is used, where $I$ is the initial amount invested, $r$ % is the interest rate, and $V$ is the value of the investment at the end of $t$ years.

Find the interest rate required for an amount of money invested for 8 years to double in value.
parts.solutionMd:
Doubling means the final value is $2 I$, so set the model equal to that

$I ( 1 + \frac{r}{100} )^{8} = 2 I$

The initial amount cancels, so the answer does not depend on how much is invested

$( 1 + \frac{r}{100} )^{8} = 2$

**[M1]**

Raise both sides to the power $\frac{1}{8}$ (taking the 8th root, `\sqrt[8]{}`)

$1 + \frac{r}{100} = 2^{\frac{1}{8}} = 1 . 0905077 . . .$

**[M1]**

Subtract 1, then multiply by 100

**Final answer:** $r = 9 . 05$** % (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of the model with the final value as twice the initial value, reaching $( 1 + \frac{r}{100} )^{8} = 2$. Using a particular starting amount, such as 100 and 200, is equally acceptable.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method to undo the power of 8, either by raising both sides to the power $\frac{1}{8}$ or by taking logarithms and dividing by 8.
> 
> **A1**: An answer which rounds to 9.05. The percentage sign is not required.

parts.problemMd:
An investor is comparing two options offered by a local bank.

![Two option cards side by side. Option 1 is a 10 year investment at an interest rate of 3.4 percent, with the account credited with a 500 dollar bonus at the end of the 10 years. Option 2 is a 10 year investment at an interest rate of 3.85 percent with no bonus](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-maths-20-pure-3/algebra-and-functions/further-modelling-with-functions/assets/003-two-option-cards-side-by-side-option-1-is-a-10-y.png)

(i) Find the least amount of money an investor would need in order for Option 2 to give a greater return than Option 1.

(ii) What advice would you give to a customer with 8100 dollars to invest? Justify your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Write the value of each option after 10 years, taking $I$ as the amount invested

$V_{1} = I ( 1 . 034 )^{10} + 500$

$V_{2} = I ( 1 . 0385 )^{10}$

**[M1]**

Option 2 gives a greater return when its value is the larger of the two

$I ( 1 . 0385 )^{10} > I ( 1 . 034 )^{10} + 500$

Collect the terms in $I$ on one side and factorise

$I ( 1 . 0385^{10} - 1 . 034^{10} ) > 500$

**[M1]**

Divide by the bracket, which is positive, so the inequality keeps its direction

$I > \frac{500}{1.0385^{10}-1.034^{10}} = 8064 . 028 . . .$

**Final answer:** **The least amount needed is 8064.03 dollars**

**[A1]**

(ii)

Compare the customer's 8100 dollars with that threshold

$8100 > 8064 . 03$

**[B1]**

The amount clears the threshold, so the option without the bonus wins

**Final answer:** **Advise the customer to choose Option 2, since 8100 dollars is above the amount at which the higher interest rate outweighs the 500 dollar bonus**

**[B1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Notice that the amount invested cancels in part (a) but not in part (b). In part (a) both sides grow in proportion to $I$, so the doubling rate is the same whatever you invest. In part (b) the 500 dollar bonus is a fixed amount rather than a proportion, which is exactly why a threshold exists at all: the bonus matters more to a small investor and less to a large one.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct expressions for the value of both options after 10 years, with the 500 added to Option 1 only.
> 
> **M1**: Correct formation of the inequality and collection of the terms in $I$, reaching $I ( 1 . 0385^{10} - 1 . 034^{10} ) > 500$ or equivalent. An equation rather than an inequality is accepted throughout, provided the final answer is identified as a least amount.
> 
> **A1**: An answer which rounds to 8064.03. Accept a value stated to the nearest dollar above, such as 8065, and accept the answer given as an inequality.
> 
> **B1**: A comparison of 8100 with the threshold found in (i), following through from that value.
> 
> **B1**: A conclusion recommending Option 2, justified by that comparison. A recommendation with no supporting comparison does not earn this mark. If the threshold found in (i) was above 8100, follow through and credit a correctly justified recommendation of Option 1.

parts.problemMd:
The flight path of a hot air balloon is planned according to the graph below.

The path is made up of three segments, ascent, cruising and descent.

![Graph of altitude in feet against time t in minutes for a hot air balloon flight, showing a steep ascent, then a cruising section which rises and falls in a regular wave pattern with six peaks and five troughs, then a descent to the ground. The point A where the ascent meets the cruise and the point B where the cruise meets the descent are both labelled](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-maths-20-pure-3/algebra-and-functions/further-modelling-with-functions/assets/001-graph-of-altitude-in-feet-against-time-t-in-minu.png)

Point $A ( A_{t} , c )$ is the point where the flight path changes from ascent to cruising.

Point $B ( B_{t} , c )$ is the point where the flight path changes from cruising to descent.

The functions for the ascent and cruising segments of the flight are given below.

Ascent: $f ( t ) = 8 ( t - 6 )^{3} + 1728$ for $0 \leq t \leq A_{t}$

Cruise: $g ( t ) = 3456 + 200  \text{sin}  ( t - 12 )$ for $A_{t} \leq t \leq B_{t}$

where $f ( t )$ and $g ( t )$ give the altitude in feet at a time $t$ minutes after the commencement of the balloon's flight.

The balloon begins and ends the cruising segment of its flight at an altitude midway between its minimum and maximum cruising altitudes.

Use the information given to deduce

(i) the values of $A_{t}$, $B_{t}$ and $c$,

(ii) the difference between the maximum and minimum cruising altitudes.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The sine term is zero at the midway altitude, so the cruise begins and ends where $\text{sin}  ( t - 12 ) = 0$

$t - 12 = 0 ,  π ,  2 π ,  3 π ,  . . .$

The graph places the start of the cruise between 10 and 15 minutes, so take the first of these

$A_{t} = 12$

**[B1]**

The cruise completes $5 \frac{1}{2}$ cycles on the graph, and one cycle of $\text{sin}  ( t - 12 )$ takes $2 π$

$B_{t} = 12 + 5 . 5 \times 2 π$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $B_{t} = 12 + 11 π = 46 . 6$** minutes (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

The altitude $c$ is the value of $g$ at either end of the cruise, where the sine is zero

**Final answer:** $c = 3456$** feet**

**[B1]**

(ii)

The sine varies between $- 1$ and 1, so the cruising altitude varies 200 feet either side of 3456

$\text{Maximum} = 3456 + 200 = 3656$

$\text{Minimum} = 3456 - 200 = 3256$

Subtract to find the difference

**Final answer:** $3656 - 3256 = 400$** feet**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The value $A_{t} = 12$. Accept this from either solving $\text{sin}  ( t - 12 ) = 0$ or from solving $8 ( t - 6 )^{3} + 1728 = 3456$, which gives the same value.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of the period $2 π$ together with the 5.5 cycles read from the graph.
> 
> **A1**: The value $B_{t} = 12 + 11 π$, or an answer which rounds to 46.6. The exact form is preferred but the decimal is fully acceptable.
> 
> **B1**: The value $c = 3456$ feet.
> 
> **B1**: The difference of 400 feet. Accept this stated directly as twice the amplitude, without the maximum and minimum being found separately.

parts.problemMd:
The total flight time is planned to be 60 minutes. The descent part of the journey is modelled by a linear function, $h ( t )$, where $B_{t} \leq t \leq 60$.

Find an equation for $h ( t )$.
parts.solutionMd:
The descent runs from the end of the cruise to the ground, so it passes through two known points

$( B_{t} , c ) = ( 12 + 11 π ,  3456 )$* and *$( 60 ,  0 )$

Find the gradient from these two points

$m = \frac{0-3456}{60-(12+11π)}$

**[M1]**

Simplify the denominator

$m = - \frac{3456}{48-11π} = - 257 . 1$* (1 d.p.)*

**[A1]**

Use the equation of a line with gradient $m$ through the point $( x_{1} , y_{1} )$, which is $y - y_{1} = m ( x - x_{1} )$, taking the point $( 60 , 0 )$

$h ( t ) - 0 = - \frac{3456}{48-11π} ( t - 60 )$

**[M1]**

Take the minus sign inside the bracket to leave a positive coefficient

**Final answer:** $h ( t ) = \frac{3456}{48-11π} ( 60 - t )$** for **$12 + 11 π \leq t \leq 60$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct gradient calculation using the two endpoints of the descent, with the value of $B_{t}$ from part (a) followed through.
> 
> **A1**: The gradient, either exactly as $- \frac{3456}{48-11π}$ or as an answer which rounds to $- 257$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of a straight line equation with the gradient and either endpoint.
> 
> **A1**: Any correct form of the equation. Accept the exact form, the expanded form $h ( t ) = 15426 - 257 . 1 t$, or $h ( t ) = - 257 . 1 ( t - 60 )$. The domain is not required for the mark.

parts.problemMd: Describe a problem with attempting to model hot air balloon flights in this manner.
parts.solutionMd:
Consider what a real flight has to contend with that the model ignores

**Final answer:** **A real balloon is affected by the weather, particularly wind speed and direction, and the pilot must also find a safe place to land and avoid obstacles, so an actual flight is unlikely to follow so precise a path**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Any sensible practical objection. Accept the effect of wind or weather, the need to choose a landing site, avoiding obstacles, or the point that a real balloon could not follow a smooth sine wave while cruising. A comment only that the model is unrealistic, with no reason, does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd:
Expand

$( 1 - 2 x )^{-1}$

in ascending powers of $x$, up to and including the term in $x^{2}$, simplifying the coefficients.
parts.solutionMd:
Quote the general binomial expansion for a rational index

$( 1 + x )^{n} = 1 + n x + \frac{n(n-1)}{2!} x^{2} +  . . .$

To match $( 1 - 2 x )^{-1}$ to this form, take $n = - 1$ and replace $x$ by $- 2 x$

$( 1 - 2 x )^{-1} = 1 + ( - 1 ) ( - 2 x ) + \frac{(-1)(-2)}{2!} ( - 2 x )^{2} +  . . .$

**[M1]**

Evaluate each coefficient, using $2 ! = 2 \times 1$

`= 1 + 2x + \frac{2}{2}\left(4x^{2}\right) + \; ...`

State the expansion as far as the term in $x^{2}$

$( 1 - 2 x )^{-1} \approx 1 + 2 x + 4 x^{2}$

**[A1 A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct unsimplified version of the $x$ or the $x^{2}$ term, with $n = - 1$ and $- 2 x$ substituted into the general expansion.
> 
> **A1**: Correct first two terms, $1 + 2 x$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct term in $x^{2}$, that is $+ 4 x^{2}$. Accept the terms written in any order, and ignore any higher powers of $x$ you have gone on to write.

parts.problemMd:
Expand

$( 1 + x )^{-2}$

in ascending powers of $x$, up to and including the term in $x^{2}$, simplifying the coefficients.
parts.solutionMd:
Quote the general binomial expansion for a rational index

$( 1 + x )^{n} = 1 + n x + \frac{n(n-1)}{2!} x^{2} +  . . .$

Here the bracket is already in the form $( 1 + x )^{n}$, so take $n = - 2$

$( 1 + x )^{-2} = 1 + ( - 2 ) x + \frac{(-2)(-3)}{2!} x^{2} +  . . .$

**[M1]**

Evaluate each coefficient, using $2 ! = 2 \times 1$

$= 1 - 2 x + \frac{6}{2} x^{2} +  . . .$

State the expansion as far as the term in $x^{2}$

$( 1 + x )^{-2} \approx 1 - 2 x + 3 x^{2}$

**[A1 A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct unsimplified version of the $x$ or the $x^{2}$ term, with $n = - 2$ substituted into the general expansion.
> 
> **A1**: Correct first two terms, $1 - 2 x$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct term in $x^{2}$, that is $+ 3 x^{2}$. The two negative factors multiply to give a positive coefficient, so $- 3 x^{2}$ does not earn this mark. Accept the terms in any order, and ignore any higher powers of $x$.

parts.problemMd: State the set of values of $x$ for which the expansion in part (a) is valid.
parts.solutionMd:
The expansion of $( 1 + y )^{n}$ is valid only when `|y| < 1`, and here $y$ is $x$ itself

`|x| < 1`

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct set of values. Accept any equivalent form, for example $- 1 < x < 1$. The inequality must be strict, so `|x| \leqslant 1` does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd:
Show that

$\sqrt{4-4x} = 2 ( 1 - x )^{\frac{1}{2}}$
parts.solutionMd:
Write the square root as a power of one half

$\sqrt{4-4x} = ( 4 - 4 x )^{\frac{1}{2}}$

Factorise inside the bracket, taking out the common factor of $4$

`= \left[4(1 - x)\right]^{\frac{1}{2}}`

**[M1]**

Separate the factors using the index law $( a b )^{n} = a^{n} b^{n}$

$= 4^{\frac{1}{2}} ( 1 - x )^{\frac{1}{2}}$

Evaluate $4^{\frac{1}{2}} = 2$ to reach the required form

**Final answer:** $\sqrt{4-4x} = 2 ( 1 - x )^{\frac{1}{2}}$** as required**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct factorisation of $4$ out of the bracket, giving `\left[4(1-x)\right]^{\frac{1}{2}}` or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: Complete argument reaching the printed result, with the index law applied to split the factors and $4^{\frac{1}{2}}$ evaluated as $2$. Because the answer is given, both of these steps must be visible.

parts.problemMd:
Hence obtain the expansion of

$\sqrt{4-4x}$

in ascending powers of $x$, up to and including the term in $x^{2}$, simplifying the coefficients.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the result from part (a), so that only $( 1 - x )^{\frac{1}{2}}$ needs expanding

$\sqrt{4-4x} = 2 ( 1 - x )^{\frac{1}{2}}$

Apply the general binomial expansion with $n = \frac{1}{2}$, replacing $x$ by $- x$

`= 2\left[1 + \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)(-x) + \frac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)}{2!}(-x)^{2} + \; ...\right]`

**[M1]**

Evaluate each coefficient inside the bracket

`= 2\left[1 - \frac{x}{2} - \frac{x^{2}}{8} + \; ...\right]`

Multiply through by $2$

$\sqrt{4-4x} \approx 2 - x - \frac{x^{2}}{4}$

**[A1 A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct unsimplified version of the $x$ or the $x^{2}$ term, using $n = \frac{1}{2}$ with $- x$ substituted.
> 
> **A1**: Correct first two terms, $2 - x$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct term in $x^{2}$, that is $- \frac{x^{2}}{4}$. Accept $- 0 . 25 x^{2}$. The factor of $2$ must have been multiplied through, so $- \frac{x^{2}}{8}$ does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd:
Expand

$( 1 + 2 x )^{-\frac{1}{2}}$

in ascending powers of $x$, up to and including the term in $x^{3}$, simplifying the coefficients.
parts.solutionMd:
Quote the general binomial expansion, taken as far as the term in $x^{3}$

$( 1 + x )^{n} = 1 + n x + \frac{n(n-1)}{2!} x^{2} + \frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{3!} x^{3} +  . . .$

To match the given bracket, take $n = - \frac{1}{2}$ and replace $x$ by $2 x$

`(1 + 2x)^{-\frac{1}{2}} = 1 + \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)(2x) + \frac{\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)}{2!}(2x)^{2} + \frac{\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)\left(-\frac{5}{2}\right)}{3!}(2x)^{3} + \; ...`

**[M1]**

Raise the whole of $2 x$ to each power, so that $( 2 x )^{2} = 4 x^{2}$ and $( 2 x )^{3} = 8 x^{3}$

`= 1 - x + \frac{3}{8}\left(4x^{2}\right) - \frac{15}{48}\left(8x^{3}\right) + \; ...`

Simplify each coefficient

$( 1 + 2 x )^{-\frac{1}{2}} \approx 1 - x + \frac{3x^{2}}{2} - \frac{5x^{3}}{2}$

**[A1 A1 A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct unsimplified version of the $x^{2}$ or the $x^{3}$ term, with $n = - \frac{1}{2}$ and $2 x$ substituted into the general expansion.
> 
> **A1**: Correct first two terms, $1 - x$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct term in $x^{2}$, that is $+ \frac{3x^{2}}{2}$. Accept $1 . 5 x^{2}$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct term in $x^{3}$, that is $- \frac{5x^{3}}{2}$. Accept $- 2 . 5 x^{3}$. The question asks you to simplify, so an unsimplified coefficient left as a product of fractions does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd:
Expand

`\left(1 - \frac{1}{2}x\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}`

in ascending powers of $x$, up to and including the term in $x^{2}$, simplifying the coefficients.
parts.solutionMd:
Quote the general binomial expansion for a rational index

$( 1 + x )^{n} = 1 + n x + \frac{n(n-1)}{2!} x^{2} +  . . .$

To match the given bracket, take $n = \frac{1}{3}$ and replace $x$ by $- \frac{x}{2}$

`\left(1 - \frac{x}{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}} = 1 + \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(-\frac{x}{2}\right) + \frac{\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)}{2!}\left(-\frac{x}{2}\right)^{2} + \; ...`

**[M1]**

Square the whole of $- \frac{x}{2}$, giving $\frac{x^{2}}{4}$

`= 1 - \frac{x}{6} - \frac{1}{9}\left(\frac{x^{2}}{4}\right) + \; ...`

Simplify each coefficient

`\left(1 - \frac{1}{2}x\right)^{\frac{1}{3}} \approx 1 - \frac{x}{6} - \frac{x^{2}}{36}`

**[A1 A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct unsimplified version of the $x$ or the $x^{2}$ term, with $n = \frac{1}{3}$ and $- \frac{x}{2}$ substituted into the general expansion.
> 
> **A1**: Correct first two terms, $1 - \frac{x}{6}$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct term in $x^{2}$, that is $- \frac{x^{2}}{36}$. Both negative signs matter here: the coefficient `\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)` is negative while squaring $- \frac{x}{2}$ makes that factor positive, so the term is negative overall.

parts.problemMd: State the set of values of $x$ for which the expansion in part (a) is valid.
parts.solutionMd:
The expansion of $( 1 + y )^{n}$ is valid only when `|y| < 1`, and here $y$ is $- \frac{x}{2}$

`\left|-\frac{x}{2}\right| < 1`

Multiply through by $2$

`|x| < 2`

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct set of values. Accept any equivalent form, for example $- 2 < x < 2$, and condone the unsimplified `\left|\frac{x}{2}\right| < 1`. The inequality must be strict. The answer `|x| < 1`, which ignores the $\frac{1}{2}$ multiplying $x$, does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
Only the $x^{2}$ term is needed, so quote just that term of the general binomial expansion

$\frac{n(n-1)}{2!} x^{2}$

Take $n = - 3$ and replace $x$ by $- 3 x$

$\frac{(-3)(-4)}{2!} ( - 3 x )^{2}$

**[M1]**

Square the whole of $- 3 x$, giving $9 x^{2}$, and evaluate the fraction

$= 6 \times 9 x^{2} = 54 x^{2}$

State the coefficient asked for

$54$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> **A1**: $54$. Accept the answer given as the term $54 x^{2}$. The whole of $- 3 x$ must be squared, so an answer of $6$, which omits the factor $( - 3 )^{2} = 9$, does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd:
The function $\text{f} ( x )$ is given by

$\text{f} ( x ) = ( 1 - p x )^{-4}$

where $p$ is an integer.

Find the coefficient of $x^{3}$ in the binomial expansion of $\text{f} ( x )$, in terms of $p$.
parts.solutionMd:
Only the $x^{3}$ term is needed, so quote just that term of the general binomial expansion

$\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{3!} x^{3}$

Take $n = - 4$ and replace $x$ by $- p x$

$\frac{(-4)(-5)(-6)}{3!} ( - p x )^{3}$

**[M1]**

Evaluate the fraction, and cube the whole of $- p x$

`= \frac{-120}{6} \times \left(-p^{3}x^{3}\right) = -20 \times \left(-p^{3}x^{3}\right)`

The two negatives cancel, leaving a positive coefficient

$20 p^{3}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> **A1**: $20 p^{3}$. Accept the answer given as the term $20 p^{3} x^{3}$. The sign must be positive: the negative numerator and the cube of $- p x$ cancel, so $- 20 p^{3}$ does not earn this mark. The whole of $- p x$ must be cubed, so $- 20 p$ does not earn it either.

parts.problemMd:
Expand

`\left(1 - \frac{1}{3}x\right)^{-2}`

in ascending powers of $x$, up to and including the term in $x^{2}$, simplifying the coefficients.
parts.solutionMd:
Quote the general binomial expansion for a rational index

$( 1 + x )^{n} = 1 + n x + \frac{n(n-1)}{2!} x^{2} +  . . .$

To match the given bracket, take $n = - 2$ and replace $x$ by $- \frac{x}{3}$

`\left(1 - \frac{x}{3}\right)^{-2} = 1 + (-2)\left(-\frac{x}{3}\right) + \frac{(-2)(-3)}{2!}\left(-\frac{x}{3}\right)^{2} + \; ...`

**[M1]**

Square the whole of $- \frac{x}{3}$, giving $\frac{x^{2}}{9}$, and evaluate the fraction

`= 1 + \frac{2x}{3} + 3\left(\frac{x^{2}}{9}\right) + \; ...`

Simplify each coefficient

`\left(1 - \frac{1}{3}x\right)^{-2} \approx 1 + \frac{2x}{3} + \frac{x^{2}}{3}`

**[A1 A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct unsimplified version of the $x$ or the $x^{2}$ term, with $n = - 2$ and $- \frac{x}{3}$ substituted into the general expansion.
> 
> **A1**: Correct first two terms, $1 + \frac{2x}{3}$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct term in $x^{2}$, that is $+ \frac{x^{2}}{3}$. Both terms are positive, because the coefficient $( - 2 ) ( - 3 )$ is positive and squaring $- \frac{x}{3}$ removes the remaining sign.

parts.problemMd:
Express

$\frac{5-x}{(1+x)(1-x)}$

in partial fractions.
parts.solutionMd:
Both factors of the denominator are linear, so each contributes a constant over that factor

$\frac{5-x}{(1+x)(1-x)} \equiv \frac{A}{1+x} + \frac{B}{1-x}$

**[B1]**

Multiply through by $( 1 + x ) ( 1 - x )$ to clear the denominators

$5 - x = A ( 1 - x ) + B ( 1 + x )$

To find $B$, substitute $x = 1$, which removes the term in $A$

$4 = 2 B$

**[M1]**

To find $A$, substitute $x = - 1$, which removes the term in $B$

$6 = 2 A$

State the decomposition

$\frac{5-x}{(1+x)(1-x)} \equiv \frac{3}{1+x} + \frac{2}{1-x}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct form stated or implied, that is a constant over $1 + x$ plus a constant over $1 - x$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for finding one of the constants. Substituting a value of $x$ that removes a term, or comparing coefficients, are equally acceptable.
> 
> **A1**: Both constants correct, giving $\frac{3}{1+x} + \frac{2}{1-x}$.

parts.problemMd:
Expand each of the following in ascending powers of $x$, up to and including the term in $x^{2}$, simplifying the coefficients.

(i) $3 ( 1 + x )^{-1}$

(ii) $2 ( 1 - x )^{-1}$
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Apply the general binomial expansion inside the bracket with $n = - 1$, keeping the factor of $3$ outside

`3(1 + x)^{-1} = 3\left[1 + (-1)x + \frac{(-1)(-2)}{2!}x^{2} + \; ...\right]`

**[M1]**

Evaluate the coefficients, then multiply through by $3$

`= 3\left[1 - x + x^{2} + \; ...\right]`

$3 ( 1 + x )^{-1} \approx 3 - 3 x + 3 x^{2}$

**[A1]**

(ii)

Apply the same expansion with $n = - 1$, this time replacing $x$ by $- x$

`2(1 - x)^{-1} = 2\left[1 + (-1)(-x) + \frac{(-1)(-2)}{2!}(-x)^{2} + \; ...\right]`

**[M1]**

Evaluate the coefficients, then multiply through by $2$

`= 2\left[1 + x + x^{2} + \; ...\right]`

$2 ( 1 - x )^{-1} \approx 2 + 2 x + 2 x^{2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct unsimplified expansion of $( 1 + x )^{-1}$, with $n = - 1$ substituted.
> 
> **A1**: $3 - 3 x + 3 x^{2}$. The factor of $3$ must be multiplied through.
> 
> **M1**: Correct unsimplified expansion of $( 1 - x )^{-1}$, with $n = - 1$ and $- x$ substituted.
> 
> **A1**: $2 + 2 x + 2 x^{2}$. All three terms are positive here, because each power of $- x$ is paired with a negative coefficient.

parts.problemMd: State the set of values of $x$ for which the expansion in part (c) is valid.

in partial fractions.

parts.problemMd:
It is given that

$\text{f} ( x ) = \sqrt{1+ax}$

and

`\text{g}(x) = \sqrt[3]{1 - ax}`

where $a$ is a non-zero constant.

In their binomial expansions, the coefficient of the $x^{2}$ term for $\text{f} ( x )$ is equal to the coefficient of the $x$ term for $\text{g} ( x )$.

Find the value of $a$.
parts.solutionMd:
Write each root as a power so the binomial expansion can be applied

$\text{f} ( x ) = ( 1 + a x )^{\frac{1}{2}}$

$\text{g} ( x ) = ( 1 - a x )^{\frac{1}{3}}$

For $\text{f} ( x )$ only the $x^{2}$ term is needed, so quote that term of the general expansion

$\frac{n(n-1)}{2!} x^{2}$

Take $n = \frac{1}{2}$ with $a x$ in place of $x$

`\frac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)}{2!}(ax)^{2}`

**[M1]**

Square the whole of $a x$ and evaluate the fraction

$= - \frac{a^{2}}{8} x^{2}$

**[A1]**

For $\text{g} ( x )$ the term in $x$ is $n x$, so take $n = \frac{1}{3}$ with $- a x$ in place of $x$

`\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)(-ax) = -\frac{a}{3}x`

**[B1]**

Equate the two coefficients, as the question states they are equal

$- \frac{a^{2}}{8} = - \frac{a}{3}$

Multiply through by $- 24$ to clear the fractions

$3 a^{2} = 8 a$

**[M1]**

Factorise, then reject $a = 0$ because the question states $a$ is non-zero

$a ( 3 a - 8 ) = 0$

$a = \frac{8}{3}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct unsimplified $x^{2}$ term, or its coefficient, for $\text{f} ( x )$, using $n = \frac{1}{2}$ with $a x$ substituted.
> 
> **A1**: Coefficient of $x^{2}$ for $\text{f} ( x )$ correct as $- \frac{a^{2}}{8}$.
> 
> **B1**: Coefficient of $x$ for $\text{g} ( x )$ correct as $- \frac{a}{3}$.
> 
> **M1**: The two coefficients equated and rearranged into a solvable equation in $a$, for example $3 a^{2} = 8 a$. Both sides are negative, so the negatives may be cancelled at this stage.
> 
> **A1**: $a = \frac{8}{3}$. Accept $2 . 67$ or better, or $2 \frac{2}{3}$. The root $a = 0$ must be rejected, or divided out with a statement that $a$ is non-zero. Giving both values without rejecting $a = 0$ does not earn this mark.

parts.solutionMd:

$\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}} = ( 1 - x )^{-2}$

Apply the general binomial expansion with $n = - 2$, replacing $x$ by $- x$

$= 1 + ( - 2 ) ( - x ) + \frac{(-2)(-3)}{2!} ( - x )^{2} + \frac{(-2)(-3)(-4)}{3!} ( - x )^{3} +  . . .$

**[M1]**

Each odd power of $- x$ is paired with a negative coefficient, so every term comes out positive

$= 1 + 2 x + 3 x^{2} + 4 x^{3} +  . . .$

State the expansion as far as the term in $x^{3}$

$\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}} \approx 1 + 2 x + 3 x^{2} + 4 x^{3}$

**[A1 A1 A1]**

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:

`= 1 + \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)(2x) + \frac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)}{2!}(2x)^{2} + \; ...`

`= 1 + x - \frac{1}{8}\left(4x^{2}\right) + \; ...`

Simplify the coefficient of $x^{2}$

parts.problemMd: Using a suitable value of $x$, use your expansion from part (a) to estimate $\sqrt{1.06}$, giving your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd:
Expand

$\frac{1}{(4+8x)^{2}}$

in ascending powers of $x$, up to and including the term in $x^{3}$, simplifying the coefficients.
parts.solutionMd:
Write the fraction as a bracket with a negative index

$\frac{1}{(4+8x)^{2}} = ( 4 + 8 x )^{-2}$

The general binomial expansion needs a bracket starting with $1$, so take out the common factor of $4$

`= \left[4(1 + 2x)\right]^{-2} = 4^{-2}(1 + 2x)^{-2}`

Evaluate $4^{-2}$ to bring the constant outside

$= \frac{1}{16} ( 1 + 2 x )^{-2}$

**[B1]**

Apply the general binomial expansion inside the bracket with $n = - 2$, replacing $x$ by $2 x$

`= \frac{1}{16}\left[1 + (-2)(2x) + \frac{(-2)(-3)}{2!}(2x)^{2} + \frac{(-2)(-3)(-4)}{3!}(2x)^{3} + \; ...\right]`

**[M1]**

Raise the whole of $2 x$ to each power, so that $( 2 x )^{2} = 4 x^{2}$ and $( 2 x )^{3} = 8 x^{3}$

`= \frac{1}{16}\left[1 - 4x + 12x^{2} - 32x^{3} + \; ...\right]`

Multiply each term by $\frac{1}{16}$

$\frac{1}{(4+8x)^{2}} \approx \frac{1}{16} - \frac{x}{4} + \frac{3x^{2}}{4} - 2 x^{3}$

**[A1 A1 A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct first term $\frac{1}{16}$, reached by taking the factor of $4$ outside the bracket. Accept $4^{-2}$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct unsimplified version of the $x^{2}$ or the $x^{3}$ term of $( 1 + 2 x )^{-2}$, with $n = - 2$ and $2 x$ substituted.
> 
> **A1**: Correct term in $x$, that is $- \frac{x}{4}$. Accept $- 0 . 25 x$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct term in $x^{2}$, that is $+ \frac{3x^{2}}{4}$. Accept $0 . 75 x^{2}$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct term in $x^{3}$, that is $- 2 x^{3}$. The factor of $\frac{1}{16}$ must have been multiplied through all four terms. Leaving the answer as `\frac{1}{16}\left[1 - 4x + 12x^{2} - 32x^{3}\right]` does not earn this mark, because the question asks you to simplify the coefficients.

parts.problemMd:

$( 1 + x ) ( 1 + 2 x )^{-3}$

parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd:
The function $\text{f} ( x )$ is given by

$\text{f} ( x ) = \sqrt{4-sx}$

where $s$ is a non-zero integer.

(i) Find the coefficient of $x$ in the binomial expansion of $\text{f} ( x )$, in terms of $s$.

(ii) Find the coefficient of $x^{2}$ in the binomial expansion of $\text{f} ( x )$, in terms of $s$.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Write the root as a power, then take out the factor of $4$ so the bracket starts with $1$

`\sqrt{4 - sx} = (4 - sx)^{\frac{1}{2}} = \left[4\left(1 - \frac{sx}{4}\right)\right]^{\frac{1}{2}} = 2\left(1 - \frac{sx}{4}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}`

parts.solutionMd:

**[A1]**

(ii)

The expansion is valid when the quantity added to $1$ has modulus below $1$

`\left|-\frac{x}{2}\right| < 1`

**[A1]**

parts.problemMd:
Expand

`\left(1 - \frac{1}{3}x\right)^{-1}(2 - x)^{-2}`

in ascending powers of $x$, up to and including the term in $x^{2}$, simplifying the coefficients.
parts.solutionMd:
Quote the general binomial expansion for a rational index

$( 1 + x )^{n} = 1 + n x + \frac{n(n-1)}{2!} x^{2} +  . . .$

Expand the first bracket, taking $n = - 1$ with $- \frac{x}{3}$ in place of $x$

`\left(1 - \frac{x}{3}\right)^{-1} = 1 + (-1)\left(-\frac{x}{3}\right) + \frac{(-1)(-2)}{2!}\left(-\frac{x}{3}\right)^{2} + \; ...`

Simplify each coefficient

$= 1 + \frac{x}{3} + \frac{x^{2}}{9}$

The second bracket does not start with $1$, so take out the factor of $2$ first

`(2 - x)^{-2} = \left[2\left(1 - \frac{x}{2}\right)\right]^{-2} = \frac{1}{4}\left(1 - \frac{x}{2}\right)^{-2}`

Expand inside that bracket, taking $n = - 2$ with $- \frac{x}{2}$ in place of $x$

`= \frac{1}{4}\left[1 + (-2)\left(-\frac{x}{2}\right) + \frac{(-2)(-3)}{2!}\left(-\frac{x}{2}\right)^{2} + \; ...\right]`

**[M1]**

Simplify inside the bracket, then multiply each term by $\frac{1}{4}$

`= \frac{1}{4}\left[1 + x + \frac{3x^{2}}{4}\right] = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{x}{4} + \frac{3x^{2}}{16}`

Multiply the two expansions together

`\left(1 + \frac{x}{3} + \frac{x^{2}}{9}\right)\left(\frac{1}{4} + \frac{x}{4} + \frac{3x^{2}}{16}\right)`

Collect the products giving each term up to $x^{2}$

`= \frac{1}{4} + \left(1 \times \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{4}\right)x + \left(1 \times \frac{3}{16} + \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{9} \times \frac{1}{4}\right)x^{2}`

**[A1]**

Combine each bracket over a common denominator, using $144$ for the $x^{2}$ coefficient

`\left(1 - \frac{1}{3}x\right)^{-1}(2 - x)^{-2} \approx \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{3}x + \frac{43}{144}x^{2}`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Both brackets expanded to the term in $x^{2}$, with the factor of $2$ correctly taken out of the second one.
> 
> **A1**: The two expansions multiplied together, with all the products contributing to the $x$ and $x^{2}$ terms collected. Three separate products contribute to the $x^{2}$ term.
> 
> **A1**: $\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{3} x + \frac{43}{144} x^{2}$. Accept equivalent fractions.

parts.problemMd:

$\frac{12-x}{(x+2)(3-x)}$

in partial fractions.
parts.solutionMd:
Both factors of the denominator are linear, so each contributes a constant over that factor

$\frac{12-x}{(x+2)(3-x)} \equiv \frac{A}{x+2} + \frac{B}{3-x}$

**[B1]**

Multiply through by $( x + 2 ) ( 3 - x )$ to clear the denominators

$12 - x = A ( 3 - x ) + B ( x + 2 )$

To find $B$, substitute $x = 3$, which removes the term in $A$

$9 = 5 B  \Rightarrow  B = \frac{9}{5}$

**[M1]**

To find $A$, substitute $x = - 2$, which removes the term in $B$

$14 = 5 A  \Rightarrow  A = \frac{14}{5}$

State the decomposition

$\frac{12-x}{(x+2)(3-x)} \equiv \frac{14}{5(x+2)} + \frac{9}{5(3-x)}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> **M1**: Correct method for finding one of the constants, by substituting a value of $x$ that removes a term or by comparing coefficients.
> 
> **A1**: Both constants correct. Accept the answer written as $\frac{14}{5(x+2)} + \frac{9}{5(3-x)}$ or as $\frac{\frac{14}{5}}{x+2} + \frac{\frac{9}{5}}{3-x}$.

Absorb each constant into its coefficient

$\begin{array}{l} = \frac{14}{5} \\times 1 \frac{1}{2} ( 1 + \frac{x}{2} )^{- 1} + \frac{9}{5} \\times 1 \frac{1}{3} ( 1 - \frac{x}{3} )^{- 1} = \frac{7}{5} ( 1 + \frac{x}{2} )^{- 1} + \frac{3}{5} ( 1 - \frac{x}{3} )^{- 1} \end{array}$

Simplify inside the bracket, then multiply through by $\frac{7}{5}$

`= \frac{7}{5}\left[1 - \frac{x}{2} + \frac{x^{2}}{4}\right] = \frac{7}{5} - \frac{7x}{10} + \frac{7x^{2}}{20}`

Expand the second with $n = - 1$ and $- \frac{x}{3}$ in place of $x$

Simplify inside the bracket, then multiply through by $\frac{3}{5}$

**[A1]**

Add the two expansions, combining each pair of coefficients over a common denominator

$\frac{12-x}{(x+2)(3-x)} \approx 2 - \frac{x}{2} + \frac{5x^{2}}{12}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

The index applies to the constant too, so $2^{-1} = \frac{1}{2}$ and $3^{-1} = \frac{1}{3}$. Following through on your answer to part (a) is allowed.

Square the whole of $- \frac{x}{2}$, giving $\frac{x^{2}}{4}$, and evaluate the fraction

`= 1 - \frac{x}{6} - \frac{1}{9}\left(\frac{x^{2}}{4}\right) + \; ...`

Simplify each coefficient

`\left(1 - \frac{1}{2}x\right)^{\frac{1}{3}} \approx 1 - \frac{x}{6} - \frac{x^{2}}{36}`

**[A1 A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> **A1**: Correct first two terms, $1 - \frac{x}{6}$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct term in $x^{2}$, that is $- \frac{x^{2}}{36}$. The coefficient is negative while the squared bracket is positive, so the term is negative overall.

parts.problemMd:

up to and including the term in $x^{2}$.
parts.solutionMd:

$= 1 - \frac{x}{6} - \frac{x^{2}}{36} - x + \frac{x^{2}}{6}$

**[M1]**

**[A1]**

parts.problemMd:
The functions $\text{f} ( x )$ and $\text{g} ( x )$ are given as follows.

$\text{f} ( x ) = ( 4 + 3 x )^{\frac{1}{2}}$

$\text{g} ( x ) = ( 9 - 2 x )^{-\frac{1}{2}}$

Expand $\text{f} ( x )$ in ascending powers of $x$, up to and including the term in $x^{2}$.
parts.solutionMd:
The bracket does not start with $1$, so take out the factor of $4$ and evaluate $4^{\frac{1}{2}}$

`(4 + 3x)^{\frac{1}{2}} = \left[4\left(1 + \frac{3x}{4}\right)\right]^{\frac{1}{2}} = 2\left(1 + \frac{3x}{4}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}`

**[B1]**

Apply the general binomial expansion inside the bracket with $n = \frac{1}{2}$, replacing $x$ by $\frac{3x}{4}$

`= 2\left[1 + \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(\frac{3x}{4}\right) + \frac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)}{2!}\left(\frac{3x}{4}\right)^{2} + \; ...\right]`

**[M1]**

Square the whole of $\frac{3x}{4}$, then multiply each term by $2$

$\text{f} ( x ) \approx 2 + \frac{3x}{4} - \frac{9x^{2}}{64}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The factor of $4$ taken outside correctly, reaching `2\left(1 + \frac{3x}{4}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}` or equivalent.
> 
> **M1**: Correct unsimplified version of the $x$ or the $x^{2}$ term of the bracket, with $n = \frac{1}{2}$ and $\frac{3x}{4}$ substituted.
> 
> **A1**: $2 + \frac{3x}{4} - \frac{9x^{2}}{64}$. The factor of $2$ must be multiplied through all three terms.

parts.problemMd: Expand $\text{g} ( x )$ in ascending powers of $x$, up to and including the term in $x^{2}$.
parts.solutionMd:
$\text{g} ( x ) = ( 9 - 2 x )^{-\frac{1}{2}}$

Take out the factor of $9$, remembering that the negative index inverts it

`(9 - 2x)^{-\frac{1}{2}} = \left[9\left(1 - \frac{2x}{9}\right)\right]^{-\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{1}{3}\left(1 - \frac{2x}{9}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}`

**[B1]**

Apply the general binomial expansion with $n = - \frac{1}{2}$, replacing $x$ by $- \frac{2x}{9}$

`= \frac{1}{3}\left[1 + \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(-\frac{2x}{9}\right) + \frac{\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)}{2!}\left(-\frac{2x}{9}\right)^{2} + \; ...\right]`

**[M1]**

Simplify each coefficient, then multiply through by $\frac{1}{3}$

$\text{g} ( x ) \approx \frac{1}{3} + \frac{x}{27} + \frac{x^{2}}{162}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The factor of $9$ taken outside correctly, reaching `\frac{1}{3}\left(1 - \frac{2x}{9}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}` or equivalent. Note that $9^{-\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{1}{3}$, not $3$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct unsimplified version of the $x$ or the $x^{2}$ term of the bracket, with $n = - \frac{1}{2}$ and $- \frac{2x}{9}$ substituted.
> 
> **A1**: $\frac{1}{3} + \frac{x}{27} + \frac{x^{2}}{162}$. All three terms are positive, because each power of $- \frac{2x}{9}$ meets a coefficient of matching sign.

parts.problemMd:
Find the expansion of

$\sqrt{\frac{4+3x}{9-2x}}$

in ascending powers of $x$, up to and including the term in $x^{2}$.
parts.solutionMd:
Splitting the root over the fraction turns the quotient into the product $\text{f} ( x )  \text{g} ( x )$

`\sqrt{\frac{4 + 3x}{9 - 2x}} = (4 + 3x)^{\frac{1}{2}}(9 - 2x)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \approx \left(2 + \frac{3x}{4} - \frac{9x^{2}}{64}\right)\left(\frac{1}{3} + \frac{x}{27} + \frac{x^{2}}{162}\right)`

**[M1]**

Collect the products giving terms up to $x^{2}$, taking $5184$ as the common denominator for the $x^{2}$ coefficient

$\sqrt{\frac{4+3x}{9-2x}} \approx \frac{2}{3} + \frac{35x}{108} - \frac{35x^{2}}{5184}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Your expansions from parts (a) and (b) multiplied together, with at least the terms in $x$ and $x^{2}$ picked out. Following through on incorrect expansions is allowed.

> **A1**: $\frac{2}{3} + \frac{35x}{108} - \frac{35x^{2}}{5184}$. All three products contributing to the $x^{2}$ term are needed. Accept equivalent fractions.

parts.problemMd: State the set of values of $x$ for which the expansion in part (c) is valid.
parts.solutionMd:
Each bracket carries its own condition. The first gives

`\left|\frac{3x}{4}\right| < 1 \; \Rightarrow \; |x| < \frac{4}{3}`

The second gives a wider one

The product is valid only where both hold, so take the stricter

`|x| < \frac{4}{3}`

**[A1]**

> 
> **A1**: `|x| < \frac{4}{3}`. Accept any equivalent form, for example $- \frac{4}{3} < x < \frac{4}{3}$. The inequality must be strict. The stricter of the two ranges is needed, so `|x| < \frac{9}{2}` does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd:
In the expansion of

`\left(1 - \frac{4}{3}x\right)^{n}`

where $n$ is a real number, the coefficient of $x^{2}$ is $- \frac{16}{81}$.

Find the possible values of $n$.
parts.solutionMd:
Only the $x^{2}$ term is needed, so quote just that term with $- \frac{4x}{3}$ in place of $x$

`\frac{n(n-1)}{2!}\left(-\frac{4x}{3}\right)^{2} = \frac{n(n-1)}{2} \times \frac{16x^{2}}{9} = \frac{8n(n-1)}{9}x^{2}`

Set this coefficient equal to the value given in the question

$\frac{8n(n-1)}{9} = - \frac{16}{81}$

**[M1]**

Multiply through by $\frac{9}{8}$, then clear the remaining fraction to reach a quadratic in $n$

$n ( n - 1 ) = - \frac{2}{9}  \Rightarrow  9 n^{2} - 9 n + 2 = 0$

**[A1]**

Factorise to find both roots

$( 3 n - 1 ) ( 3 n - 2 ) = 0$

**Final answer:** $n = \frac{1}{3}$** or **$n = \frac{2}{3}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct $x^{2}$ coefficient in terms of $n$, set equal to $- \frac{16}{81}$. The whole of $- \frac{4x}{3}$ must be squared, so a factor of $\frac{16}{9}$ should be present.
> 
> **A1**: Correct quadratic in $n$, that is $9 n^{2} - 9 n + 2 = 0$ or any equivalent form such as $n ( n - 1 ) = - \frac{2}{9}$.
> 
> **A1**: Both values, $n = \frac{1}{3}$ and $n = \frac{2}{3}$. The question asks for the possible values, so both are needed and giving only one does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd:
Express

$\frac{4+5x-x^{2}}{(1-x)(1+x)^{2}}$

in partial fractions.
parts.solutionMd:
The factor $( 1 + x )$ is repeated, so it contributes two terms, one over each power

$\frac{4+5x-x^{2}}{(1-x)(1+x)^{2}} \equiv \frac{A}{1-x} + \frac{B}{1+x} + \frac{C}{(1+x)^{2}}$

**[B1]**

Multiply through by $( 1 - x ) ( 1 + x )^{2}$ to clear the denominators

$4 + 5 x - x^{2} = A ( 1 + x )^{2} + B ( 1 - x ) ( 1 + x ) + C ( 1 - x )$

To find $C$, substitute $x = - 1$, which removes the terms in $A$ and $B$

$- 2 = 2 C  \Rightarrow  C = - 1$

**[M1 A1]**

To find $A$, substitute $x = 1$, which removes the terms in $B$ and $C$

$8 = 4 A  \Rightarrow  A = 2$

**[A1]**

No value of $x$ isolates $B$, so substitute $x = 0$ and use the two constants already found

$4 = A + B + C = 2 + B - 1  \Rightarrow  B = 3$

State the decomposition

$\frac{4+5x-x^{2}}{(1-x)(1+x)^{2}} \equiv \frac{2}{1-x} + \frac{3}{1+x} - \frac{1}{(1+x)^{2}}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct form stated or implied, with three terms including one over $( 1 + x )$ and one over $( 1 + x )^{2}$. Omitting the term over the single power of $( 1 + x )$ does not earn this mark.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for finding one of the constants, by substituting a value of $x$ that removes terms or by comparing coefficients.
> 
> **A1**: One constant correct.
> 
> **A1**: A second constant correct.
> 
> **A1**: The third constant correct, giving $\frac{2}{1-x} + \frac{3}{1+x} - \frac{1}{(1+x)^{2}}$.

parts.problemMd:
Use the binomial expansion to find the first three terms, in ascending powers of $x$, in each of

$( 1 - x )^{-1}$

$( 1 + x )^{-1}$

and

$( 1 + x )^{-2}$
parts.solutionMd:
Apply the general binomial expansion with $n = - 1$, replacing $x$ by $- x$

$( 1 - x )^{-1} = 1 + ( - 1 ) ( - x ) + \frac{(-1)(-2)}{2!} ( - x )^{2} +  . . .$

**[M1]**

Every power of $- x$ meets a negative coefficient, so all the terms are positive

$( 1 - x )^{-1} \approx 1 + x + x^{2}$

**[A1]**

Apply the same expansion with $n = - 1$, keeping $x$ as it is, so the signs alternate

$( 1 + x )^{-1} \approx 1 - x + x^{2}$

**[A1]**

Now take $n = - 2$ with $x$ unchanged

$( 1 + x )^{-2} = 1 + ( - 2 ) x + \frac{(-2)(-3)}{2!} x^{2} +  . . .$

$( 1 + x )^{-2} \approx 1 - 2 x + 3 x^{2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct unsimplified version of the $x$ or the $x^{2}$ term of any one of the three expansions.
> 
> **A1**: $1 + x + x^{2}$.
> 
> **A1**: $1 - x + x^{2}$.
> 
> **A1**: $1 - 2 x + 3 x^{2}$.

in ascending powers of $x$, up to and including the term in $x^{2}$.
parts.solutionMd:
Substitute the three expansions into the decomposition from part (a), each with its own multiplier

parts.problemMd: State the set of values of $x$ for which the expansion in part (c) is valid.
parts.solutionMd:
All three expansions require the quantity added to $1$ to have modulus below $1$, and each gives the same condition

parts.problemMd:
Expand

$( 2 + 3 x )^{-1} ( 3 - 2 x )^{-2}$

in ascending powers of $x$, up to and including the term in $x^{2}$, simplifying the coefficients.
parts.solutionMd:
Expand each bracket separately, then multiply. Neither starts with $1$, so take out the constant from each

`(2 + 3x)^{-1} = \left[2\left(1 + \frac{3x}{2}\right)\right]^{-1}`

`= \frac{1}{2}\left(1 + \frac{3x}{2}\right)^{-1} = \frac{1}{2}\left[1 + (-1)\left(\frac{3x}{2}\right) + \frac{(-1)(-2)}{2!}\left(\frac{3x}{2}\right)^{2} + \; ...\right]`

Simplify inside the bracket, then multiply through by $\frac{1}{2}$

`= \frac{1}{2}\left[1 - \frac{3x}{2} + \frac{9x^{2}}{4}\right] = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{3x}{4} + \frac{9x^{2}}{8}`

Repeat for the second bracket

`(3 - 2x)^{-2} = \left[3\left(1 - \frac{2x}{3}\right)\right]^{-2}`

`= \frac{1}{9}\left(1 - \frac{2x}{3}\right)^{-2} = \frac{1}{9}\left[1 + (-2)\left(-\frac{2x}{3}\right) + \frac{(-2)(-3)}{2!}\left(-\frac{2x}{3}\right)^{2} + \; ...\right]`

Simplify inside the bracket, then multiply through by $\frac{1}{9}$

`= \frac{1}{9}\left[1 + \frac{4x}{3} + \frac{4x^{2}}{3}\right] = \frac{1}{9} + \frac{4x}{27} + \frac{4x^{2}}{27}`

**[M1]**

Multiply the two expansions, collecting the products that give terms up to $x^{2}$

`\approx \frac{1}{18} + \left(\frac{2}{27} - \frac{1}{12}\right)x + \left(\frac{2}{27} - \frac{3}{27} + \frac{1}{8}\right)x^{2}`

**[A1]**

Combine each bracket over a common denominator

$( 2 + 3 x )^{-1} ( 3 - 2 x )^{-2} \approx \frac{1}{18} - \frac{x}{108} + \frac{19x^{2}}{216}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Both brackets expanded to the term in $x^{2}$, with the constant correctly taken out of each.
> 
> **A1**: The two expansions multiplied, with all the contributing products collected. Three separate products contribute to the $x^{2}$ term.
> 
> **A1**: $\frac{1}{18} - \frac{x}{108} + \frac{19x^{2}}{216}$. Accept equivalent fractions.

parts.problemMd: Find the percentage error in using your expansion from part (a) to approximate the value of $( 2 + 3 x )^{-1} ( 3 - 2 x )^{-2}$ when $x = 0 . 1$, giving your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.solutionMd:
Evaluate the original expression exactly at $x = 0 . 1$

$( 2 . 3 )^{-1} ( 2 . 8 )^{-2} = \frac{1}{2.3\times7.84} = 0 . 0554570$

**[M1]**

Evaluate the expansion from part (a) at the same value

$\frac{1}{18} - \frac{0.1}{108} + \frac{19(0.1)^{2}}{216} = 0 . 0555093$

Percentage error compares the difference with the exact value

`\frac{|0.0555093 - 0.0554570|}{0.0554570} \times 100 = 0.0943`

**[M1]**

Round to 1 decimal place

`0.1\%`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: The exact value found by substituting $x = 0 . 1$ into the original expression, and the approximate value found from your expansion. Both are needed.
> 
> **M1**: Correct percentage error method, that is the difference divided by the exact value and multiplied by $100$. Following through on your earlier values is allowed.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to `0.1\%`. Because the two values agree to three decimal places, full precision must be carried through the working. Rounding either value early loses this mark.
