> **B1**: All three $x$-axis crossings $( - 1 , 0 )$, $( 2 , 0 )$ and $( 3 , 0 )$, correct and labelled.

> **B1**: Correct positive-cubic shape through those crossings with the $y$-intercept $( 0 , 6 )$ labelled. Stationary points are not required, as the question says.

parts.problemMd: Show that $( x + 3 )$ is a factor of the function $\text{f} ( x ) = 6 x^{3} + 23 x^{2} + 11 x - 12$ and hence, or otherwise, fully factorise $\text{f} ( x )$.
parts.solutionMd:
By the factor theorem, $( x + 3 )$ is a factor exactly when $\text{f} ( - 3 ) = 0$, so evaluate $\text{f} ( - 3 )$

$\text{f} ( - 3 ) = 6 ( - 3 )^{3} + 23 ( - 3 )^{2} + 11 ( - 3 ) - 12$

$= - 162 + 207 - 33 - 12 = 0$

$\text{f} ( - 3 ) = 0 \text{, so} ( x + 3 ) \text{is a factor}$

**[B1]**

Now divide $\text{f} ( x )$ by $( x + 3 )$; write $\text{f} ( x )$ as $( x + 3 )$ multiplied by an unknown quadratic

$6 x^{3} + 23 x^{2} + 11 x - 12 = ( x + 3 ) ( a x^{2} + b x + c )$

**[M1]**

Compare the coefficient of $x^{3}$

$a = 6$

Compare the constant term

$3 c = - 12 \Rightarrow c = - 4$

Compare the coefficient of $x^{2}$

$3 a + b = 23 \Rightarrow b = 5$

These give the quadratic factor

$\text{f} ( x ) = ( x + 3 ) ( 6 x^{2} + 5 x - 4 )$

Factorise the quadratic; $6 \times ( - 4 ) = - 24$, and $8$ and $- 3$ multiply to $- 24$ and add to $5$

$6 x^{2} + 5 x - 4 = ( 2 x - 1 ) ( 3 x + 4 )$

$\text{f} ( x ) = ( x + 3 ) ( 2 x - 1 ) ( 3 x + 4 )$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Substituting $x = - 3$ and reaching $0$, which shows $( x + 3 )$ is a factor. A written conclusion is good practice but is not required for the mark; an arithmetic slip loses it even if the last line reads $0$.
> 
> **M1**: Writing $\text{f} ( x ) = ( x + 3 ) ( a x^{2} + b x + c )$ and comparing coefficients, or dividing by $( x + 3 )$ by long division.
> 
> **A1**: Fully factorised $\text{f} ( x ) = ( x + 3 ) ( 2 x - 1 ) ( 3 x + 4 )$, factors in any order. Accept the equivalent `3(x+3)(2x-1)\left(x+\frac{4}{3}\right)` or similar, provided it multiplies back to $\text{f} ( x )$.

parts.problemMd: Factorise completely $15 x^{3} + 19 x^{2} - 10 x$.
parts.solutionMd:
Every term has a factor of $x$, so take that out first

$15 x^{3} + 19 x^{2} - 10 x = x ( 15 x^{2} + 19 x - 10 )$

**[M1]**

Factorise the quadratic; $15 \times ( - 10 ) = - 150$, and $25$ and $- 6$ multiply to $- 150$ and add to $19$

$15 x^{2} + 19 x - 10 = ( 5 x - 2 ) ( 3 x + 5 )$

Combine with the common factor

$x ( 5 x - 2 ) ( 3 x + 5 )$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Taking out the common factor of $x$ to reach $x ( 15 x^{2} + 19 x - 10 )$, or otherwise beginning a valid factorisation.
> 
> **A1**: Fully factorised $x ( 5 x - 2 ) ( 3 x + 5 )$, factors in any order. The $x$ must be there: "completely" means all three factors, so $( 5 x - 2 ) ( 3 x + 5 )$ on its own does not score.

parts.problemMd:
$\text{f} ( x ) = x^{3} - 28 x + 48$

Find the remainder when $\text{f} ( x )$ is divided by $( x - 3 )$.
parts.solutionMd:
**Method 1 - Remainder Theorem**

The remainder on dividing by $( x - 3 )$ is the value of $\text{f} ( x )$ at $x = 3$

$\text{f} ( 3 ) = ( 3 )^{3} - 28 ( 3 ) + 48 = 27 - 84 + 48$

**[M1]**

$- 9$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Using the remainder theorem, substituting $x = 3$ into $\text{f} ( x )$ (or commencing long division by $( x - 3 )$).
> 
> **A1**: Correct remainder $- 9$. A bare value with no substitution or division seen does not score.

**Method 2 - Long Division**

Divide $\text{f} ( x )$ by $( x - 3 )$, writing the missing $x^{2}$ term as $0 x^{2}$ so that the columns line up; the number left at the foot of the division is the remainder

![Long division tableau dividing x ^3 + zero x ^2 - 28x + 48 by x - 3, giving quotient x ^2 + 3x - 19 and a remainder of - 9](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-maths-20-pure-3/algebra-and-functions/polynomials/assets/020-long-division-tableau-dividing-x-cubed-plus-zero.png)

**[M1]**

The final line of the division is the remainder

$- 9$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Commencing division of $\text{f} ( x )$ by $( x - 3 )$ and working through to the constant at the foot.
> 
> **A1**: Correct remainder $- 9$.

$x^{3} + 0 x^{2} - 28 x + 48 = ( x + 6 ) ( a x^{2} + b x + c )$

**[M1]**

Compare the coefficient of $x^{3}$

$a = 1$

Compare the constant term

$6 c = 48 \Rightarrow c = 8$

Compare the coefficient of $x^{2}$

$6 a + b = 0 \Rightarrow b = - 6$

These give the quadratic factor

$\text{f} ( x ) = ( x + 6 ) ( x^{2} - 6 x + 8 )$

**[A1]**

Factorise the quadratic, using two numbers that multiply to $8$ and add to $- 6$, namely $- 2$ and $- 4$

$x^{2} - 6 x + 8 = ( x - 2 ) ( x - 4 )$

**[M1]**

Combine the factors

$\text{f} ( x ) = ( x + 6 ) ( x - 2 ) ( x - 4 )$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Writing $\text{f} ( x ) = ( x + 6 ) ( a x^{2} + b x + c )$ and comparing coefficients, or dividing by $( x + 6 )$. The missing $x^{2}$ term must be handled as $0 x^{2}$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct quadratic factor $x^{2} - 6 x + 8$.
> 
> **M1**: Factorising the quadratic into two linear factors.

parts.problemMd:
Show that $( 5 x - 2 )$ is a factor of $25 x^{3} + 55 x^{2} - 56 x + 12$.

Hence find all the real solutions to the equation $25 x^{3} + 55 x^{2} - 56 x + 12 = 0$.
parts.solutionMd:
The factor $( 5 x - 2 )$ is zero at $x = \frac{2}{5}$, so by the factor theorem evaluate the cubic there and check it is zero

`25\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^3 + 55\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^2 - 56\left(\frac{2}{5}\right) + 12`

**[M1]**

Work out the arithmetic

$= \frac{8}{5} + \frac{44}{5} - \frac{112}{5} + \frac{60}{5} = 0$

$\text{The value is} 0 \text{, so} ( 5 x - 2 ) \text{is a factor}$

**[A1]**

Now divide the cubic by $( 5 x - 2 )$; write it as $( 5 x - 2 )$ multiplied by an unknown quadratic

$25 x^{3} + 55 x^{2} - 56 x + 12 = ( 5 x - 2 ) ( a x^{2} + b x + c )$

**[M1]**

Compare the coefficient of $x^{3}$

$5 a = 25 \Rightarrow a = 5$

Compare the constant term

$- 2 c = 12 \Rightarrow c = - 6$

Compare the coefficient of $x^{2}$

$- 2 a + 5 b = 55 \Rightarrow b = 13$

These give the quadratic factor

$25 x^{3} + 55 x^{2} - 56 x + 12 = ( 5 x - 2 ) ( 5 x^{2} + 13 x - 6 )$

Factorise the quadratic; $5 \times ( - 6 ) = - 30$, and $15$ and $- 2$ multiply to $- 30$ and add to $13$

$5 x^{2} + 13 x - 6 = ( 5 x - 2 ) ( x + 3 )$

**[A1]**

The factor $( 5 x - 2 )$ appears twice, so write the cubic in its fully factorised form and set each distinct factor to zero

$( 5 x - 2 )^{2} ( x + 3 ) = 0$

$x = \frac{2}{5} ,  - 3$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Substituting $x = \frac{2}{5}$ into the cubic. The fractional substitution must be seen.
> 
> **A1**: Reaching $0$ with no errors, which shows $( 5 x - 2 )$ is a factor. A written conclusion is good practice but is not required for the mark; an arithmetic slip loses it even if the last line reads $0$.
> 
> **M1**: Writing the cubic as $( 5 x - 2 ) ( a x^{2} + b x + c )$ and comparing coefficients, or dividing by $( 5 x - 2 )$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct quadratic factor $5 x^{2} + 13 x - 6$, or the fully factorised $( 5 x - 2 )^{2} ( x + 3 )$.
> 
> **A1**: Both solutions $x = \frac{2}{5}$ and $x = - 3$, and no extras. Accept $0 . 4$ for $\frac{2}{5}$. Do not penalise a candidate for giving only two solutions, because there are only two. Listing $\frac{2}{5}$ twice is condoned.

parts.problemMd:
$\text{f} ( x ) = x^{3} + r x^{2} + s x - 30$

Given that $\text{f} ( 2 ) = 0$ and $\text{f} ( - 3 ) = - 240$, find the values of $r$ and $s$.
parts.solutionMd:
Since $\text{f} ( 2 ) = 0$, substitute $x = 2$ and set the result to zero

$8 + 4 r + 2 s - 30 = 0$

**[M1]**

Simplify to obtain the first equation

$2 r + s = 11$

**[A1]**

Since $\text{f} ( - 3 ) = - 240$, substitute $x = - 3$ and set the result to $- 240$

$- 27 + 9 r - 3 s - 30 = - 240$

**[M1]**

Simplify to obtain the second equation

$3 r - s = - 61$

**[A1]**

Add the two equations to eliminate $s$

$5 r = - 50 \Rightarrow r = - 10$

**[M1]**

Substitute back into the first equation to find $s$

$2 ( - 10 ) + s = 11$

$r = - 10 ,  s = 31$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Substituting $x = 2$ into $\text{f} ( x )$ and equating to zero.
> 
> **A1**: Correct first equation, e.g. $2 r + s = 11$.
> 
> **M1**: Substituting $x = - 3$ into $\text{f} ( x )$ and equating to $- 240$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct second equation, e.g. $3 r - s = - 61$.
> 
> **M1**: Solving the two equations simultaneously by elimination or substitution.
> 
> **A1**: Both $r = - 10$ and $s = 31$.

parts.problemMd:

parts.problemMd: Show that $3 x^{3} + 16 x^{2} - 22 x$ can be written in the form $( 3 x + 1 ) ( a x^{2} + b x + c ) + d$, where $a , b , c$ and $d$ are constants to be found.
parts.solutionMd:
Write out the required identity, noting that the left hand side has no constant term

$3 x^{3} + 16 x^{2} - 22 x + 0 = ( 3 x + 1 ) ( a x^{2} + b x + c ) + d$

**[M1]**

Compare the coefficient of $x^{3}$

$3 a = 3 \Rightarrow a = 1$

**[A1]**

Compare the coefficient of $x^{2}$

$3 b + a = 16 \Rightarrow b = 5$

Compare the coefficient of $x$

$3 c + b = - 22 \Rightarrow c = - 9$

**[A1]**

Compare the constant terms; the left hand side has none, so the two must cancel

$c + d = 0 \Rightarrow d = 9$

$3 x^{3} + 16 x^{2} - 22 x = ( 3 x + 1 ) ( x^{2} + 5 x - 9 ) + 9$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Writing the identity $3 x^{3} + 16 x^{2} - 22 x = ( 3 x + 1 ) ( a x^{2} + b x + c ) + d$ and comparing coefficients, or dividing $3 x^{3} + 16 x^{2} - 22 x$ by $( 3 x + 1 )$ by long division.
> 
> **A1**: $a = 1$.
> 
> **A1**: $b = 5$ and $c = - 9$.
> 
> **A1**: $d = 9$, with the full identity stated. Accept the values listed separately rather than substituted back in.

**Method 1 - Long Division**

Divide by $( 2 x - 1 )$, writing the missing $x^{3}$ and $x$ terms as $0 x^{3}$ and $0 x$ so the columns line up

![Long division tableau dividing 4x to the fourth + zero x ^3 - 37x ^2 + zero x + 9 by 2x - 1, giving quotient 2x ^3 + x ^2 - 18x - 9 and remainder zero](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-maths-20-pure-3/algebra-and-functions/polynomials/assets/018-long-division-tableau-dividing-4x-to-the-fourth-.png)

**[M1]**

Read the quotient from the top of the tableau; the remainder is zero

$2 x^{3} + x^{2} - 18 x - 9$

**[A1 A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Commencing division of $4 x^{4} - 37 x^{2} + 9$ by $( 2 x - 1 )$, by any valid method, dividing $4 x^{4}$ by $2 x$ to start the quotient with $2 x^{3}$.
> 
> **A1**: A correct partial quotient (at least $2 x^{3} + x^{2}$).
> 
> **A1**: Fully correct quotient $2 x^{3} + x^{2} - 18 x - 9$ with zero remainder.

**Method 2 - Inspection**

Write the quartic as $( 2 x - 1 )$ multiplied by an unknown cubic

$4 x^{4} - 37 x^{2} + 9 = ( 2 x - 1 ) ( a x^{3} + b x^{2} + c x + d )$

**[M1]**

Compare coefficients term by term, from $x^{4}$ down to the constant

$2 a = 4 \Rightarrow a = 2$

$- a + 2 b = 0 \Rightarrow b = 1$

$- b + 2 c = - 37 \Rightarrow c = - 18$

$- c + 2 d = 0 \Rightarrow d = - 9$

$2 x^{3} + x^{2} - 18 x - 9$

**[A1 A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Writing $4 x^{4} - 37 x^{2} + 9 = ( 2 x - 1 ) ( a x^{3} + b x^{2} + c x + d )$ and comparing coefficients.
> 
> **A1**: At least two coefficients correct.
> 
> **A1**: Fully correct quotient $2 x^{3} + x^{2} - 18 x - 9$.

parts.problemMd:

Compare the constant term

**[A1]**

parts.problemMd: Find the coordinates of the points of intersection between the curve with equation $y = x^{3} - x^{2} - 4 x + 4$ and the line with equation $y = 2 x + 4$.
parts.solutionMd:
The graphs meet where their $y$-values are equal, so set the two expressions equal

$x^{3} - x^{2} - 4 x + 4 = 2 x + 4$

**[M1]**

Rearrange so that one side is zero; the constant terms cancel

$x^{3} - x^{2} - 6 x = 0$

**[A1]**

Every term has a factor of $x$, so take it out and factorise the quadratic

$x ( x^{2} - x - 6 ) = 0$

$x ( x - 3 ) ( x + 2 ) = 0$

**[M1]**

Set each factor to zero to get the three $x$-values

$x = 0 ,  3 ,  - 2$

Substitute each into the line $y = 2 x + 4$, which is the simpler of the two equations

$( 0 , 4 ) ,  ( 3 , 10 ) ,  ( - 2 , 0 )$

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Substitute back into the line rather than the cubic, as it is far less work and both must give the same answer.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Setting the two expressions for $y$ equal to each other.
> 
> **A1**: Correct simplified cubic equal to zero, $x^{3} - x^{2} - 6 x = 0$.
> 
> **M1**: Taking out the factor of $x$ and factorising the resulting quadratic (or otherwise solving for all three roots).
> 
> **A1**: All three points $( 0 , 4 )$, $( 3 , 10 )$ and $( - 2 , 0 )$, as coordinate pairs. Accept them in any order. $x$-values alone, without the matching $y$-values, do not score this mark.

parts.problemMd:

Also label any points where the graphs intersect the coordinate axes.
parts.solutionMd:
The line $y = 2 x + 4$ has gradient $2$; it crosses the axes at $( - 2 , 0 )$ and $( 0 , 4 )$

**[B1]**

To find where the curve crosses the $x$-axis, factorise the cubic by grouping the terms in pairs

$x^{3} - x^{2} - 4 x + 4 = x^{2} ( x - 1 ) - 4 ( x - 1 )$

Take out the common factor of $( x - 1 )$

$= ( x - 1 ) ( x^{2} - 4 )$

Factorise the difference of two squares

$= ( x - 1 ) ( x - 2 ) ( x + 2 )$

The curve crosses the $x$-axis where each factor is zero

$( - 2 , 0 ) ,  ( 1 , 0 ) ,  ( 2 , 0 )$

**[B1]**

Find the curve's $y$-intercept by substituting $x = 0$

$( 0 , 4 )$

**[B1]**

The coefficient of $x^{3}$ is positive, so the curve rises from lower left to upper right; draw both graphs on one diagram and mark the three intersection points found in part (a)

parts.problemMd:
It is given that

$\frac{\text{f}(x)}{\text{g}(x)} = 2 x + 3 - \frac{4}{x+1}$

Why would assuming that $\text{g} ( x ) = x + 1$ be a logical first step in attempting to determine the precise forms of $\text{f} ( x )$ and $\text{g} ( x )$?
parts.solutionMd:
Any division can be written as $\frac{\text{dividend}}{\text{divisor}} = \text{quotient} + \frac{\text{remainder}}{\text{divisor}}$, so the divisor is whatever sits underneath the remainder term

$\text{The remainder term is} \frac{4}{x+1} \text{, so the divisor g} ( x ) \text{is} x + 1$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Identifying that in the standard division form the divisor appears as the denominator of the remainder term, and that here that denominator is $( x + 1 )$. Accept any wording carrying that idea, for example "the remainder is written over the thing you divided by". Simply asserting "because it is the denominator" with no link to the division form is enough at this level, but a bare "it looks right" is not.

parts.problemMd: By first making the assumption from part (a), find $\text{f} ( x )$.
parts.solutionMd:
Take $\text{g} ( x ) = x + 1$ and multiply every term by it to clear the fractions

$\text{f} ( x ) = ( x + 1 ) ( 2 x + 3 ) - 4$

**[M1]**

Expand and simplify

$\text{f} ( x ) = 2 x^{2} + 5 x + 3 - 4$

$\text{f} ( x ) = 2 x^{2} + 5 x - 1$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Multiplying through by $( x + 1 )$ to reach $\text{f} ( x ) = ( x + 1 ) ( 2 x + 3 ) - 4$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct $\text{f} ( x ) = 2 x^{2} + 5 x - 1$.

parts.problemMd: Explain, with an example, why the forms of $\text{f} ( x )$ and $\text{g} ( x )$ determined in parts (a) and (b) are not the only possible forms for those functions.
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The equation only fixes the ratio **$\frac{\text{f}(x)}{\text{g}(x)}$**, so multiplying both functions by the same non-zero factor leaves that ratio unchanged**

**[B1]**

**Final answer:** **For example, doubling both gives a different pair of functions satisfying the same equation**

$\text{f} ( x ) = 4 x^{2} + 10 x - 2 \text{and g} ( x ) = 2 x + 2$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Explaining that only the ratio of $\text{f} ( x )$ to $\text{g} ( x )$ is determined, so both may be multiplied by the same non-zero factor. Accept "any common multiple of both works" or equivalent.
> 
> **B1**: A correct concrete example, i.e. any pair $k ( 2 x^{2} + 5 x - 1 )$ and $k ( x + 1 )$ with $k \neq 1$. A common polynomial factor is equally acceptable, e.g. $\text{f} ( x ) = ( 2 x^{2} + 5 x - 1 ) ( x - 3 )$ with $\text{g} ( x ) = ( x + 1 ) ( x - 3 )$. The example must actually be stated; the explanation alone does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd:
When $x^{3} + a x^{2} + 4 x - 1$ is divided by $( x + 2 )$ the quotient is $x^{2} - 4 x + 12$ and the remainder is $b$.

Find the values of $a$ and $b$.
parts.solutionMd:
Any division can be written as $\text{dividend} = ( \text{divisor} ) ( \text{quotient} ) + \text{remainder}$, so write that identity out

$x^{3} + a x^{2} + 4 x - 1 = ( x + 2 ) ( x^{2} - 4 x + 12 ) + b$

**[M1]**

Expand the right hand side

$= x^{3} - 4 x^{2} + 12 x + 2 x^{2} - 8 x + 24 + b$

$= x^{3} - 2 x^{2} + 4 x + 24 + b$

Compare the coefficient of $x^{2}$

$a = - 2$

**[A1]**

Compare the constant terms

$24 + b = - 1$

$b = - 25$

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Once you have expanded, the coefficient of $x$ comes out as $4$ on both sides without you having used it. That is a free check that you multiplied out correctly, so glance at it before writing down your answers.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Writing the division identity $x^{3} + a x^{2} + 4 x - 1 = ( x + 2 ) ( x^{2} - 4 x + 12 ) + b$ and expanding the product. Accept an equivalent route, such as dividing $x^{3} + a x^{2} + 4 x - 1$ by $( x + 2 )$ and matching the given quotient.
> 
> **A1**: $a = - 2$.
> 
> **A1**: $b = - 25$.

parts.problemMd:
The polynomial $p x^{3} + ( 5 p + 1 ) x^{2} + 5 q x - 2 q - 2$, where $p$ and $q$ are constants, is denoted by $\text{f} ( x )$.

It is given that $( x + 4 )$ is a factor of $\text{f} ( x )$, and that when $\text{f} ( x )$ is divided by $( x + 1 )$ the remainder is $- 12$.

Find the values of $p$ and $q$.
parts.solutionMd:
Since $( x + 4 )$ is a factor, the factor theorem gives $\text{f} ( - 4 ) = 0$, so substitute $x = - 4$

$p ( - 4 )^{3} + ( 5 p + 1 ) ( - 4 )^{2} + 5 q ( - 4 ) - 2 q - 2 = 0$

**[M1]**

Expand and collect like terms

$- 64 p + 80 p + 16 - 20 q - 2 q - 2 = 0$

$16 p - 22 q = - 14$

Divide through by $2$ to obtain the first equation

$8 p - 11 q = - 7$

**[A1]**

When $\text{f} ( x )$ is divided by $( x + 1 )$ the remainder is $- 12$, so by the remainder theorem $\text{f} ( - 1 ) = - 12$

$p ( - 1 )^{3} + ( 5 p + 1 ) ( - 1 )^{2} + 5 q ( - 1 ) - 2 q - 2 = - 12$

**[M1]**

Expand and collect like terms to obtain the second equation

$- p + 5 p + 1 - 5 q - 2 q - 2 = - 12$

$4 p - 7 q = - 11$

**[A1]**

Solve the two equations simultaneously; doubling the second gives $8 p - 14 q = - 22$, so subtracting eliminates $p$

$( 8 p - 11 q ) - ( 8 p - 14 q ) = - 7 - ( - 22 )$

$3 q = 15 \Rightarrow q = 5$

Substitute back into the second equation to find $p$

$4 p - 7 ( 5 ) = - 11 \Rightarrow 4 p = 24$

$p = 6 ,  q = 5$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Using the factor theorem, substituting $x = - 4$ into $\text{f} ( x )$ and equating to zero. Dividing by $( x + 4 )$ and equating the constant remainder to zero is equally acceptable.
> 
> **A1**: A correct simplified equation in $p$ and $q$, e.g. $8 p - 11 q = - 7$ or the unsimplified $16 p - 22 q = - 14$.
> 
> **M1**: Using the remainder theorem, substituting $x = - 1$ into $\text{f} ( x )$ and equating to $- 12$. Dividing by $( x + 1 )$ and equating the constant remainder to $- 12$ is equally acceptable.
> 
> **A1**: A correct simplified equation in $p$ and $q$, e.g. $4 p - 7 q = - 11$.
> 
> **A1**: Both $p = 6$ and $q = 5$, from correct working throughout. There is no follow-through here: if either equation is wrong, this mark is lost even if the wrong pair is then solved perfectly.

parts.problemMd:
On the same diagram, sketch the graphs of $4 y = x^{3} - 5 x^{2} - 12 x + 36$ and $x + y - 6 = 0$.

Label the coordinates of any points of intersection between the two graphs.

Also label any points where the graphs intersect the coordinate axes.
parts.solutionMd:
To find where the curve crosses the $x$-axis, factorise the cubic; the crossings do not depend on the factor of $\frac{1}{4}$

Test values to find a factor: $x = 2$ gives $( 2 )^{3} - 5 ( 2 )^{2} - 12 ( 2 ) + 36 = 0$, so $( x - 2 )$ is a factor

$x^{3} - 5 x^{2} - 12 x + 36 = ( x - 2 ) ( x^{2} + b x + c )$

Compare the coefficient of $x^{2}$

$b - 2 = - 5 \Rightarrow b = - 3$

Compare the constant term

$- 2 c = 36 \Rightarrow c = - 18$

Factorise the quadratic $x^{2} - 3 x - 18$; $- 6$ and $3$ multiply to $- 18$ and add to $- 3$

$x^{3} - 5 x^{2} - 12 x + 36 = ( x - 2 ) ( x - 6 ) ( x + 3 )$

**[M1]**

The curve crosses the $x$-axis where each factor is zero

$( - 3 , 0 ) ,  ( 2 , 0 ) ,  ( 6 , 0 )$

**[A1]**

Find the cubic's $y$-intercept; because $4 y = 36$ at $x = 0$, divide by $4$

$( 0 , 9 )$

**[B1]**

Rearrange the line to $y = 6 - x$; it has negative gradient and crosses the axes at $( 6 , 0 )$ and $( 0 , 6 )$

**[B1]**

Find the intersections by setting $6 - x = \frac{1}{4} ( x^{3} - 5 x^{2} - 12 x + 36 )$ and clearing the fraction

$24 - 4 x = x^{3} - 5 x^{2} - 12 x + 36$

$x^{3} - 5 x^{2} - 8 x + 12 = 0$

**[M1]**

To solve, factorise; $x = 6$ is already known to lie on both graphs, so $( x - 6 )$ is a factor. Divide by it, writing the cubic as $( x - 6 )$ times a quadratic

$x^{3} - 5 x^{2} - 8 x + 12 = ( x - 6 ) ( x^{2} + b x + c )$

Compare the coefficient of $x^{2}$

$b - 6 = - 5 \Rightarrow b = 1$

Compare the constant term

$- 6 c = 12 \Rightarrow c = - 2$

Factorise the quadratic $x^{2} + x - 2$; $2$ and $- 1$ multiply to $- 2$ and add to $1$

$( x - 6 ) ( x - 1 ) ( x + 2 ) = 0 \Rightarrow x = 6 ,  1 ,  - 2$

**[A1]**

Substitute each into the line $y = 6 - x$ to get the intersection points

$( 6 , 0 ) ,  ( 1 , 5 ) ,  ( - 2 , 8 )$

**[A1]**

Draw both graphs on one diagram: a positive cubic through its three crossings and $y$-intercept, and the descending line, meeting at the three intersection points

![Sketch of a positive cubic and a descending line on the same diagram. The cubic crosses the x-axis at (-3, 0), (2, 0) and (6, 0) and the y-axis at (0, 9). The line y = 6 - x crosses the x-axis at (6, 0) and the y-axis at (0, 6). The two graphs meet at (-2, 8), (1, 5) and (6, 0)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-maths-20-pure-3/algebra-and-functions/polynomials/assets/003-sketch-of-a-positive-cubic-and-a-descending-stra.png)

**[B1 B1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Two things may trip people here. First, the cubic is written as $4 y = \dots$, so every $y$-value is a quarter of the cubic expression, making the $y$-intercept $9$, not $36$.
> 
> Secondly the point $( 6 , 0 )$ does three things: it is a crossing of the cubic, the $x$-intercept of the line, and one of the three intersections. Spotting that gives you a factor of the intersection cubic for free.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Factorising the cubic $x^{3} - 5 x^{2} - 12 x + 36$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct cubic crossings $( - 3 , 0 )$, $( 2 , 0 )$, $( 6 , 0 )$.
> 
> **B1**: The cubic's $y$-intercept $( 0 , 9 )$, with the division by $4$ applied.
> 
> **B1**: The line drawn correctly with negative gradient, crossing at $( 6 , 0 )$ and $( 0 , 6 )$.
> 
> **M1**: Setting the two expressions equal and reaching $x^{3} - 5 x^{2} - 8 x + 12 = 0$.
> 
> **A1**: Factorising and solving for all three $x$-values $6 , 1 , - 2$.
> 
> **A1**: All three intersection points $( 6 , 0 )$, $( 1 , 5 )$, $( - 2 , 8 )$ as coordinate pairs.
> 
> **B1**: Correct positive-cubic shape drawn on the same diagram as the line.
> 
> **B1**: A fully correct diagram with both graphs, all axis crossings and all three intersections labelled.

parts.problemMd:
$\text{f} ( x ) = 6 x^{4} + 7 x^{3} - 27 x^{2} - 28 x + 12$

Find the remainder when $\text{f} ( x )$ is divided by $( 2 x + 3 )$.
parts.solutionMd:
**Method 1 - Remainder Theorem**

The factor $( 2 x + 3 )$ is zero at $x = - \frac{3}{2}$, so the remainder is `\text{f}\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)`

`\text{f}\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right) = 6\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)^4 + 7\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)^3 - 27\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)^2 - 28\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right) + 12`

**[M1]**

Work out the arithmetic

$= \frac{243}{8} - \frac{189}{8} - \frac{243}{4} + 42 + 12 = 0$

$0$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Using the remainder theorem, substituting $x = - \frac{3}{2}$ into $\text{f} ( x )$ (or commencing long division by $( 2 x + 3 )$).
> 
> **A1**: Correct remainder $0$. (A remainder of $0$ also shows $( 2 x + 3 )$ is a factor, which is used implicitly in part (b).)

**Method 2 - Long Division**

Divide $\text{f} ( x )$ by $( 2 x + 3 )$; the constant left at the foot is the remainder

![Long division tableau dividing 6x to the fourth + 7x ^3 - 27x ^2 - 28x + 12 by 2x + 3, giving quotient 3x ^3 - x ^2 - 12x + 4 and a remainder of zero](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-maths-20-pure-3/algebra-and-functions/polynomials/assets/019-long-division-tableau-dividing-6x-to-the-fourth-.png)

**[M1]**

The final line of the division is the remainder

$0$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Commencing division of $\text{f} ( x )$ by $( 2 x + 3 )$ and working through to the constant at the foot.
> 
> **A1**: Correct remainder $0$.

parts.problemMd: Given that $( x + 2 )$ is a factor of $\text{f} ( x )$, factorise $\text{f} ( x )$ completely.
parts.solutionMd:
Since $( x + 2 )$ is a factor, divide $\text{f} ( x )$ by it; write $\text{f} ( x )$ as $( x + 2 )$ multiplied by an unknown cubic

$6 x^{4} + 7 x^{3} - 27 x^{2} - 28 x + 12 = ( x + 2 ) ( a x^{3} + b x^{2} + c x + d )$

**[M1]**

Compare the coefficient of $x^{4}$

$a = 6$

Compare the coefficient of $x^{3}$

$2 a + b = 7 \Rightarrow b = - 5$

Compare the constant term

$2 d = 12 \Rightarrow d = 6$

Compare the coefficient of $x$

$2 c + d = - 28 \Rightarrow c = - 17$

These give the cubic factor

$\text{f} ( x ) = ( x + 2 ) ( 6 x^{3} - 5 x^{2} - 17 x + 6 )$

**[A1]**

From part (a), $( 2 x + 3 )$ is also a factor (the remainder was $0$), so divide the cubic by it

$6 x^{3} - 5 x^{2} - 17 x + 6 = ( 2 x + 3 ) ( 3 x^{2} - 7 x + 2 )$

**[M1]**

Factorise the quadratic; $3 \times 2 = 6$, and $- 6$ and $- 1$ multiply to $6$ and add to $- 7$

$3 x^{2} - 7 x + 2 = ( 3 x - 1 ) ( x - 2 )$

**[A1]**

Combine all four linear factors

$\text{f} ( x ) = ( x + 2 ) ( 2 x + 3 ) ( 3 x - 1 ) ( x - 2 )$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Dividing $\text{f} ( x )$ by $( x + 2 )$ (or comparing coefficients) to begin reducing the quartic.
> 
> **A1**: Correct cubic factor $6 x^{3} - 5 x^{2} - 17 x + 6$.
> 
> **M1**: Using $( 2 x + 3 )$ from part (a), or otherwise, to reduce the cubic to a quadratic factor.
> 
> **A1**: Correct quadratic factor $3 x^{2} - 7 x + 2$, or its factors $( 3 x - 1 ) ( x - 2 )$.
> 
> **A1**: Fully factorised $\text{f} ( x ) = ( x + 2 ) ( 2 x + 3 ) ( 3 x - 1 ) ( x - 2 )$, factors in any order.

Substitute $x = - 1$ and $x = - 2$ into $\text{f} ( x )$ and show each gives zero

$\text{f} ( - 1 ) = 2 + 15 - 10 - 105 + 98 = 0$

$\text{f} ( - 2 ) = 32 + 120 - 40 - 210 + 98 = 0$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Both $\text{f} ( - 1 ) = 0$ and $\text{f} ( - 2 ) = 0$ shown, with the substitutions seen. As both results are given, the working must be seen for each.

parts.problemMd: Hence, solve $\text{f} ( x ) = 0$.
parts.solutionMd:
From part (a), $( x + 1 )$ and $( x + 2 )$ are both factors, so their product $( x + 1 ) ( x + 2 ) = x^{2} + 3 x + 2$ is a factor; divide $\text{f} ( x )$ by it, writing $\text{f} ( x )$ as $( x^{2} + 3 x + 2 )$ multiplied by an unknown quadratic

$2 x^{4} - 15 x^{3} - 10 x^{2} + 105 x + 98 = ( x^{2} + 3 x + 2 ) ( a x^{2} + b x + c )$

**[M1]**

Compare the coefficient of $x^{4}$

$a = 2$

Compare the constant term

$2 c = 98 \Rightarrow c = 49$

Compare the coefficient of $x^{3}$

$3 a + b = - 15 \Rightarrow b = - 21$

These give the quadratic factor

$\text{f} ( x ) = ( x^{2} + 3 x + 2 ) ( 2 x^{2} - 21 x + 49 )$

**[A1]**

Factorise the quadratic $2 x^{2} - 21 x + 49$; $2 \times 49 = 98$, and $- 14$ and $- 7$ multiply to $98$ and add to $- 21$

$2 x^{2} - 21 x + 49 = ( 2 x - 7 ) ( x - 7 )$

**[M1 A1]**

Write $\text{f} ( x )$ fully factorised

$\text{f} ( x ) = ( x + 1 ) ( x + 2 ) ( 2 x - 7 ) ( x - 7 )$

**[A1]**

Set each factor to zero to solve $\text{f} ( x ) = 0$

$x = - 1 ,  - 2 ,  \frac{7}{2} ,  7$

**[A1 A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Using $( x + 1 ) ( x + 2 ) = x^{2} + 3 x + 2$ as a factor and dividing (or comparing coefficients).
> 
> **A1**: Correct quadratic quotient $2 x^{2} - 21 x + 49$.
> 
> **M1**: Attempting to factorise $2 x^{2} - 21 x + 49$ into two linear factors.
> 
> **A1**: Correct factors $( 2 x - 7 ) ( x - 7 )$.
> 
> **A1**: Fully factorised $\text{f} ( x ) = ( x + 1 ) ( x + 2 ) ( 2 x - 7 ) ( x - 7 )$.
> 
> **A1**: Two correct solutions.
> 
> **A1**: All four solutions $x = - 1 , - 2 , \frac{7}{2} , 7$ and no extras.

parts.problemMd:
When $2 x^{3} + ( a + b ) x^{2} + ( a - b ) x - 3$ is divided by $x + 4$ the quotient is $2 x^{2} + ( 2 a + 3 ) x + ( 2 b - 5 )$ and the remainder is $c$.

Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$.
parts.solutionMd:
Write out the division identity, dividend $= ( \text{divisor} ) ( \text{quotient} ) + \text{remainder}$

`2x^3 + (a+b)x^2 + (a-b)x - 3 = (x+4)\left(2x^2 + (2a+3)x + (2b-5)\right) + c`

**[M1]**

Expand the right hand side and collect like terms

$= 2 x^{3} + ( 2 a + 11 ) x^{2} + ( 8 a + 2 b + 7 ) x + ( 8 b - 20 + c )$

Compare the coefficient of $x^{2}$

$2 a + 11 = a + b \Rightarrow b = a + 11$

Compare the coefficient of $x$

$8 a + 2 b + 7 = a - b \Rightarrow 7 a + 3 b = - 7$

Substitute $b = a + 11$ and solve for $a$

$7 a + 3 ( a + 11 ) = - 7$

$a = - 4 ,  b = 7$

**[M1 A1]**

Compare the constant terms to find $c$

$8 b - 20 + c = - 3 \Rightarrow 8 ( 7 ) - 20 + c = - 3$

$c = - 39$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Writing the division identity dividend $= ( x + 4 ) ( \text{quotient} ) + c$ and expanding the product.
> 
> **M1**: Comparing coefficients of $x^{2}$ and $x$ to form two simultaneous equations in $a$ and $b$.
> 
> **A1**: Both $a = - 4$ and $b = 7$.
> 
> **A1**: $c = - 39$, from comparing the constant terms.

parts.problemMd:
$( x - 2 )$ and $( x + 3 )$ are factors of $\text{f} ( x )$, where $\text{f} ( x ) = x^{4} - 9 x^{3} + 9 x^{2} + 85 x - 150$.

Sketch the graph of $y = \text{f} ( x )$, labelling any points where the graph intersects the coordinate axes. (There is no need to label any stationary points.)
parts.solutionMd:
Both $( x - 2 )$ and $( x + 3 )$ are factors, so their product $( x - 2 ) ( x + 3 ) = x^{2} + x - 6$ divides $\text{f} ( x )$; divide to find the remaining quadratic

$x^{4} - 9 x^{3} + 9 x^{2} + 85 x - 150 = ( x^{2} + x - 6 ) ( x^{2} + b x + c )$

**[M1]**

Compare the coefficient of $x^{3}$

$b + 1 = - 9 \Rightarrow b = - 10$

Compare the constant term

$- 6 c = - 150 \Rightarrow c = 25$

These give the quadratic factor

$\text{f} ( x ) = ( x^{2} + x - 6 ) ( x^{2} - 10 x + 25 )$

Factorise both quadratics; the second is a perfect square

$\text{f} ( x ) = ( x - 2 ) ( x + 3 ) ( x - 5 )^{2}$

**[A1]**

Set each factor to zero; the repeated factor $( x - 5 )^{2}$ gives a point where the curve touches the axis, the others where it crosses

$\text{crosses at} ( - 3 , 0 ) \text{and} ( 2 , 0 ) , \text{touches at} ( 5 , 0 )$

**[B1]**

Find the $y$-intercept by substituting $x = 0$

$( 0 , - 150 )$

**[B1]**

The coefficient of $x^{4}$ is positive, so the curve falls from the upper left and rises to the upper right; draw it crossing at $- 3$ and $2$ and touching at $5$

![Sketch of a positive quartic that crosses the x-axis at (-3, 0) and (2, 0), touches the x-axis at (5, 0), and crosses the y-axis at (0, -150). The curve comes down from upper left, dips below the axis between -3 and 2, rises to touch at (5, 0), then rises again. Not drawn to scale](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-maths-20-pure-3/algebra-and-functions/polynomials/assets/001-sketch-of-a-positive-quartic-that-crosses-the-x-.png)

**[B1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The squared factor $( x - 5 )^{2}$ is the key: a repeated root means the curve *touches* the $x$-axis there rather than crossing it. Miss that and your sketch has the wrong shape even with every coordinate correct.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Using the product $( x - 2 ) ( x + 3 )$ as a quadratic factor and dividing (or comparing coefficients) to find the remaining quadratic.
> 
> **A1**: Fully factorised $\text{f} ( x ) = ( x - 2 ) ( x + 3 ) ( x - 5 )^{2}$.
> 
> **B1**: All three $x$-axis points correct: crosses at $( - 3 , 0 )$ and $( 2 , 0 )$, touches at $( 5 , 0 )$.
> 
> **B1**: The $y$-intercept $( 0 , - 150 )$.
> 
> **B1**: Correct positive-quartic shape, crossing at the two single roots and touching (not crossing) at the repeated root. A curve that crosses at $( 5 , 0 )$ does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd: Sketch the graph of $y = 3 x^{3} + 2 x^{2} - 3 x + 10$, labelling any points where the graph intersects the coordinate axes.
parts.solutionMd:
Look for a factor; testing $x = - 2$ gives $3 ( - 8 ) + 2 ( 4 ) - 3 ( - 2 ) + 10 = 0$, so $( x + 2 )$ is a factor. Divide it out

$3 x^{3} + 2 x^{2} - 3 x + 10 = ( x + 2 ) ( 3 x^{2} - 4 x + 5 )$

**[M1]**

Check whether the quadratic factor gives further crossings by evaluating its discriminant

$b^{2} - 4 a c = ( - 4 )^{2} - 4 ( 3 ) ( 5 ) = 16 - 60 = - 44$

Since the discriminant is negative, $3 x^{2} - 4 x + 5$ has no real roots, so the only crossing is where $x + 2 = 0$

$( - 2 , 0 )$

**[A1]**

Find the $y$-intercept by substituting $x = 0$

$( 0 , 10 )$

**[B1]**

The coefficient of $x^{3}$ is positive, so the curve rises from lower left to upper right, crossing the axis only at $( - 2 , 0 )$

![Sketch of a positive cubic crossing the x-axis once at (-2, 0) and the y-axis at (0, 10). To the right of the crossing the curve has a shallow local maximum and local minimum but both stay above the x-axis, so there are no further crossings](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-maths-20-pure-3/algebra-and-functions/polynomials/assets/005-sketch-of-a-positive-cubic-crossing-the-x-axis-o.png)

**[B1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A positive cubic can cross the $x$-axis once, twice or three times. Once you have one factor, check the quadratic that is left: a negative discriminant means it never reaches the axis, so there is exactly one crossing.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Finding the factor $( x + 2 )$ and dividing to reach the quadratic factor $3 x^{2} - 4 x + 5$.
> 
> **A1**: Establishing $( - 2 , 0 )$ as the only $x$-axis crossing, supported by showing the quadratic factor has a negative discriminant (or equivalent reasoning that it has no real roots).
> 
> **B1**: The $y$-intercept $( 0 , 10 )$.
> 
> **B1**: Correct positive-cubic shape crossing the $x$-axis exactly once, at $( - 2 , 0 )$. A sketch showing extra crossings does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd: Fully factorise $4 x^{3} + 17 x^{2} + 20 x + 4$.
parts.solutionMd:
Look for a factor; testing $x = - 2$ gives $4 ( - 8 ) + 17 ( 4 ) + 20 ( - 2 ) + 4 = 0$, so $( x + 2 )$ is a factor. Divide it out, writing the cubic as $( x + 2 )$ multiplied by an unknown quadratic

$4 x^{3} + 17 x^{2} + 20 x + 4 = ( x + 2 ) ( a x^{2} + b x + c )$

**[M1]**

Compare the coefficient of $x^{3}$

$a = 4$

Compare the constant term

$2 c = 4 \Rightarrow c = 2$

Compare the coefficient of $x^{2}$

$2 a + b = 17 \Rightarrow b = 9$

These give the quadratic factor

$4 x^{3} + 17 x^{2} + 20 x + 4 = ( x + 2 ) ( 4 x^{2} + 9 x + 2 )$

**[A1]**

Factorise the quadratic; $4 \times 2 = 8$, and $8$ and $1$ multiply to $8$ and add to $9$

$4 x^{2} + 9 x + 2 = ( 4 x + 1 ) ( x + 2 )$

Combine, noting that $( x + 2 )$ now appears twice

$4 x^{3} + 17 x^{2} + 20 x + 4 = ( 4 x + 1 ) ( x + 2 )^{2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Finding a factor (e.g. $( x + 2 )$) and dividing to reach a quadratic factor, or comparing coefficients.
> 
> **A1**: Correct quadratic factor $4 x^{2} + 9 x + 2$.
> 
> **A1**: Fully factorised $( 4 x + 1 ) ( x + 2 )^{2}$, in any order. The square must be shown, so $( 4 x + 1 ) ( x + 2 )$ alone is not fully factorised.

parts.problemMd: Sketch the graph of $y = 4 x^{3} + 17 x^{2} + 20 x + 4$. Label any points where the graph crosses the coordinate axes.
parts.solutionMd:
From part (a) the factors give the $x$-axis behaviour: a crossing where $4 x + 1 = 0$ and a touch where $( x + 2 )^{2} = 0$

`\text{crosses at } \left(-\frac{1}{4}, 0\right), \text{ touches at } (-2, 0)`

Find the $y$-intercept by substituting $x = 0$, then draw a positive cubic through these points

$( 0 , 4 )$

![Sketch of a positive cubic that touches the x-axis at (-2, 0), crosses it at (negative one quarter, 0), and crosses the y-axis at (0, 4). The curve rises from lower left to touch at (-2, 0), dips slightly, then rises through the crossing and continues up to the right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-maths-20-pure-3/algebra-and-functions/polynomials/assets/002-sketch-of-a-positive-cubic-that-touches-the-x-ax.png)

**[B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: All axis points correct and labelled: touches at $( - 2 , 0 )$, crosses at `\left(-\frac{1}{4}, 0\right)`, $y$-intercept $( 0 , 4 )$.
> 
> **B1**: Correct positive-cubic shape, touching (not crossing) at $( - 2 , 0 )$ and crossing at `\left(-\frac{1}{4}, 0\right)`. Follow through from part (a)'s factors.

parts.problemMd:
On the same diagram, sketch the graphs of $y = x^{3} - 3 x^{2} - 6 x + 8$ and $y = \frac{3}{x^{2}}$.

Label any points where the graphs intersect the coordinate axes.
parts.solutionMd:
Test values to find a factor of the cubic: $x = 1$ gives $( 1 )^{3} - 3 ( 1 )^{2} - 6 ( 1 ) + 8 = 0$, so $( x - 1 )$ is a factor

Divide by $( x - 1 )$, writing the cubic as $( x - 1 )$ multiplied by an unknown quadratic

$x^{3} - 3 x^{2} - 6 x + 8 = ( x - 1 ) ( x^{2} + b x + c )$

Compare the coefficient of $x^{2}$

$b - 1 = - 3 \Rightarrow b = - 2$

Compare the constant term

$- c = 8 \Rightarrow c = - 8$

Factorise the quadratic $x^{2} - 2 x - 8$; $- 4$ and $2$ multiply to $- 8$ and add to $- 2$

$x^{3} - 3 x^{2} - 6 x + 8 = ( x - 1 ) ( x - 4 ) ( x + 2 )$

**[M1]**

Set each factor to zero to find where the curve crosses the $x$-axis

$( - 2 , 0 ) ,  ( 1 , 0 ) ,  ( 4 , 0 )$

**[A1]**

Find the cubic's $y$-intercept by substituting $x = 0$

$( 0 , 8 )$

**[B1]**

For $y = \frac{3}{x^{2}}$, note that $x^{2} > 0$ for all $x \neq 0$, so the graph lies entirely above the $x$-axis in two branches, with the $y$-axis ($x = 0$) and the $x$-axis as asymptotes; draw it on the same diagram as the cubic

![Sketch of a positive cubic and the reciprocal curve y = 3 / x ^2 on the same diagram. The cubic crosses the x-axis at (-2, 0), (1, 0) and (4, 0) and the y-axis at (0, 8). The reciprocal curve has two branches, both above the x-axis, approaching the y-axis as a vertical asymptote and the x-axis as a horizontal asymptote. The two graphs cross three *, twice on the left branch and once on the far right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-maths-20-pure-3/algebra-and-functions/polynomials/assets/004-sketch-of-a-positive-cubic-and-the-reciprocal-cu.png)

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Factorising the cubic $x^{3} - 3 x^{2} - 6 x + 8$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct cubic crossings $( - 2 , 0 )$, $( 1 , 0 )$ and $( 4 , 0 )$, with a correct positive-cubic shape.
> 
> **B1**: The $y$-intercept $( 0 , 8 )$ labelled.
> 
> **B1**: A correct $y = \frac{3}{x^{2}}$: two branches, both above the $x$-axis, with the $y$-axis and $x$-axis as asymptotes, drawn on the same diagram.

parts.problemMd:
Write down the number of solutions to the equation

$x^{5} - 3 x^{4} - 6 x^{3} + 8 x^{2} = 3$.
parts.solutionMd:
Divide both sides by $x^{2}$; this is valid because $x = 0$ is not a solution (the left-hand side would be $0$, not $3$)

$x^{3} - 3 x^{2} - 6 x + 8 = \frac{3}{x^{2}}$

The two sides are exactly the two graphs from part (a)

![Sketch of a positive cubic and the reciprocal curve y = 3 / x ^2 on the same diagram. The cubic crosses the x-axis at (-2, 0), (1, 0) and (4, 0) and the y-axis at (0, 8). The reciprocal curve has two branches, both above the x-axis, approaching the y-axis as a vertical asymptote and the x-axis as a horizontal asymptote. The two graphs cross three *, twice on the left branch and once on the far right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-maths-20-pure-3/algebra-and-functions/polynomials/assets/004-sketch-of-a-positive-cubic-and-the-reciprocal-cu.png)

The number of solutions is the number of times those graphs cross

$3$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $3$, following from a correct part (a) sketch. The count follows through from the candidate's own diagram; award the mark if their sketch clearly shows that many intersections and the reasoning (divide by $x^{2}$, read off the graphs) is sound, even if their graph is slightly inaccurate.

parts.problemMd: Factorise completely $x^{5} y - x y^{5}$.
parts.solutionMd:
Every term has a common factor of $x y$, so take that out first

$x^{5} y - x y^{5} = x y ( x^{4} - y^{4} )$

**[M1]**

$x^{4} - y^{4}$ is a difference of two squares, $( x^{2} )^{2} - ( y^{2} )^{2}$

$= x y ( x^{2} - y^{2} ) ( x^{2} + y^{2} )$

**[A1]**

$x^{2} - y^{2}$ is itself a difference of two squares; $x^{2} + y^{2}$ does not factorise over the reals, so leave it

$x y ( x - y ) ( x + y ) ( x^{2} + y^{2} )$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Taking out the common factor $x y$ to reach $x y ( x^{4} - y^{4} )$.
> 
> **A1**: One correct difference-of-squares step, reaching $x y ( x^{2} - y^{2} ) ( x^{2} + y^{2} )$.
> 
> **A1**: Fully factorised $x y ( x - y ) ( x + y ) ( x^{2} + y^{2} )$, factors in any order. The $x^{2} + y^{2}$ must be present and left unfactorised, since it has no real factors, so "completely" means stopping there. Splitting $x^{2} + y^{2}$ further loses this mark.

parts.problemMd:
$\text{f} ( x ) = 3 x^{4} + x^{3} - 12 x^{2} - 49 x - 15$

Show that $\text{f} ( x ) = ( 3 x + 1 ) ( a x^{3} + b x^{2} + c x + d )$ where $a , b , c$ and $d$ are constants to be found.
parts.solutionMd:
Since $( 3 x + 1 )$ is a factor, write $\text{f} ( x )$ as $( 3 x + 1 )$ multiplied by an unknown cubic

$3 x^{4} + x^{3} - 12 x^{2} - 49 x - 15 = ( 3 x + 1 ) ( a x^{3} + b x^{2} + c x + d )$

**[M1]**

Expanding $( 3 x + 1 ) ( a x^{3} + b x^{2} + c x + d )$ gives $3 a x^{4} + ( 3 b + a ) x^{3} + ( 3 c + b ) x^{2} + ( 3 d + c ) x + d$; compare each coefficient with $\text{f} ( x )$

$3 a = 3 \Rightarrow a = 1$

$3 b + a = 1 \Rightarrow b = 0$

$d = - 15$

$3 d + c = - 49 \Rightarrow c = - 4$

$\text{f} ( x ) = ( 3 x + 1 ) ( x^{3} - 4 x - 15 )$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Writing $\text{f} ( x ) = ( 3 x + 1 ) ( a x^{3} + b x^{2} + c x + d )$ and comparing coefficients, or dividing by $( 3 x + 1 )$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct $a = 1 , b = 0 , c = - 4 , d = - 15$, giving $\text{f} ( x ) = ( 3 x + 1 ) ( x^{3} - 4 x - 15 )$. The $b = 0$ (no $x^{2}$ term in the cubic) must be correct.

parts.problemMd: Given that $( x - 3 )$ is a factor of $\text{f} ( x )$, factorise $\text{f} ( x )$ completely.
parts.solutionMd:
From part (a), $\text{f} ( x ) = ( 3 x + 1 ) ( x^{3} - 4 x - 15 )$. Since $( x - 3 )$ is a factor of $\text{f} ( x )$ but not of $( 3 x + 1 )$, it must be a factor of the cubic; divide the cubic by it, writing the missing $x^{2}$ term as $0 x^{2}$

$x^{3} + 0 x^{2} - 4 x - 15 = ( x - 3 ) ( x^{2} + b x + c )$

**[M1]**

Compare the coefficient of $x^{2}$

$b - 3 = 0 \Rightarrow b = 3$

Compare the constant term

$- 3 c = - 15 \Rightarrow c = 5$

These give the quadratic factor

$x^{3} - 4 x - 15 = ( x - 3 ) ( x^{2} + 3 x + 5 )$

**[A1]**

Check whether the quadratic factorises further by its discriminant

$b^{2} - 4 a c = 3^{2} - 4 ( 1 ) ( 5 ) = 9 - 20 = - 11$

**[M1]**

Since the discriminant is negative, $x^{2} + 3 x + 5$ has no real factors, so the full factorisation is

$\text{f} ( x ) = ( 3 x + 1 ) ( x - 3 ) ( x^{2} + 3 x + 5 )$

**[A1 A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Using $( x - 3 )$ as a factor of the cubic $x^{3} - 4 x - 15$ and dividing (or comparing coefficients).
> 
> **A1**: Correct quadratic factor $x^{2} + 3 x + 5$.
> 
> **M1**: Testing the quadratic factor for further factorisation (discriminant, or an equivalent argument that it has no real roots).
> 
> **A1**: Recognising $x^{2} + 3 x + 5$ is irreducible (negative discriminant), so it is left as a quadratic.
> 
> **A1**: Fully factorised $\text{f} ( x ) = ( 3 x + 1 ) ( x - 3 ) ( x^{2} + 3 x + 5 )$, factors in any order.

parts.problemMd: Hence show that the equation $\text{f} ( x ) = 0$ has exactly $2$ real roots.
parts.solutionMd:
Set the fully factorised form to zero; a product is zero when one of its factors is zero

$( 3 x + 1 ) ( x - 3 ) ( x^{2} + 3 x + 5 ) = 0$

The two linear factors give real roots, while $x^{2} + 3 x + 5 = 0$ has discriminant $- 11 < 0$ from part (b), so contributes none

**Final answer:** **The only real roots are **$x = - \frac{1}{3}$** and **$x = 3$**, so **$\text{f} ( x ) = 0$** has exactly two real roots**

**[B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Identifying the two real roots $x = - \frac{1}{3}$ and $x = 3$ from the linear factors.
> 
> **B1**: Concluding "exactly 2" by explicitly ruling out the quadratic factor via its negative discriminant. Both the two real roots and the reason the quadratic gives none are needed, because this is a "show" part, so the count must be justified, not just stated.

parts.problemMd: Given that $3$ is a root of the equation $2 x^{3} - x^{2} - 11 x - 12 = 0$, prove that the equation has no other real roots.
parts.solutionMd:
Since $3$ is a root, $( x - 3 )$ is a factor; divide the cubic by it, writing it as $( x - 3 )$ multiplied by an unknown quadratic

$2 x^{3} - x^{2} - 11 x - 12 = ( x - 3 ) ( a x^{2} + b x + c )$

**[M1]**

Compare the coefficient of $x^{3}$

$a = 2$

Compare the constant term

$- 3 c = - 12 \Rightarrow c = 4$

Compare the coefficient of $x^{2}$

$- 3 a + b = - 1 \Rightarrow b = 5$

These give the quadratic factor

$2 x^{3} - x^{2} - 11 x - 12 = ( x - 3 ) ( 2 x^{2} + 5 x + 4 )$

**[A1]**

Any further real root must come from $2 x^{2} + 5 x + 4 = 0$; test whether that has real roots using its discriminant

$b^{2} - 4 a c = 5^{2} - 4 ( 2 ) ( 4 ) = 25 - 32 = - 7$

**[M1]**

Since the discriminant is negative, $2 x^{2} + 5 x + 4 = 0$ has no real roots, so the only real root of the cubic is $x = 3$

**Final answer:** **The discriminant is **$- 7 < 0$**, so there are no other real roots**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Using $( x - 3 )$ as a factor and dividing (or comparing coefficients) to reach the quadratic factor.
> 
> **A1**: Correct quadratic factor $2 x^{2} + 5 x + 4$.
> 
> **M1**: Computing the discriminant of the quadratic factor.
> 
> **A1**: Concluding from the negative discriminant that the quadratic has no real roots, so the cubic has no real root other than $x = 3$. A conclusion in words is required here, because this is a "prove" question, so the negative discriminant must be explicitly linked to "no other real roots".

parts.problemMd: Show that $( 9 x^{2} - 4 )$ is a factor of $9 x^{4} - 40 x^{2} + 16$ and hence find all the real solutions to the equation $9 x^{4} - 40 x^{2} + 16 = 0$.
parts.solutionMd:
The expression is a quadratic in $x^{2}$; writing $y = x^{2}$ turns it into $9 y^{2} - 40 y + 16$

$9 x^{4} - 40 x^{2} + 16 = 9 ( x^{2} )^{2} - 40 ( x^{2} ) + 16$

**[M1]**

By the factor theorem in $y$, test $y = \frac{4}{9}$ (that is, $x^{2} = \frac{4}{9}$)

`9\left(\frac{4}{9}\right)^2 - 40\left(\frac{4}{9}\right) + 16 = \frac{16}{9} - \frac{160}{9} + \frac{144}{9} = 0`

**Final answer:** **so **$( 9 x^{2} - 4 )$** is a factor**

**[A1]**

The quadratic in $y$ therefore factorises completely as $( 9 y - 4 ) ( y - 4 )$; replacing $y$ with $x^{2}$ and setting the result equal to zero

$9 x^{4} - 40 x^{2} + 16 = ( 9 x^{2} - 4 ) ( x^{2} - 4 ) = 0$

**[M1]**

Factorise each difference of two squares and solve

$( 3 x - 2 ) ( 3 x + 2 ) ( x - 2 ) ( x + 2 ) = 0$

$x = \frac{2}{3} ,  - \frac{2}{3} ,  2 ,  - 2$

**[A1 A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Recognising the expression as a quadratic in $x^{2}$ (substitution $y = x^{2}$ or working directly in $x^{2}$).
> 
> **A1**: Showing $( 9 x^{2} - 4 )$ is a factor, by evaluating at $x^{2} = \frac{4}{9}$ or by dividing.
> 
> **M1**: Reaching the fully factorised $( 9 x^{2} - 4 ) ( x^{2} - 4 )$, or dividing $9 x^{4} - 40 x^{2} + 16$ by $( 9 x^{2} - 4 )$ to obtain $x^{2} - 4$.
> 
> **A1**: Two correct solutions.
> 
> **A1**: All four solutions $x = \pm \frac{2}{3} , \pm 2$ and no extras. Accept decimals $\pm 0 . 667$.

parts.problemMd: Show that $( a x - 2 )$ is a factor of $3 a x^{2} + ( a - 6 ) x - 2$.
parts.solutionMd:
The factor $( a x - 2 )$ is zero at $x = \frac{2}{a}$, so by the factor theorem evaluate the quadratic there and check it is zero

`3a\left(\frac{2}{a}\right)^2 + (a-6)\left(\frac{2}{a}\right) - 2`

**[M1]**

Work out each term

$= \frac{12}{a} + 2 - \frac{12}{a} - 2 = 0$

**Final answer:** **The value is **$0$**, so **$( a x - 2 )$** is a factor**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Substituting $x = \frac{2}{a}$ into the quadratic (or writing it as $( a x - 2 ) ( 3 x + 1 )$ and expanding to verify).
> 
> **A1**: Reaching $0$ with no errors, which shows $( a x - 2 )$ is a factor. A written conclusion is good practice but is not required for the mark.

parts.problemMd: Given that $x = - \frac{1}{a-4}$ is a root of $3 a x^{2} + ( a - 6 ) x - 2$, find the possible values of $a$.
parts.solutionMd:
Part (a) shows $( a x - 2 )$ is a factor, so divide the quadratic by it to find the other factor

$3 a x^{2} + ( a - 6 ) x - 2 = ( a x - 2 ) ( 3 x + 1 )$

Setting each factor to zero gives the two roots $x = \frac{2}{a}$ and $x = - \frac{1}{3}$

**[M1]**

The given root $x = - \frac{1}{a-4}$ must equal one of these; equating it to $- \frac{1}{3}$

$- \frac{1}{a-4} = - \frac{1}{3}$

$a - 4 = 3 \Rightarrow a = 7$

**[M1]**

Equating it instead to $\frac{2}{a}$

$- \frac{1}{a-4} = \frac{2}{a}$

$- a = 2 ( a - 4 )$

$- a = 2 a - 8$

$3 a = 8 \Rightarrow a = \frac{8}{3}$

Both values give a genuine root of the quadratic, so

**Final answer:** $a = 7$** or **$a = \frac{8}{3}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Dividing by $( a x - 2 )$ to obtain the other factor $( 3 x + 1 )$, and hence the roots $x = \frac{2}{a}$ and $x = - \frac{1}{3}$.
> 
> **M1**: Equating $- \frac{1}{a-4}$ to a root and solving for $a$ (either case).
> 
> **A1**: Both $a = 7$ and $a = \frac{8}{3}$. Giving only $a = 7$ (equating to $- \frac{1}{3}$ alone) is incomplete and scores M1 M1 A0, since $x = - \frac{1}{a-4}$ can equally be the root $\frac{2}{a}$, which gives $a = \frac{8}{3}$.

parts.problemMd:
$z_{1} = 3 + 4 i$ and $z_{2} = 5 - 3 i$

Work out the values of $z_{1} + z_{2}$ and $z_{1} - z_{2}$.
parts.solutionMd:
To add two complex numbers, collect the real parts and the imaginary parts separately

$z_{1} + z_{2} = ( 3 + 4 i ) + ( 5 - 3 i ) = ( 3 + 5 ) + ( 4 - 3 ) i$

$z_{1} + z_{2} = 8 + i$

**[B1]**

Subtract in the same way, taking care with the double negative in the imaginary part

$z_{1} - z_{2} = ( 3 + 4 i ) - ( 5 - 3 i ) = ( 3 - 5 ) + ( 4 - ( - 3 ) ) i$

$z_{1} - z_{2} = - 2 + 7 i$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $z_{1} + z_{2} = 8 + i$. Accept $8 + 1 i$ or the terms written in the other order.
> 
> **B1**: $z_{1} - z_{2} = - 2 + 7 i$. The commonest slip is treating $- ( - 3 i )$ as $- 3 i$, which gives $- 2 + i$ and does not score.

parts.problemMd: On a sketch of an Argand diagram, show the points representing $z_{1}$, $z_{2}$, $z_{1} + z_{2}$ and $z_{1} - z_{2}$.
parts.solutionMd:
On an Argand diagram the real part of a complex number is measured along the horizontal axis and the imaginary part along the vertical axis, so each number is plotted as a point

`z_{1} = 3 + 4i \longrightarrow (3, 4)`

`z_{2} = 5 - 3i \longrightarrow (5, -3)`

Use the two answers from part (a) for the remaining points

`z_{1} + z_{2} = 8 + i \longrightarrow (8, 1)`

`z_{1} - z_{2} = -2 + 7i \longrightarrow (-2, 7)`

Draw axes labelled Re and Im, mark a scale on each, then plot and label the four points

![Argand diagram with a horizontal Re axis and a vertical Im axis, both marked with a scale. Four labelled points are plotted: z1 at (3, 4), z2 at (5, -3), z1 + z2 at (8, 1) and z1 - z2 at (-2, 7)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-maths-20-pure-3/complex-numbers/argand-diagrams/assets/005-argand-diagram-with-a-horizontal-re-axis-and-a-v.png)

**[B1 B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: An Argand diagram with the horizontal axis labelled Re (or "real") and the vertical axis labelled Im (or "imaginary"), and some indication of scale. Marks on the axes, a numbered scale, or correctly labelled points are all enough.
> 
> **B1**: $z_{1}$ plotted at $( 3 , 4 )$ and $z_{2}$ plotted at $( 5 , - 3 )$, both labelled.
> 
> **B1**: $z_{1} + z_{2}$ plotted at $( 8 , 1 )$ and $z_{1} - z_{2}$ plotted at $( - 2 , 7 )$, both labelled. This mark follows through from your answers to part (a), so two points that are correctly plotted from wrong values in part (a) still score.

parts.problemMd: On a separate sketch of an Argand diagram, show $z_{1}$, $z_{2}$, $z_{1} + z_{2}$ and $z_{1} - z_{2}$ as position vectors.
parts.solutionMd:
A complex number can also be shown as the position vector running from the origin to the point representing it, so the four points from part (b) become four arrows that all start at the origin

Draw the arrow to $( 3 , 4 )$ for $z_{1}$ and the arrow to $( 5 , - 3 )$ for $z_{2}$

Draw the arrow to $( 8 , 1 )$ for $z_{1} + z_{2}$

Draw the arrow to $( - 2 , 7 )$ for $z_{1} - z_{2}$

![Argand diagram with a horizontal Re axis and a vertical Im axis, both marked with a scale. Four labelled arrows are drawn from the origin: to (3, 4) labelled z1, to (5, -3) labelled z2, to (8, 1) labelled z1 + z2, and to (-2, 7) labelled z1 - z2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-maths-20-pure-3/complex-numbers/argand-diagrams/assets/006-argand-diagram-with-a-horizontal-re-axis-and-a-v.png)

**[B1 B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $z_{1}$ and $z_{2}$ drawn as arrows from the origin to $( 3 , 4 )$ and $( 5 , - 3 )$, both labelled.
> 
> **B1**: $z_{1} + z_{2}$ drawn as an arrow from the origin to $( 8 , 1 )$ and labelled.
> 
> **B1**: $z_{1} - z_{2}$ drawn as an arrow from the origin to $( - 2 , 7 )$ and labelled. The last two marks follow through from your answers to part (a). Allow dots instead of arrows.

parts.problemMd:
Find the modulus of each of the following, giving your answers as exact values.

(i) $3 - 4 i$

(ii) $1 + i$

(iii) $- 7 i$

(iv) $- \frac{24}{25} + \frac{7}{25} i$

(v) $2$

(vi) $23 i$

(vii) $- 5 - 7 i$

(viii) $- 15$
parts.solutionMd:
The modulus of $z = a + b i$ is its distance from the origin on an Argand diagram, so square the real part, square the imaginary part, add, and take the positive square root

(i)

Substitute $a = 3$ and $b = - 4$

`|3 - 4i| = \sqrt{3^{2} + (-4)^{2}} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = \sqrt{25}`

`|3 - 4i| = 5`

(ii)

Substitute $a = 1$ and $b = 1$

`|1 + i| = \sqrt{1^{2} + 1^{2}} = \sqrt{2}`

`|1 + i| = \sqrt{2}`

**[B1]**

(iii)

A pure imaginary number has real part 0

`|-7i| = \sqrt{0^{2} + (-7)^{2}} = \sqrt{49}`

`|-7i| = 7`

(iv) Substitute the two fractions and put them over a common denominator

`\left|-\frac{24}{25} + \frac{7}{25}i\right| = \sqrt{\left(-\frac{24}{25}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{7}{25}\right)^{2}} = \sqrt{\frac{576}{625} + \frac{49}{625}}`

$= \sqrt{\frac{625}{625}} = \sqrt{1}$

`\left|-\frac{24}{25} + \frac{7}{25}i\right| = 1`

**[B1]**

(v) A real number has imaginary part 0

`|2| = \sqrt{2^{2} + 0^{2}} = \sqrt{4}`

`|2| = 2`

(vi) Another pure imaginary number

`|23i| = \sqrt{0^{2} + 23^{2}} = \sqrt{529}`

`|23i| = 23`

**[B1]**

(vii) Both parts are negative, but squaring makes both contributions positive

`|-5 - 7i| = \sqrt{(-5)^{2} + (-7)^{2}} = \sqrt{25 + 49}`

`|-5 - 7i| = \sqrt{74}`

(viii) A negative real number still has a positive modulus

`|-15| = \sqrt{(-15)^{2} + 0^{2}} = \sqrt{225}`

`|-15| = 15`

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Both $5$ and $\sqrt{2}$ correct.
> 
> **B1**: Both $7$ and $1$ correct.
> 
> **B1**: Both $2$ and $23$ correct.
> 
> **B1**: Both $\sqrt{74}$ and $15$ correct.
> 
> Each mark needs both of its answers right. The question asks for exact values, so $\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{74}$ must be left in surd form and decimals such as $1 . 41$ or $8 . 60$ do not score. A modulus is a distance, so it is never negative: answers of $- 7$, $- 15$ or $- 5 - 7 i$ do not score. Working is not required, and a correct answer alone earns the mark.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows how the principal argument of a complex number $z$, the argument lying in the interval $- π < \mathrm{arg} z \leq π$, is obtained from the acute angle $θ$ in each quadrant.

![Diagram of an Argand diagram divided into four quadrants, showing that the principal argument equals theta in the first quadrant, pi minus theta in the second, minus pi plus theta in the third and minus theta in the fourth, with the positive real axis at 0 and the positive imaginary axis at pi over 2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-maths-20-pure-3/complex-numbers/argand-diagrams/assets/004-diagram-of-an-argand-diagram-divided-into-four-q.png)

Write down the principal arguments of

(i) $5 i$

(ii) $3$

(iii) $- 7$

(iv) $- 4 i$
parts.solutionMd:
Each of these four numbers lies on an axis, so the argument can be read straight off the Argand diagram without any calculation

(i)

$5 i$ lies on the positive imaginary axis, a quarter turn anticlockwise from the positive real axis

$\mathrm{arg} ( 5 i ) = \frac{π}{2}$

(ii)

$3$ lies on the positive real axis, which is where arguments are measured from

$\mathrm{arg} ( 3 ) = 0$

**[B1]**

(iii)

$- 7$ lies on the negative real axis, a half turn from the positive real axis. The principal interval is $- π < \mathrm{arg} z \leq π$, so this takes the value $π$ rather than $- π$

$\mathrm{arg} ( - 7 ) = π$

(iv) $- 4 i$ lies on the negative imaginary axis, a quarter turn clockwise, so the argument is negative

$\mathrm{arg} ( - 4 i ) = - \frac{π}{2}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Both $\frac{π}{2}$ and $0$ correct.
> 
> **B1**: Both $π$ and $- \frac{π}{2}$ correct.
> 
> Each mark needs both of its answers right. No working is expected here. Answers must lie in the principal interval $- π < \mathrm{arg} z \leq π$: for $- 7$ accept $π$ only, since $- π$ is excluded from the interval, and for $- 4 i$ accept $- \frac{π}{2}$ but not $\frac{3π}{2}$. Answers in degrees do not score.

parts.problemMd:
Find the principal arguments of the following complex numbers, giving your answers as exact values.

(i) $2 + 2 i$

(ii) $\sqrt{3} - i$

(iii) $- 4 + 4 \sqrt{3} i$

(iv) $- \frac{7}{2} - \frac{7}{2} i$
parts.solutionMd:
For a number not on an axis, find the acute angle $θ$ that its position vector makes with the real axis using `\theta = \tan^{-1}\left|\frac{b}{a}\right|`, then adjust according to the quadrant

(i)

Both parts are positive, so $2 + 2 i$ is in the first quadrant and the argument is $θ$ itself

`\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2}{2}\right) = \tan^{-1}(1) = \frac{\pi}{4}`

$\mathrm{arg} ( 2 + 2 i ) = \frac{π}{4}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

The real part is positive and the imaginary part negative, so $\sqrt{3} - i$ is in the fourth quadrant and the argument is $- θ$

`\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = \frac{\pi}{6}`

$\mathrm{arg} ( \sqrt{3} - i ) = - \frac{π}{6}$

**[B1]**

(iii)

The real part is negative and the imaginary part positive, so $- 4 + 4 \sqrt{3} i$ is in the second quadrant and the argument is $π - θ$

`\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{4}\right) = \tan^{-1}(\sqrt{3}) = \frac{\pi}{3}`

$π - θ = π - \frac{π}{3}$

$\mathrm{arg} ( - 4 + 4 \sqrt{3} i ) = \frac{2π}{3}$

**[B1]**

(iv) Both parts are negative, so $- \frac{7}{2} - \frac{7}{2} i$ is in the third quadrant and the argument is $- π + θ$

`\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{7/2}{7/2}\right) = \tan^{-1}(1) = \frac{\pi}{4}`

$- π + θ = - π + \frac{π}{4}$

`\arg\left(-\frac{7}{2} - \frac{7}{2}i\right) = -\frac{3\pi}{4}`

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $\frac{π}{4}$
> 
> **B1**: $- \frac{π}{6}$
> 
> **B1**: $\frac{2π}{3}$
> 
> **B1**: $- \frac{3π}{4}$
> 
> The question asks for exact values, so answers must be in terms of $π$ and a decimal such as $0 . 785$ does not score. All four answers must lie in $- π < \mathrm{arg} z \leq π$, so $\frac{7π}{4}$ for (ii), $\frac{5π}{4}$ for (iv) and similar out-of-interval equivalents do not score. Answers in degrees do not score. The commonest error is quoting the acute angle $θ$ without the quadrant adjustment, which gives $\frac{π}{3}$ in (iii) and $\frac{π}{4}$ in (iv).

parts.problemMd:
Find the principal arguments of the following complex numbers, giving your answers correct to 3 significant figures.

(i) $3 + 4 i$

(ii) $- 8 - 15 i$

(iii) $12 - 5 i$

(iv) $- \frac{7}{25} + \frac{24}{25} i$
parts.solutionMd:
Use the same method, but this time the acute angle does not come out as a neat multiple of $π$, so work in radians and round only at the end

(i)

Both parts are positive, so $3 + 4 i$ is in the first quadrant and the argument is $θ$

`\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{4}{3}\right) = 0.927295\ldots`

$\mathrm{arg} ( 3 + 4 i ) = 0 . 927$

**[B1]**

(ii)

Both parts are negative, so $- 8 - 15 i$ is in the third quadrant and the argument is $- π + θ$

`\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{15}{8}\right) = 1.080839\ldots`

$- π + θ = - π + 1 . 080839 \dots = - 2 . 060753 \dots$

$\mathrm{arg} ( - 8 - 15 i ) = - 2 . 06$

**[B1]**

(iii)

The real part is positive and the imaginary part negative, so $12 - 5 i$ is in the fourth quadrant and the argument is $- θ$

`\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{5}{12}\right) = 0.394791\ldots`

$\mathrm{arg} ( 12 - 5 i ) = - 0 . 395$

**[B1]**

(iv) The real part is negative and the imaginary part positive, so this number is in the second quadrant and the argument is $π - θ$

`\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{24/25}{7/25}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{24}{7}\right) = 1.287002\ldots`

$π - θ = π - 1 . 287002 \dots = 1 . 854590 \dots$

`\arg\left(-\frac{7}{25} + \frac{24}{25}i\right) = 1.85`

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Answers which round to $0 . 927$
> 
> **B1**: Answers which round to $- 2 . 06$
> 
> **B1**: Answers which round to $- 0 . 395$
> 
> **B1**: Answers which round to $1 . 85$
> 
> Answers are required in radians correct to 3 significant figures, and answers in degrees do not score. Do not round the acute angle before adjusting for the quadrant, since rounding early can shift the final digit. All four answers must lie in $- π < \mathrm{arg} z \leq π$, so $4 . 22$ in place of $- 2 . 06$ and $5 . 89$ in place of $- 0 . 395$ do not score. As in part (b), quoting the acute angle without the quadrant adjustment is the commonest error.

parts.problemMd:
The complex number $z$ is such that $z = ( 7 - p ) + ( 1 + 7 p ) i$, where $p$ is a real constant.

Show that `|z| = \sqrt{50 + 50p^{2}}`.
parts.solutionMd:
The modulus is the square root of the sum of the squares of the real and imaginary parts, so square each part and add

`|z|^{2} = (7 - p)^{2} + (1 + 7p)^{2}`

**[M1]**

Expand both brackets in full

$= ( 49 - 14 p + p^{2} ) + ( 1 + 14 p + 49 p^{2} )$

Collect like terms, noting that the two terms in $p$ cancel

$= 50 + 50 p^{2}$

Take the positive square root, since a modulus is never negative

`|z| = \sqrt{50 + 50p^{2}}`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Squaring both the real part $7 - p$ and the imaginary part $1 + 7 p$ and adding them. Award this for the correct structure even if a bracket is later expanded wrongly.
> 
> **A1**: Both brackets expanded correctly and simplified to $50 + 50 p^{2}$, leading to the printed result. Because the answer is given, the expansion must be visible and the two $14 p$ terms must be seen to cancel. A bare statement of the result scores nothing.

parts.problemMd: Given that `|z| = 10`, find the two possible values of $p$.
parts.solutionMd:
Set the expression from part (a) equal to 10 and square both sides to clear the root

$\sqrt{50+50p^{2}} = 10$

$50 + 50 p^{2} = 100$

**[M1]**

Rearrange to make $p^{2}$ the subject

$50 p^{2} = 50$

$p^{2} = 1$

Take the square root, remembering both signs

**Final answer:** $p = 1$** or **$p = - 1$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Equating $\sqrt{50+50p^{2}}$ to 10 and squaring to reach a correct equation in $p^{2}$.
> 
> **A1**: Both $p = 1$ and $p = - 1$. Only one value scores nothing for this mark, since the question asks for two, and $p = \pm 1$ is accepted as a single statement of both.

parts.problemMd: For each of the values of $p$ found in part (b), find the argument of the corresponding complex number $z$, giving your answers correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
Substitute each value of $p$ back into $z$ to see which complex number it produces

Taking $p = 1$ first

$z = ( 7 - 1 ) + ( 1 + 7 ) i = 6 + 8 i$

Both parts are positive, so this lies in the first quadrant and the argument is the acute angle itself

`\arg z = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{8}{6}\right) = 0.927295\ldots`

$\mathrm{arg} z = 0 . 927$

**[B1]**

Now take $p = - 1$

$z = ( 7 + 1 ) + ( 1 - 7 ) i = 8 - 6 i$

The real part is positive and the imaginary part negative, so this lies in the fourth quadrant and the argument is the negative of the acute angle

`\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{6}{8}\right) = 0.643501\ldots`

$\mathrm{arg} z = - 0 . 644$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Answers which round to $0 . 927$, from $p = 1$ giving $z = 6 + 8 i$.
> 
> **B1**: Answers which round to $- 0 . 644$, from $p = - 1$ giving $z = 8 - 6 i$. The negative sign is needed: $0 . 644$ on its own does not score.
> 
> Answers are in radians correct to 3 significant figures, and answers in degrees do not score. Both marks follow through from your values of $p$ in part (b). Do not round before adjusting for the quadrant.

parts.problemMd: Given also that the point representing $z$ lies in the fourth quadrant of the Argand diagram, write down the value of $p$.
parts.solutionMd:
In the fourth quadrant the real part is positive and the imaginary part is negative, which of the two numbers in part (c) is true only for $8 - 6 i$

$p = - 1$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $p = - 1$. No working is expected here, and a correct answer alone scores. A negative argument in part (c) is equally acceptable as the justification. $p = 1$ gives $6 + 8 i$, which lies in the first quadrant, and does not score.

parts.problemMd:
A complex number $z$ may be written in modulus-argument form as

$z = r ( \mathrm{cos} θ + i \mathrm{sin} θ )$

where `r = |z|` and $θ = \mathrm{arg} z$.

Express the complex number $- 5 + 12 i$ in modulus-argument form. Give $θ$ in radians correct to 3 significant figures, in the interval $- π < θ \leq π$.
parts.solutionMd:
The value of $r$ is the modulus, so square the real and imaginary parts, add, and take the positive square root

`r = |-5 + 12i| = \sqrt{(-5)^{2} + 12^{2}} = \sqrt{25 + 144} = \sqrt{169}`

$r = 13$

**[B1]**

The value of $θ$ is the argument, so start from the acute angle the position vector makes with the real axis

`\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{12}{5}\right) = 1.176005\ldots`

The real part is negative and the imaginary part positive, so $- 5 + 12 i$ lies in the second quadrant and the argument is $π$ minus that acute angle

$θ = π - 1 . 176005 \dots = 1 . 965587 \dots$

**[M1]**

Round to 3 significant figures and substitute both values into the form

$- 5 + 12 i = 13 ( \mathrm{cos} 1 . 97 + i \mathrm{sin} 1 . 97 )$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $r = 13$.
> 
> **M1**: A correct method for the argument, meaning `\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{12}{5}\right)` or `\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{12}{-5}\right)` together with a quadrant adjustment that places the angle in the second quadrant. Quoting `\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{12}{5}\right) = 1.18` with no adjustment does not score.
> 
> **A1**: The full form $13 ( \mathrm{cos} 1 . 97 + i \mathrm{sin} 1 . 97 )$, with $θ$ an answer which rounds to $1 . 97$. Both the modulus and the argument must appear in the form for this mark, so a correct $r$ and $θ$ listed separately without being assembled does not score. Accept the equivalent exponential form $13 e^{1.97i}$.

parts.problemMd:
A complex number $z$ has modulus 14 and argument $- \frac{π}{6}$.

Express $z$ in the form $a + b i$, where $a$ and $b$ are real numbers given as exact values.
parts.solutionMd:
Substitute $r = 14$ and $θ = - \frac{π}{6}$ into the modulus-argument form, then multiply out the bracket so the real and imaginary parts separate

`z = 14\left(\cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right) + i\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)`

`z = 14\cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right) + \left(14\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)i`

**[M1]**

Use the exact values `\cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}` and `\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\frac{1}{2}`

`z = 14 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \left(14 \times \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\right)i`

$z = 7 \sqrt{3} - 7 i$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Substituting $r = 14$ and $θ = - \frac{π}{6}$ into $r \mathrm{cos} θ + ( r \mathrm{sin} θ ) i$, or equivalent. Award this even if an exact trigonometric value is then misquoted.
> 
> **A1**: $7 \sqrt{3} - 7 i$. The question asks for exact values, so $12 . 1 - 7 i$ does not score. A positive imaginary part, from using $\mathrm{sin} \frac{π}{6}$ instead of `\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)`, does not score.

parts.problemMd:
Explain why each of the following is not in modulus-argument form.

(i) `z_{1} = -4\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{4} + i\sin\frac{\pi}{4}\right)`

(ii) `z_{2} = 5\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{3} - i\sin\frac{\pi}{3}\right)`

(iii) `z_{3} = 7\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{6} + i\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)`
parts.solutionMd:
In each case compare what is written against the required form $r ( \mathrm{cos} θ + i \mathrm{sin} θ )$, where $r$ is the modulus and the same $θ$ appears in both trigonometric terms

(i)

The number in front of the bracket has to be the modulus $r$

**Final answer:** **A modulus is a distance, so it can never be negative, and **$- 4$** cannot be the modulus of **$z_{1}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

The required form has a plus sign between the two terms inside the bracket

**Final answer:** **The sign in front of **$i \mathrm{sin} \frac{π}{3}$** is a minus, and modulus-argument form must have **$+ i \mathrm{sin} θ$

**[B1]**

(iii)

The same angle $θ$ must appear in both the cosine and the sine

**Final answer:** **The two angles **$\frac{π}{6}$** and **$- \frac{π}{6}$** are different, so they cannot both be the argument of **$z_{3}$

**[B1]**

Each number can be rewritten correctly by working out its actual modulus and argument

`z_{1} = 4\left(\cos\left(-\frac{3\pi}{4}\right) + i\sin\left(-\frac{3\pi}{4}\right)\right)`

`z_{2} = 5\left(\cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{3}\right) + i\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\right)`

`z_{3} = 7\left(\cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right) + i\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)`

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: For (i), a reason identifying that the modulus cannot be negative. Accept any wording carrying that idea, such as "the modulus is a distance so it must be positive" or "$r$ cannot be $- 4$".
> 
> **B1**: For (ii), a reason identifying the minus sign before $i \mathrm{sin} θ$, where the form requires a plus.
> 
> **B1**: For (iii), a reason identifying that the angle in the cosine and the angle in the sine are different, so there is no single argument.
> 
> Each mark is for the reason, not for a corrected version of the number, so rewriting the number in correct form without saying what was wrong does not score. Only one valid reason is needed per part.

parts.problemMd:
For two complex numbers $z_{1}$ and $z_{2}$,

`|z_{1}z_{2}| = |z_{1}||z_{2}|`

$\mathrm{arg} ( z_{1} z_{2} ) = \mathrm{arg} ( z_{1} ) + \mathrm{arg} ( z_{2} )$

`\left|\frac{z_{1}}{z_{2}}\right| = \frac{|z_{1}|}{|z_{2}|}`

`\arg\left(\frac{z_{1}}{z_{2}}\right) = \arg(z_{1}) - \arg(z_{2})`

Use these results to work out the following, giving your answers in modulus-argument form.

(i) `5\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{3} + i\sin\frac{\pi}{3}\right) \times 4\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{2} + i\sin\frac{\pi}{2}\right)`

(ii) `12\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{2} + i\sin\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \div 3\left(\cos\frac{3\pi}{4} + i\sin\frac{3\pi}{4}\right)`

(iii) `\sqrt{3}\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{6} + i\sin\frac{\pi}{6}\right) \times \sqrt{6}\left(\cos\left(-\frac{3\pi}{4}\right) + i\sin\left(-\frac{3\pi}{4}\right)\right)`

(iv) $\frac{6.25(\mathrm{cos}3.05+i\mathrm{sin}3.05)}{0.5(\mathrm{cos}1.42+i\mathrm{sin}1.42)}$
parts.solutionMd:
Each number is already in modulus-argument form, so read off its modulus and argument, then multiply or divide the moduli and add or subtract the arguments

(i)

Multiply the moduli, then add the arguments

$5 \times 4 = 20$

$\frac{π}{3} + \frac{π}{2} = \frac{2π}{6} + \frac{3π}{6} = \frac{5π}{6}$

`20\left(\cos\frac{5\pi}{6} + i\sin\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)`

**[B1]**

(ii)

Divide the moduli, then subtract the arguments

$12 \div 3 = 4$

$\frac{π}{2} - \frac{3π}{4} = \frac{2π}{4} - \frac{3π}{4} = - \frac{π}{4}$

`4\left(\cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\right) + i\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right)`

**[B1]**

(iii)

Multiply the moduli, simplifying the surd

$\sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{6} = \sqrt{18} = 3 \sqrt{2}$

Add the arguments, taking care with the negative one

`\frac{\pi}{6} + \left(-\frac{3\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{2\pi}{12} - \frac{9\pi}{12} = -\frac{7\pi}{12}`

`3\sqrt{2}\left(\cos\left(-\frac{7\pi}{12}\right) + i\sin\left(-\frac{7\pi}{12}\right)\right)`

**[B1]**

(iv) This one is written as a fraction, so divide the moduli and subtract the arguments

$6 . 25 \div 0 . 5 = 12 . 5$

$3 . 05 - 1 . 42 = 1 . 63$

$12 . 5 ( \mathrm{cos} 1 . 63 + i \mathrm{sin} 1 . 63 )$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: `20\left(\cos\frac{5\pi}{6} + i\sin\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)`
> 
> **B1**: `4\left(\cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\right) + i\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right)`
> 
> **B1**: `3\sqrt{2}\left(\cos\left(-\frac{7\pi}{12}\right) + i\sin\left(-\frac{7\pi}{12}\right)\right)`
> 
> **B1**: $12 . 5 ( \mathrm{cos} 1 . 63 + i \mathrm{sin} 1 . 63 )$
> 
> Each answer must be assembled into modulus-argument form, so a correct modulus and argument written separately does not score. In (iii) the modulus should be simplified to $3 \sqrt{2}$, although $\sqrt{18}$ is condoned. Accept the equivalent exponential forms, for example $20 e^{\frac{5π}{6}i}$. All four arguments already lie in $- π < θ \leq π$, and equivalent arguments differing by $2 π$ are accepted.

parts.problemMd:
On an Argand diagram, sketch the locus of points for which

`|z - (1 - 3i)| = 4`
parts.solutionMd:
The modulus `|z - z_{1}|` measures the distance from the fixed point $z_{1}$ to $z$, so this equation says that $z$ stays a fixed distance from one point

Compare the equation with `|z - z_{1}| = k` to read off the fixed point and the distance

$z_{1} = 1 - 3 i$

$k = 4$

So the locus is a circle of radius 4 centred at the point representing $1 - 3 i$, which is $( 1 , - 3 )$

The four points directly above, below, left and right of the centre make the circle easy to place

$1 + i$

$1 - 7 i$

$- 3 - 3 i$

$5 - 3 i$

![Argand diagram with Re and Im axes marked with an integer scale, showing a circle of radius 4 centred at the point 1 minus 3i. The centre is marked and labelled, and the points 1 plus i, 1 minus 7i, minus 3 minus 3i and 5 minus 3i are labelled on the circle](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-maths-20-pure-3/complex-numbers/argand-diagrams/assets/001-argand-diagram-with-re-and-im-axes-marked-with-a.png)

**[B1 B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A circle drawn, with its centre not at the origin.
> 
> **B1**: The centre in the correct place, at the point representing $1 - 3 i$. There must be some indication of scale for this mark, so mark the centre with its coordinates, label points on the circle, or number the axes.
> 
> **B1**: A radius of 4, consistent with the scale you have used.
> 
> The axes should be labelled Re and Im, or real and imaginary. A freehand circle is fine provided it is recognisably circular and its centre and radius are clear.

parts.problemMd:
Use your sketch from part (a) to write down a complex number $z$ satisfying each of the following.

(i) `|z - (1 - 3i)| < 4`

(ii) `|z - (1 - 3i)| > 4`
parts.solutionMd:
![Argand diagram with Re and Im axes marked with an integer scale, showing a circle of radius 4 centred at the point 1 minus 3i. The centre is marked and labelled, and the points 1 plus i, 1 minus 7i, minus 3 minus 3i and 5 minus 3i are labelled on the circle](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-maths-20-pure-3/complex-numbers/argand-diagrams/assets/001-argand-diagram-with-re-and-im-axes-marked-with-a.png)

The left-hand side is the distance from $1 - 3 i$ to $z$, so each inequality asks for a point at less than, or more than, distance 4 from the centre

(i)

Less than 4 means inside the circle, so choose any point in the shaded interior, for example the point $( - 1 , - 1 )$

$z = - 1 - i$

**[B1]**

(ii)

More than 4 means outside the circle, so choose any point beyond it, for example the point $( 4 , 3 )$

$z = 4 + 3 i$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Any complex number lying strictly inside the circle, meaning any $z$ with `|z - (1 - 3i)| < 4`. The answer given here is $- 1 - i$, but there are infinitely many correct answers and any valid one scores.
> 
> **B1**: Any complex number lying strictly outside the circle, meaning any $z$ with `|z - (1 - 3i)| > 4`. The answer given here is $4 + 3 i$, and again any valid one scores.
> 
> No working is expected here. A point on the circle itself, such as $5 - 3 i$, satisfies neither inequality and does not score. The answer must be a complex number, so a pair of coordinates such as $( - 1 , - 1 )$ is condoned only if it is clear which complex number is meant.

parts.problemMd:
On an Argand diagram, sketch the locus of points for which

`|z - (3 + 5i)| = |z - (-3 - i)|`
parts.solutionMd:
Each side measures a distance, so the equation says $z$ is the same distance from $3 + 5 i$ as it is from $- 3 - i$

Compare with `|z - z_{1}| = |z - z_{2}|` to read off the two fixed points

$z_{1} = 3 + 5 i$

$z_{2} = - 3 - i$

Points equidistant from two fixed points form the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them, so find the midpoint of that segment
