$\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}  \text{cos}  θ - \frac{1}{2}  \text{sin}  θ \equiv \text{cos}  \frac{π}{6}  \text{cos}  θ - \text{sin}  \frac{π}{6}  \text{sin}  θ$

**[M1]**

This is the expansion of $\text{cos}  ( A + B )$ read backwards

`\equiv \text{cos} \left( \theta + \dfrac{\pi}{6} \right)`

**[A1]**

Treat the second bracket the same way

$\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}  \text{sin}  θ + \frac{1}{2}  \text{cos}  θ \equiv \text{cos}  \frac{π}{6}  \text{sin}  θ + \text{sin}  \frac{π}{6}  \text{cos}  θ$

**[M1]**

This time it is the expansion of $\text{sin}  ( A + B )$

`\equiv \text{sin} \left( \theta + \dfrac{\pi}{6} \right)`

**[A1]**

Substitute both back into the original expression, restating the left hand side in full

`\dfrac{1}{\left( \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \; \text{cos} \; \theta - \dfrac{1}{2} \; \text{sin} \; \theta \right)^2} + \dfrac{1}{\left( \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \; \text{sin} \; \theta + \dfrac{1}{2} \; \text{cos} \; \theta \right)^2} \equiv \dfrac{1}{\text{cos}^2 \left( \theta + \dfrac{\pi}{6} \right)} + \dfrac{1}{\text{sin}^2 \left( \theta + \dfrac{\pi}{6} \right)}`

Combine over a common denominator

`\equiv \dfrac{\text{sin}^2 \left( \theta + \dfrac{\pi}{6} \right) + \text{cos}^2 \left( \theta + \dfrac{\pi}{6} \right)}{\text{cos}^2 \left( \theta + \dfrac{\pi}{6} \right) \text{sin}^2 \left( \theta + \dfrac{\pi}{6} \right)}`

**[M1]**

The numerator is $1$ by the Pythagorean identity, and the denominator is a single square

`\equiv \dfrac{1}{\left( \text{cos} \left( \theta + \dfrac{\pi}{6} \right) \text{sin} \left( \theta + \dfrac{\pi}{6} \right) \right)^2}`

**[A1]**

The product of a sine and cosine of the same angle is half the sine of the double angle, so use $\text{sin}  2 A \equiv 2  \text{sin}  A  \text{cos}  A$ with $A = θ + \frac{π}{6}$

`\equiv \dfrac{1}{\left( \dfrac{1}{2} \; \text{sin} \left( 2\theta + \dfrac{\pi}{3} \right) \right)^2}`

**[M1]**

Square the bracket, so the $\frac{1}{4}$ in the denominator becomes a factor of $4$

`\equiv \dfrac{4}{\text{sin}^2 \left( 2\theta + \dfrac{\pi}{3} \right)}`

**[A1]**

Use the definition $\text{cosec}  A = \frac{1}{\text{sin}A}$

`\equiv 4 \; \text{cosec}^2 \left( 2\theta + \dfrac{\pi}{3} \right)`

This is the required result

`\dfrac{1}{\left( \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \; \text{cos} \; \theta - \dfrac{1}{2} \; \text{sin} \; \theta \right)^2} + \dfrac{1}{\left( \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \; \text{sin} \; \theta + \dfrac{1}{2} \; \text{cos} \; \theta \right)^2} \equiv 4 \; \text{cosec}^2 \left( 2\theta + \dfrac{\pi}{3} \right)`

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Seeing $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $\frac{1}{2}$ sitting next to a sine and a cosine should make you think of the compound angle formulae running backwards. Exact values of common angles turning up as coefficients is nearly always the setter telling you to compress two terms into one.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct identification of $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $\frac{1}{2}$ as $\text{cos}  \frac{π}{6}$ and $\text{sin}  \frac{π}{6}$ in the first bracket.
> 
> **A1**: First bracket correctly written as `\text{cos} \left( \theta + \dfrac{\pi}{6} \right)`.
> 
> **M1**: The same identification applied to the second bracket.
> 
> **A1**: Second bracket correctly written as `\text{sin} \left( \theta + \dfrac{\pi}{6} \right)`.
> 
> **M1**: Correct combination of the two fractions over a common denominator.
> 
> **A1**: Correct use of the Pythagorean identity to reduce the numerator to $1$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $\text{sin}  2 A \equiv 2  \text{sin}  A  \text{cos}  A$ with $A = θ + \frac{π}{6}$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct squaring to give `\dfrac{4}{\text{sin}^2 \left( 2\theta + \dfrac{\pi}{3} \right)}`.
> 
> **A1**: Correct use of the definition of $\text{cosec}$ to reach the printed result, from full and correct working.
> 
> Writing each bracket in the R form, as `\text{cos} \left( \theta + \dfrac{\pi}{6} \right)` and `\text{sin} \left( \theta + \dfrac{\pi}{6} \right)` found by comparing coefficients, is equally acceptable and earns the first four marks. Because the result is given, the combined fraction and the double angle step must both be visible.

name: Vector Equations of Lines & The Scalar Product

parts.problemMd:
The equation of a line is given in vector form as follows

`\mathbf{r} = 2 \mathbf{i} + 6 \mathbf{j} + t \left(7 \mathbf{i} + 3 \mathbf{j}\right)`

Explain briefly what the vectors $2 i + 6 j$ and $7 i + 3 j$ in the equation above tell us, respectively, about the line.
parts.solutionMd:
Compare the equation with the general vector form of a line

$r = a + t b$

In this form $a$ is the position vector of a point that the line passes through

**Final answer:** $2 i + 6 j$** is the position vector of a point on the line**

**[B1]**

The vector $b$ fixes the direction the line travels in

**Final answer:** $7 i + 3 j$** is a direction vector for the line**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct statement that $2 i + 6 j$ is the position vector of a point on the line. Accept a point the line passes through, or the point $( 2 , 6 )$ lies on the line.
> 
> **B1**: Correct statement that $7 i + 3 j$ gives the direction of the line. Accept a vector parallel to the line, or the line is parallel to $7 i + 3 j$. Describing it as a point on the line does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd: Write down, in vector form, the equation of the line passing through $( 1 , 4 )$ in the same direction as $i + 3 j$.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the vector form of a line, $r = a + s b$, where $a$ is the position vector of a point on the line and $b$ is a direction vector

Write the given point as a position vector

$a = i + 4 j$

**[M1]**

Substitute this and the given direction into the vector form

`\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{i} + 4 \mathbf{j} + s \left(\mathbf{i} + 3 \mathbf{j}\right)`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct identification of $i + 4 j$ as the position vector of a point on the line, together with $i + 3 j$ as the direction vector. This mark is available without $r =$ being written.
> 
> **A1**: Fully correct equation, which must include $r =$. Any letter may be used for the parameter. Column vector form is equally acceptable. Any other point on the line and any non-zero multiple of the direction vector are also accepted, for example `\mathbf{r} = 2 \mathbf{i} + 7 \mathbf{j} + s \left(2 \mathbf{i} + 6 \mathbf{j}\right)`.

parts.problemMd:
A line passes through the two points `A \left(3 , - 2\right)` and `B \left(5 , 7\right)`.

(i) Write down the position vectors $\overset{\rightarrow}{OA}$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{OB}$ of the two points.

(ii) Use the vector relation $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB} = \overset{\rightarrow}{OB} - \overset{\rightarrow}{OA}$ to find the vector $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$.

(iii) Use the answers from (i) and (ii) to write down an equation of the line in vector form.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

A position vector has the coordinates of the point as its components

$\overset{\rightarrow}{OA} = 3 i - 2 j$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{OB} = 5 i + 7 j$

**[B1]**

(ii)

Substitute the two position vectors into the given relation

`\overrightarrow{AB} = \left(5 \mathbf{i} + 7 \mathbf{j}\right) - \left(3 \mathbf{i} - 2 \mathbf{j}\right)`

**[M1]**

Subtract component by component, taking care with the double negative in the $j$ direction

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AB} = 2 i + 9 j$

**[A1]**

(iii)

Use the vector form of a line, $r = a + t b$, taking $\overset{\rightarrow}{OA}$ as the point on the line and $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$ as the direction

`\mathbf{r} = 3 \mathbf{i} - 2 \mathbf{j} + t \left(2 \mathbf{i} + 9 \mathbf{j}\right)`

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Both position vectors correct in part (i). Column vector form is equally acceptable.
> 
> **M1**: Correct substitution into $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB} = \overset{\rightarrow}{OB} - \overset{\rightarrow}{OA}$ in part (ii).
> 
> **A1**: Correct vector $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB} = 2 i + 9 j$. The most common error is $2 i + 5 j$, from subtracting rather than adding in the $j$ direction.
> 
> **B1**: Correct vector equation in part (iii), which must include $r =$. Any letter may be used for the parameter. Starting from $\overset{\rightarrow}{OB}$ instead is equally acceptable, as is any non-zero multiple of the direction vector, for example `\mathbf{r} = 5 \mathbf{i} + 7 \mathbf{j} + t \left(2 \mathbf{i} + 9 \mathbf{j}\right)`. Follow through on an incorrect $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$ from part (ii).

parts.problemMd: Write down, in vector form, the equation of the line through the point `\left(1 , 3 , - 6\right)` in the direction $4 i - j + 2 k$.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the vector form of a line, $r = a + t b$, where $a$ is the position vector of a point on the line and $b$ is a direction vector

Write the given point as a position vector

$a = i + 3 j - 6 k$

**[M1]**

Substitute this and the given direction into the vector form

`\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{i} + 3 \mathbf{j} - 6 \mathbf{k} + t \left(4 \mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} + 2 \mathbf{k}\right)`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct identification of $i + 3 j - 6 k$ as the position vector of a point on the line, together with the given direction vector. Available without $r =$ being written.
> 
> **A1**: Fully correct equation, which must include $r =$. Any parameter letter and column vector form are equally acceptable, as is any non-zero multiple of the direction vector.

parts.problemMd: By first calculating the vectors $\overset{\rightarrow}{OA}$, $\overset{\rightarrow}{OB}$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$, find a vector equation of the line passing through the two points `A \left(1 , 3 , 1\right)` and `B \left(3 , 4 , - 3\right)`.
parts.solutionMd:
Write each point as a position vector

$\overset{\rightarrow}{OA} = i + 3 j + k$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{OB} = 3 i + 4 j - 3 k$

**[B1]**

A direction vector for the line is the displacement from $A$ to $B$, found by subtracting the position vectors

`\overrightarrow{AB} = \overrightarrow{OB} - \overrightarrow{OA} = \left(3 \mathbf{i} + 4 \mathbf{j} - 3 \mathbf{k}\right) - \left(\mathbf{i} + 3 \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}\right)`

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AB} = 2 i + j - 4 k$

**[M1]**

Take $\overset{\rightarrow}{OA}$ as the point on the line and $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$ as the direction, then substitute into $r = a + t b$

`\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{i} + 3 \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k} + t \left(2 \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} - 4 \mathbf{k}\right)`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Both position vectors $\overset{\rightarrow}{OA}$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{OB}$ stated correctly.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$, subtracting the position vector of $A$ from that of $B$, giving $2 i + j - 4 k$. Accept $\overset{\rightarrow}{BA} = - 2 i - j + 4 k$, which is an equally valid direction for the line.
> 
> **A1**: Fully correct equation, which must include $r =$. Either point may be used as the starting point and any non-zero multiple of the direction is accepted, for example `\mathbf{r} = 3 \mathbf{i} + 4 \mathbf{j} - 3 \mathbf{k} + t \left(2 \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} - 4 \mathbf{k}\right)`.

parts.problemMd:
$A$ and $B$ are the points on the line `\mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ - 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} + t \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 4 \\ - 3 \end{pmatrix}` with $t = 1$ and $t = 3$ respectively.

(i) Find the position vectors $\overset{\rightarrow}{OA}$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{OB}$.

(ii) By first finding the vector $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$, calculate the modulus `\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\right|`.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Substitute $t = 1$ into the equation of the line to reach the point $A$

`\overrightarrow{OA} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ - 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} + 1 \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 4 \\ - 3 \end{pmatrix}`

`\overrightarrow{OA} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}`

**[B1]**

Substitute $t = 3$ to reach the point $B$

`\overrightarrow{OB} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ - 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} + 3 \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 4 \\ - 3 \end{pmatrix}`

`\overrightarrow{OB} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 11 \\ - 6 \end{pmatrix}`

**[B1]**

(ii)

Find the displacement from $A$ to $B$ by subtracting the position vectors

`\overrightarrow{AB} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 11 \\ - 6 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 8 \\ - 6 \end{pmatrix}`

**[M1]**

Use the formula for the magnitude of a vector, `\left|x \mathbf{i} + y \mathbf{j} + z \mathbf{k}\right| = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}}`

`\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\right| = \sqrt{0^{2} + 8^{2} + \left(- 6\right)^{2}} = \sqrt{100}`

This square root is exact, so evaluate it

`\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\right| = 10`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct $\overset{\rightarrow}{OA} = 2 i + 3 j$, from substituting $t = 1$.
> 
> **B1**: Correct $\overset{\rightarrow}{OB} = 2 i + 11 j - 6 k$, from substituting $t = 3$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$, subtracting the position vector of $A$ from that of $B$. Accept $\overset{\rightarrow}{BA}$, since the modulus is the same either way. Follow through on incorrect position vectors from part (i).
> 
> **A1**: Correct modulus of $10$. The square root must be evaluated, not left as $\sqrt{100}$. Column vector and component forms are equally acceptable throughout.

parts.problemMd:
Relative to the origin $O$, the points $A$, $B$ and $C$ have position vectors given by

$\overset{\rightarrow}{OA} = 2 i - j + 3 k$, $\overset{\rightarrow}{OB} = i - 2 j + 5 k$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{OC} = 6 i + 3 j + k$

Find $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{AC}$, and calculate `\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\right|` and `\left|\overrightarrow{AC}\right|`.
parts.solutionMd:
A displacement vector is found by subtracting the position vector of the starting point from that of the end point

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AB} = \overset{\rightarrow}{OB} - \overset{\rightarrow}{OA}$

Subtract component by component

`\overrightarrow{AB} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ - 2 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ - 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} - 1 \\ - 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}`

**[M1]**

Apply the same subtraction to find $\overset{\rightarrow}{AC}$

`\overrightarrow{AC} = \begin{pmatrix} 6 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ - 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 4 \\ - 2 \end{pmatrix}`

**[A1]**

Use the formula for the magnitude of a vector, `\left|x \mathbf{i} + y \mathbf{j} + z \mathbf{k}\right| = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}}`

`\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\right| = \sqrt{\left(- 1\right)^{2} + \left(- 1\right)^{2} + 2^{2}}`

Evaluate the square root, leaving the answer exact

`\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\right| = \sqrt{6}`

Apply the same formula to $\overset{\rightarrow}{AC}$

`\left|\overrightarrow{AC}\right| = \sqrt{4^{2} + 4^{2} + \left(- 2\right)^{2}} = \sqrt{36}`

This square root is exact, so simplify it

`\left|\overrightarrow{AC}\right| = 6`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for a displacement vector, subtracting the position vector of the starting point from that of the end point, for either $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$ or $\overset{\rightarrow}{AC}$.
> 
> **A1**: Both $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB} = - i - j + 2 k$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{AC} = 4 i + 4 j - 2 k$ correct. Column vector form is equally acceptable throughout.
> 
> **A1**: Both magnitudes correct, `\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\right| = \sqrt{6}` and `\left|\overrightarrow{AC}\right| = 6`. Accept $2 . 449$ or better for $\sqrt{6}$, though the exact form is preferred since it is carried into part (c).

parts.problemMd:
For two vectors $a = a_{1} i + a_{2} j + a_{3} k$ and $b = b_{1} i + b_{2} j + b_{3} k$, the scalar product `\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}` can be calculated using the formula

`\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = a_{1} b_{1} + a_{2} b_{2} + a_{3} b_{3}`

Calculate the scalar product `\overrightarrow{AB} \cdot \overrightarrow{AC}`.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the formula for the scalar product given in the question, `\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = a_{1} b_{1} + a_{2} b_{2} + a_{3} b_{3}`

`\overrightarrow{AB} \cdot \overrightarrow{AC} = \left(- 1\right)\left(4\right) + \left(- 1\right)\left(4\right) + \left(2\right)\left(- 2\right)`

Evaluate the sum

`\overrightarrow{AB} \cdot \overrightarrow{AC} = - 12`

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct value of $- 12$. The three products may be shown or implied. A positive $12$ does not earn the mark, as the sign carries the information that the angle in part (c) is obtuse.

parts.problemMd:
A defining property of the scalar product of two vectors $a$ and $b$ is

`\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = \left|\mathbf{a}\right| \left|\mathbf{b}\right| \text{cos} \; \theta`

where $θ$ is the angle between the two vectors.

Using this relationship, along with the answers to parts (a) and (b), find the angle between the vectors $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{AC}$.

Give your answer in degrees correct to 1 decimal place.
parts.solutionMd:
Rearrange the given relationship to make $\text{cos}  θ$ the subject

`\text{cos} \; \theta = \dfrac{\overrightarrow{AB} \cdot \overrightarrow{AC}}{\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\right| \left|\overrightarrow{AC}\right|}`

Substitute the scalar product from part (b) and the two magnitudes from part (a)

$\text{cos}  θ = \frac{-12}{6\sqrt{6}} = - \frac{\sqrt{6}}{3}$

**[M1]**

Take the inverse cosine, keeping the unrounded value for the rounding step

`\theta = \text{cos}^{-1} \left(- \dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{3}\right) = 144.7356 \ldots`*°*

Round to 1 decimal place, as the question requires

**Final answer:** $θ = 144 . 7$**° (1 d.p.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct rearrangement to `\text{cos} \; \theta = \dfrac{\overrightarrow{AB} \cdot \overrightarrow{AC}}{\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\right| \left|\overrightarrow{AC}\right|}`, with the scalar product and both magnitudes substituted. Follow through on incorrect values from parts (a) and (b).
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to $144 . 7$ degrees. The unrounded value is $144 . 7356 \dots$. An answer in radians does not earn this mark, since degrees are specified. Subtracting from 180 degrees to give $35 . 3$ degrees does not earn this mark either: the scalar product is negative, so the angle between the two vectors is obtuse.

parts.problemMd:
Two lines $l$ and $m$ have equations `\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} + 3 \mathbf{k} + s \left(\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}\right)` and `\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{i} - 2 \mathbf{j} + 2 \mathbf{k} + t \left(2 \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} + 3 \mathbf{k}\right)` respectively. The two lines intersect at a point $P$.

Explain why, at point $P$, the values of the parameters $s$ and $t$ must satisfy the vector equation

`\begin{pmatrix} 1 + s \\ 1 - s \\ 3 + s \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 + 2 t \\ - 2 + t \\ 2 + 3 t \end{pmatrix}`
parts.solutionMd:
Collect the components of a general point on line $l$

`\mathbf{r} = \left(1 + s\right) \mathbf{i} + \left(1 - s\right) \mathbf{j} + \left(3 + s\right) \mathbf{k}`

Do the same for a general point on line $m$

`\mathbf{r} = \left(1 + 2 t\right) \mathbf{i} + \left(- 2 + t\right) \mathbf{j} + \left(2 + 3 t\right) \mathbf{k}`

**[M1]**

Point $P$ lies on both lines, so it is reached by some value of $s$ on $l$ and some value of $t$ on $m$

*Two vectors are equal only when all three components match*

`\begin{pmatrix} 1 + s \\ 1 - s \\ 3 + s \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 + 2 t \\ - 2 + t \\ 2 + 3 t \end{pmatrix}`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct collection of components for at least one of the two lines, giving a general point in the form `\left(1 + s\right) \mathbf{i} + \left(1 - s\right) \mathbf{j} + \left(3 + s\right) \mathbf{k}` or `\left(1 + 2 t\right) \mathbf{i} + \left(- 2 + t\right) \mathbf{j} + \left(2 + 3 t\right) \mathbf{k}`.
> 
> **A1**: A complete explanation: point $P$ lies on both lines, so its position vector can be written using either equation, and equal vectors have equal components. Because the result is given, the reasoning must be visible.

parts.problemMd: Solve the simultaneous equations $1 + s = 1 + 2 t$ and $1 - s = - 2 + t$, and show that the values found for $s$ and $t$ also satisfy the equation $3 + s = 2 + 3 t$.
parts.solutionMd:
The first equation has $1$ on both sides, so it simplifies immediately

$s = 2 t$

Substitute this into the second equation to leave a single unknown

$1 - 2 t = - 2 + t$

**[M1]**

Collect the terms in $t$

$3 = 3 t$

$t = 1$

Substitute back to find $s$

$s = 2$

**[A1]**

Test these values in the third equation, working out each side separately

$3 + s = 3 + 2 = 5$

$2 + 3 t = 2 + 3 = 5$

*Both sides agree, so the third equation is satisfied*

$5 = 5$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method to reduce the two given equations to a single equation in one parameter. Any valid method is acceptable, including elimination in place of substitution.
> 
> **A1**: Both $t = 1$ and $s = 2$ correct.
> 
> **A1**: Both sides of the third equation evaluated and shown to be equal, with a conclusion. Because the result is given, the evaluation must be shown; asserting that the values work without substituting does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd: Hence, find the coordinates of the point $P$.
parts.solutionMd:
Substitute $s = 2$ into the equation of line $l$ to reach the point of intersection

`\mathbf{r} = \left(1 + 2\right) \mathbf{i} + \left(1 - 2\right) \mathbf{j} + \left(3 + 2\right) \mathbf{k} = 3 \mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} + 5 \mathbf{k}`

The question asks for coordinates, so write the components as a point

`P \left(3 , - 1 , 5\right)`

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct coordinates `\left(3 , - 1 , 5\right)`. Substituting $t = 1$ into the equation of line $m$ is an equally valid route and gives the same point. Accept the answer written as a column vector or in component form, but a position vector including $i$, $j$ and $k$ is not a set of coordinates. Follow through on incorrect parameter values from part (b).

parts.problemMd:
Two lines $l$ and $m$ have equations `\mathbf{r} = 6 \mathbf{i} - 2 \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k} + s \left(\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} - \mathbf{k}\right)` and `\mathbf{r} = 3 \mathbf{i} + 3 \mathbf{j} - 2 \mathbf{k} + t \left(3 \mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}\right)` respectively.

Show that if the two lines intersect, then at the point of intersection the parameters $s$ and $t$ must satisfy the vector equation

`\begin{pmatrix} 6 + s \\ - 2 + s \\ 1 - s \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 + 3 t \\ 3 - t \\ - 2 + t \end{pmatrix}`
parts.solutionMd:
Collect the $i$, $j$ and $k$ components of a general point on line $l$

`\mathbf{r} = \left(6 + s\right) \mathbf{i} + \left(- 2 + s\right) \mathbf{j} + \left(1 - s\right) \mathbf{k}`

Do the same for a general point on line $m$

`\mathbf{r} = \left(3 + 3 t\right) \mathbf{i} + \left(3 - t\right) \mathbf{j} + \left(- 2 + t\right) \mathbf{k}`

**[M1]**

A point of intersection lies on both lines

*The two general points must therefore have equal components*

`\begin{pmatrix} 6 + s \\ - 2 + s \\ 1 - s \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 + 3 t \\ 3 - t \\ - 2 + t \end{pmatrix}`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct collection of components for at least one of the two lines, giving a general point in the form `\left(6 + s\right) \mathbf{i} + \left(- 2 + s\right) \mathbf{j} + \left(1 - s\right) \mathbf{k}` or `\left(3 + 3 t\right) \mathbf{i} + \left(3 - t\right) \mathbf{j} + \left(- 2 + t\right) \mathbf{k}`. Column vector form is equally acceptable.
> 
> **A1**: The two general points equated to give the printed vector equation, together with a statement that a point of intersection lies on both lines and so has equal components. Because the result is given, the reasoning must be visible; simply writing the printed equation down does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd: Solve the simultaneous equations $6 + s = 3 + 3 t$ and $- 2 + s = 3 - t$, and show that the values found for $s$ and $t$ do not also satisfy the equation $1 - s = - 2 + t$.
parts.solutionMd:
Both equations contain a single $s$, so subtracting one from the other eliminates it

`\left(6 + s\right) - \left(- 2 + s\right) = \left(3 + 3 t\right) - \left(3 - t\right)`

Simplify each side

$8 = 4 t$

**[M1]**

Divide by 4 to find the parameter for line $m$

$t = 2$

Substitute this value back into the first equation to find $s$

`6 + s = 3 + 3 \left(2\right)`

$s = 3$

**[A1]**

Test these values in the third equation, working out each side separately

$1 - s = 1 - 3 = - 2$

$- 2 + t = - 2 + 2 = 0$

*The two sides disagree, so the third equation is not satisfied*

$- 2 \neq 0$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method to eliminate one parameter from the two given equations and solve for the other. Any valid method is acceptable, including substitution in place of subtraction.
> 
> **A1**: Both $t = 2$ and $s = 3$ correct.
> 
> **A1**: Both sides of the third equation evaluated and shown to differ, with a conclusion such as $- 2 \neq 0$ or the equation is not satisfied. A bare statement that the values do not work, with no evaluation shown, does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd: What do the results of part (b) tell you about the lines $l$ and $m$?
parts.solutionMd:
Part (b) found the only values that satisfy the first two equations, and they failed the third

*No pair of values for *$s$* and *$t$* satisfies all three equations at once*

**Final answer:** **The lines **$l$** and **$m$** do not intersect**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct statement that the lines do not intersect. Accept "they have no point of intersection" or "there is no point common to both lines". Stating that the lines are skew also earns this mark, since it includes the fact that they do not intersect.

parts.problemMd:
Find the equation of each of these lines in vector form.

The line joining `\left(4 , 1\right)` to `\left(7 , 6\right)`.
parts.solutionMd:
A line through two points needs a direction, which is the displacement from one to the other

`\mathbf{d} = \left(7 \mathbf{i} + 6 \mathbf{j}\right) - \left(4 \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}\right)`

**[M1]**

Subtract component by component

$d = 3 i + 5 j$

**[A1]**

Use the vector form of a line, $r = a + t b$, taking the first point as $a$ and this displacement as $b$

`\mathbf{r} = 4 \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} + t \left(3 \mathbf{i} + 5 \mathbf{j}\right)`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for a direction vector, subtracting the position vector of one point from the other.
> 
> **A1**: Correct direction $3 i + 5 j$. Accept $- 3 i - 5 j$, which points along the same line.
> 
> **A1**: Fully correct equation, which must include $r =$. Either point may be used as the starting point, any letter may be used for the parameter, column vector form is equally acceptable, and any non-zero multiple of the direction is accepted.

parts.problemMd: Find, in vector form, the equation of the line passing through `\left(2 , 5\right)` in the same direction as $2 i + j$.
parts.solutionMd:
Here the direction is given, so only the point needs writing as a position vector

$a = 2 i + 5 j$

**[M1]**

Substitute this and the given direction into $r = a + t b$

`\mathbf{r} = 2 \mathbf{i} + 5 \mathbf{j} + t \left(2 \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}\right)`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct identification of $2 i + 5 j$ as the position vector of a point on the line, together with the given direction. Available without $r =$ being written.
> 
> **A1**: Fully correct equation, which must include $r =$. Any point on the line and any non-zero multiple of the direction are accepted.

parts.problemMd:
Find the equation of each of these lines in vector form.

(i) Through `\left(3 , 1 , - 2\right)` in the direction `\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}`

(ii) Through `\left(2 , 0 , 7\right)` and `\left(5 , 2 , - 3\right)`.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The direction is given, so write the point as a position vector and substitute both into $r = a + t b$

$a = 3 i + j - 2 k$

**[M1]**

The direction has no $i$ component, so the line runs parallel to the $y z$ plane

`\mathbf{r} = 3 \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} - 2 \mathbf{k} + t \left(\mathbf{j} + 5 \mathbf{k}\right)`

**[A1]**

(ii)

Two points are given this time, so start by finding the displacement between them

`\mathbf{d} = \left(5 \mathbf{i} + 2 \mathbf{j} - 3 \mathbf{k}\right) - \left(2 \mathbf{i} + 7 \mathbf{k}\right)`

**[M1]**

Subtract component by component

$d = 3 i + 2 j - 10 k$

**[A1]**

Take the first point as the position vector and this displacement as the direction

`\mathbf{r} = 2 \mathbf{i} + 7 \mathbf{k} + t \left(3 \mathbf{i} + 2 \mathbf{j} - 10 \mathbf{k}\right)`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct identification in (i) of $3 i + j - 2 k$ as the position vector of a point on the line, with the given direction.
> 
> **A1**: Fully correct equation in (i), which must include $r =$. Writing the direction as $0 i + j + 5 k$ or as a column vector is equally acceptable.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method in (ii) for a direction vector, subtracting the position vector of one point from the other.
> 
> **A1**: Correct direction $3 i + 2 j - 10 k$, or its negative.
> 
> **A1**: Fully correct equation in (ii), which must include $r =$. Either point may be used as the starting point and any non-zero multiple of the direction is accepted.

parts.problemMd: Show that the point `\left(- 4 , - 4 , 27\right)` lies on the line found in part (a)(ii).
parts.solutionMd:
If the point is on the line, one value of $t$ must reproduce all three of its components. Use the $i$ component to find the candidate value

$2 + 3 t = - 4$

$t = - 2$

**[M1]**

Substitute this value into the other two components to check they match

`0 + 2 \left(- 2\right) = - 4`

`7 - 10 \left(- 2\right) = 27`

*All three components agree for the same value of *$t$

**Final answer:** **The point lies on the line**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method to find a value of the parameter from one component, giving $t = - 2$. Follow through on an incorrect line from part (a)(ii).
> 
> **A1**: The remaining two components verified for that same value of $t$, with a conclusion. Because the result is given, all three components must be seen to agree; finding $t$ from one component and stopping does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd:
$A$ and $B$ are the points on the line `\mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ - 2 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix} + t \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ - 1 \end{pmatrix}` with $t = 4$ and $t = 7$ respectively.

(i) Find the position vectors $\overset{\rightarrow}{OA}$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{OB}$.

(ii) Find `\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\right|`.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Substitute $t = 4$ into the equation of the line to reach the point $A$

`\overrightarrow{OA} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ - 2 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix} + 4 \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ - 1 \end{pmatrix}`

`\overrightarrow{OA} = \begin{pmatrix} 7 \\ 10 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}`

**[B1]**

Substitute $t = 7$ to reach the point $B$

`\overrightarrow{OB} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ - 2 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix} + 7 \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ - 1 \end{pmatrix}`

`\overrightarrow{OB} = \begin{pmatrix} 10 \\ 19 \\ - 2 \end{pmatrix}`

**[B1]**

(ii)

Find the displacement from $A$ to $B$ by subtracting the position vectors

`\overrightarrow{AB} = \begin{pmatrix} 10 \\ 19 \\ - 2 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} 7 \\ 10 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 9 \\ - 3 \end{pmatrix}`

Use the formula for the magnitude of a vector, `\left|x \mathbf{i} + y \mathbf{j} + z \mathbf{k}\right| = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}}`

`\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\right| = \sqrt{3^{2} + 9^{2} + \left(- 3\right)^{2}} = \sqrt{99}`

**[M1]**

Simplify the surd by taking out the largest square factor, since $99 = 9 \times 11$

`\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\right| = 3 \sqrt{11}`

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> There is a much quicker route to part (ii). Both points sit on the same line, so travelling from $A$ to $B$ just means increasing the parameter by $7 - 4 = 3$, which covers three times the direction vector.
> 
> The direction vector has magnitude `\sqrt{1^{2} + 3^{2} + \left(- 1\right)^{2}} = \sqrt{11}`, so the distance is $3 \sqrt{11}$ straight away, with no need to find $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$ at all.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct $\overset{\rightarrow}{OA} = 7 i + 10 j + k$.
> 
> **B1**: Correct $\overset{\rightarrow}{OB} = 10 i + 19 j - 2 k$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the magnitude, squaring and summing the three components of $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$ and taking the square root. An alternative complete method scores equally: multiplying the change in the parameter by the magnitude of the direction vector.
> 
> **A1**: Correct simplified surd $3 \sqrt{11}$. The surd must be simplified, so $\sqrt{99}$ alone does not earn this mark. Answers which round to $9 . 95$ are accepted, since the question specifies no accuracy.

parts.problemMd:
The coordinates of three points are `A \left(1 , 0 , - 4\right)`, `B \left(3 , - 1 , 6\right)` and `C \left(- 2 , 5 , 7\right)`.

Find $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{AC}$.
parts.solutionMd:
A displacement vector is found by subtracting the position vector of the starting point from that of the end point

`\overrightarrow{AB} = \left(3 \mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} + 6 \mathbf{k}\right) - \left(\mathbf{i} - 4 \mathbf{k}\right)`

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AB} = 2 i - j + 10 k$

**[B1]**

Apply the same subtraction to find $\overset{\rightarrow}{AC}$

`\overrightarrow{AC} = \left(- 2 \mathbf{i} + 5 \mathbf{j} + 7 \mathbf{k}\right) - \left(\mathbf{i} - 4 \mathbf{k}\right)`

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AC} = - 3 i + 5 j + 11 k$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB} = 2 i - j + 10 k$.
> 
> **B1**: Correct $\overset{\rightarrow}{AC} = - 3 i + 5 j + 11 k$. Column vector form is equally acceptable throughout. Reversed vectors $\overset{\rightarrow}{BA}$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{CA}$ do not earn these marks, since the angle asked for in part (c) is the one at $A$.

parts.problemMd: Calculate `\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\right|` and `\left|\overrightarrow{AC}\right|`, and the scalar product `\overrightarrow{AB} \cdot \overrightarrow{AC}`.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the formula for the magnitude of a vector, `\left|x \mathbf{i} + y \mathbf{j} + z \mathbf{k}\right| = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}}`

`\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\right| = \sqrt{2^{2} + \left(- 1\right)^{2} + 10^{2}}`

This surd has no square factor to take out, so leave it exact

`\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\right| = \sqrt{105}`

**[B1]**

Apply the same formula to $\overset{\rightarrow}{AC}$

`\left|\overrightarrow{AC}\right| = \sqrt{\left(- 3\right)^{2} + 5^{2} + 11^{2}}`

`\left|\overrightarrow{AC}\right| = \sqrt{155}`

**[B1]**

For the scalar product, use its component form, `\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = a_{1} b_{1} + a_{2} b_{2} + a_{3} b_{3}`

`\overrightarrow{AB} \cdot \overrightarrow{AC} = \left(2\right)\left(- 3\right) + \left(- 1\right)\left(5\right) + \left(10\right)\left(11\right)`

`\overrightarrow{AB} \cdot \overrightarrow{AC} = 99`

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct `\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\right| = \sqrt{105}`. Accept $10 . 2$ or better.
> 
> **B1**: Correct `\left|\overrightarrow{AC}\right| = \sqrt{155}`. Accept $12 . 4$ or better.
> 
> **B1**: Correct scalar product of $99$. Neither surd simplifies, so leaving both magnitudes in surd form is preferred; a decimal value must not be rounded before part (c), as premature rounding there can lose the final accuracy mark. Follow through on incorrect vectors from part (a).

parts.problemMd:
Hence, find the angle between the vectors $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{AC}$.

Give your answer in degrees correct to 1 decimal place.
parts.solutionMd:
Rearrange the definition of the scalar product, `\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = \left|\mathbf{a}\right| \left|\mathbf{b}\right| \text{cos} \; \theta`, to make the cosine the subject

`\text{cos} \; \theta = \dfrac{\overrightarrow{AB} \cdot \overrightarrow{AC}}{\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\right| \left|\overrightarrow{AC}\right|}`

Substitute the three values found in part (b)

$\text{cos}  θ = \frac{99}{\sqrt{105}\times\sqrt{155}} = 0 . 776023 \dots$

**[M1]**

Take the inverse cosine, keeping the unrounded value for the rounding step

`\theta = \text{cos}^{-1} \left(0.776023 \ldots\right) = 39.1021 \ldots`*°*

Round to 1 decimal place, as the question requires

**Final answer:** $θ = 39 . 1$**° (1 d.p.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct rearrangement to `\text{cos} \; \theta = \dfrac{\overrightarrow{AB} \cdot \overrightarrow{AC}}{\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\right| \left|\overrightarrow{AC}\right|}` with the scalar product divided by the product of the two magnitudes. Follow through on incorrect values from parts (a) and (b).
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to $39 . 1$ degrees. The unrounded value is $39 . 1021 \dots$. An answer in radians does not earn this mark, since degrees are specified.

parts.problemMd:
The vertices of triangle $A B C$ are the points with coordinates `A \left(2 , 4 , - 3\right)`, `B \left(0 , 2 , 1\right)` and `C \left(- 4 , - 2 , - 3\right)`.

(i) Show that `\overrightarrow{BA} \cdot \overrightarrow{BC} = 0`.

(ii) What does the result of part (i) tell you about the triangle $A B C$?
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Both vectors start at $B$, so subtract the position vector of $B$ from each of the others

`\overrightarrow{BA} = \left(2 \mathbf{i} + 4 \mathbf{j} - 3 \mathbf{k}\right) - \left(2 \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}\right)`

**[M1]**

Subtract component by component

$\overset{\rightarrow}{BA} = 2 i + 2 j - 4 k$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{BC} = - 4 i - 4 j - 4 k$

**[A1]**

Use the component form of the scalar product, `\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = a_{1} b_{1} + a_{2} b_{2} + a_{3} b_{3}`

`\overrightarrow{BA} \cdot \overrightarrow{BC} = \left(2\right)\left(- 4\right) + \left(2\right)\left(- 4\right) + \left(- 4\right)\left(- 4\right)`

The first two products are negative and the third is positive, and they cancel exactly

`\overrightarrow{BA} \cdot \overrightarrow{BC} = - 8 - 8 + 16 = 0`

**[A1]**

(ii)

A zero scalar product means the two vectors are perpendicular, and both of these run out of the vertex $B$

**Final answer:** **Triangle **$A B C$** is right-angled at **$B$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for at least one of $\overset{\rightarrow}{BA}$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{BC}$, subtracting the position vector of $B$ from that of the other point.
> 
> **A1**: Both $\overset{\rightarrow}{BA} = 2 i + 2 j - 4 k$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{BC} = - 4 i - 4 j - 4 k$ correct.
> 
> **A1**: The three products formed and summed to give $0$. Because the result is given, the products must be visible. Using $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{CB}$ throughout gives the same value and is accepted, but mixing one reversed vector with one correct vector is not, since that is a different scalar product.
> 
> **B1**: Correct conclusion that the triangle is right-angled at $B$. The vertex must be named; stating only that the triangle is right-angled does not earn this mark, since the zero scalar product locates the right angle at $B$ specifically.

parts.problemMd:
Two lines $l$ and $m$ have equations `\mathbf{r} = - 3 \mathbf{i} - 6 \mathbf{j} + 8 \mathbf{k} + s \left(\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} - \mathbf{k}\right)` and `\mathbf{r} = 8 \mathbf{i} - 10 \mathbf{j} + 6 \mathbf{k} + t \left(2 \mathbf{i} - 3 \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}\right)` respectively.

Show that the two lines meet and find the position vector of the point of intersection.
parts.solutionMd:
A common point must be reachable on both lines, so equate the two general points component by component

`\begin{pmatrix} - 3 + s \\ - 6 + s \\ 8 - s \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 8 + 2 t \\ - 10 - 3 t \\ 6 + t \end{pmatrix}`

**[M1]**

Take the $i$ equation and rearrange it to give $s$ in terms of $t$

$s = 11 + 2 t$

Substitute into the $j$ equation to leave a single unknown

$- 6 + 11 + 2 t = - 10 - 3 t$

**[M1]**

Collect the terms in $t$

$5 t = - 15$

$t = - 3$

Substitute back to find $s$

$s = 11 - 6 = 5$

**[A1]**

Test these values in the remaining equation, working out each side separately

$8 - 5 = 3$

`6 + \left(- 3\right) = 3`

*All three equations hold for the same pair of values*

**Final answer:** **The lines meet**

**[A1]**

Substitute $s = 5$ into the equation of line $l$ to reach the common point

`\mathbf{r} = - 3 \mathbf{i} - 6 \mathbf{j} + 8 \mathbf{k} + 5 \left(\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} - \mathbf{k}\right)`

**[M1]**

Collect the components

$r = 2 i - j + 3 k$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: The two general points equated component by component, giving three equations in $s$ and $t$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method to solve two of the three equations simultaneously for the parameters.
> 
> **A1**: Both $s = 5$ and $t = - 3$ correct. Solving a different pair of equations first is equally acceptable and reaches the same values, since the system here is consistent.
> 
> **A1**: The remaining equation verified, with a conclusion that the lines meet. Because the result is given, the verification must be shown; solving two equations and asserting that the lines meet does not earn this mark.
> 
> **M1**: Correct substitution of a parameter value back into the corresponding line equation.
> 
> **A1**: Correct position vector $2 i - j + 3 k$. Substituting $t = - 3$ into line $m$ is an equally valid route to the same point. Column vector form is accepted, but a set of coordinates is not a position vector.

parts.problemMd:
Two lines $l$ and $m$ have equations `\mathbf{r} = 8 \mathbf{i} - 5 \mathbf{j} - 6 \mathbf{k} + s \left(- \mathbf{i} + 2 \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}\right)` and `\mathbf{r} = 2 \mathbf{i} + 2 \mathbf{j} - 2 \mathbf{k} + t \left(2 \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}\right)` respectively.

(i) Show that the two lines do not intersect.

(ii) Are the two lines skew? Be sure to justify your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

If the lines met, the two general points would agree in all three components

`\begin{pmatrix} 8 - s \\ - 5 + 2 s \\ - 6 + s \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 + 2 t \\ 2 + t \\ - 2 + t \end{pmatrix}`

Rearrange the $i$ equation to give $s$ in terms of $t$

$s = 6 - 2 t$

Substitute into the $j$ equation to leave a single unknown

`- 5 + 2 \left(6 - 2 t\right) = 2 + t`

**[M1]**

Collect the terms in $t$

$7 - 4 t = 2 + t$

$t = 1$

Substitute back to find $s$

$s = 6 - 2 = 4$

**[A1]**

Test these values in the remaining equation, working out each side separately

$- 6 + s = - 6 + 4 = - 2$

$- 2 + t = - 2 + 1 = - 1$

*No single pair of values satisfies all three equations at once*

**Final answer:** $- 2 \neq - 1$**, so the lines do not intersect**

**[A1]**

(ii)

Lines that do not intersect are either parallel or skew, so compare the two direction vectors

`- \mathbf{i} + 2 \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k} \neq \lambda \left(2 \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}\right)`

*The directions are not multiples of one another, so the lines are not parallel*

**Final answer:** **Yes, the lines are skew**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: The general points equated and a correct method used to solve two of the three equations for the parameters.
> 
> **A1**: Correct values $s = 4$ and $t = 1$. Solving a different pair of equations first gives different parameter values, which is expected here because the system is inconsistent, and those are equally acceptable.
> 
> **A1**: The remaining equation shown not to hold, with a conclusion that the lines do not intersect. Because the result is given, both sides must be evaluated and compared.
> 
> **B1**: Correct answer of skew, justified by the direction vectors not being scalar multiples of one another. Accept that the direction vectors have no common factor. Do not accept "the direction vectors are different", "the direction vectors are not equal", "the parameters are not equal", "the scalar product is not zero", or "the line equations are not multiples of each other", as none of these establishes that the lines are not parallel.

parts.problemMd:
The line $l$ has equation `\mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ - 4 \\ 10 \end{pmatrix} + s \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ - 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}`.

Point $N$ is the point on line $l$ such that the line connecting $N$ and the point `P \left(3 , 4 , 1\right)` is perpendicular to $l$.

Find the position vector, $\overset{\rightarrow}{ON}$, of point $N$.
parts.solutionMd:
$N$ lies on $l$, so its position vector is what the equation of the line gives for one particular value of $s$

`\overrightarrow{ON} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 + s \\ - 4 - s \\ 10 + 3 s \end{pmatrix}`

**[M1]**

The vector from $N$ to $P$ is found by subtracting these position vectors

`\overrightarrow{NP} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} 1 + s \\ - 4 - s \\ 10 + 3 s \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 - s \\ 8 + s \\ - 9 - 3 s \end{pmatrix}`

$N P$ is perpendicular to the line, so its scalar product with the direction vector is zero

`\begin{pmatrix} 2 - s \\ 8 + s \\ - 9 - 3 s \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ - 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} = 0`

**[M1]**

Expand the scalar product and collect like terms

`\left(2 - s\right) - \left(8 + s\right) + 3 \left(- 9 - 3 s\right) = 0`

$- 33 - 11 s = 0$

Solve for the parameter

$s = - 3$

**[A1]**

Substitute this value back into the general point

`\overrightarrow{ON} = \begin{pmatrix} - 2 \\ - 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: A general point on the line written in terms of the parameter.
> 
> **M1**: A relevant scalar product set equal to zero, using $\overset{\rightarrow}{NP}$ (or $\overset{\rightarrow}{PN}$) and the direction vector of the line.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value $s = - 3$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct position vector $- 2 i - j + k$. Column vector form is equally acceptable. A set of coordinates is not a position vector, though this is condoned if the vector form appears elsewhere in the working.

parts.problemMd: Hence find the shortest distance from point $P$ to the line $l$.
parts.solutionMd:
The shortest distance is measured along the perpendicular, so substitute $s = - 3$ into the expression for $\overset{\rightarrow}{NP}$

`\overrightarrow{NP} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 + 3 \\ 8 - 3 \\ - 9 + 9 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 5 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}`

**[M1]**

Use the formula for the magnitude of a vector, `\left|x \mathbf{i} + y \mathbf{j} + z \mathbf{k}\right| = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}}`

`\left|\overrightarrow{NP}\right| = \sqrt{5^{2} + 5^{2} + 0^{2}} = \sqrt{50}`

Simplify the surd by taking out the largest square factor, since $50 = 25 \times 2$

`\left|\overrightarrow{NP}\right| = 5 \sqrt{2}`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for the distance, finding $\overset{\rightarrow}{NP}$ (or the distance from $P$ to their $N$) and applying the magnitude formula. Follow through on an incorrect $\overset{\rightarrow}{ON}$ from part (a).
> 
> **A1**: Correct simplified surd $5 \sqrt{2}$. Answers which round to $7 . 07$ are accepted, since the question specifies no accuracy, but $\sqrt{50}$ left unsimplified does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd:
In the triangle $A B C$, the vectors $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{AC}$ are given by

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AB} = - 2 i + 3 j - k$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AC} = - 5 i - 4 j - 7 k$

![Triangle ABC, with A at the lower left, B above it and C to the right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-maths-20-pure-3/vectors/vector-equations-of-lines-and-the-scalar-product/assets/005-triangle-abc-with-a-at-the-lower-left-b-above-it.png)

Show that angle $B A C = 81 . 9$°, correct to 1 decimal place.
parts.solutionMd:
Both given vectors point away from $A$, so the angle between them is the angle $B A C$. Use the scalar product, `\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = a_{1} b_{1} + a_{2} b_{2} + a_{3} b_{3} = \left|\mathbf{a}\right| \left|\mathbf{b}\right| \text{cos} \; \theta`

`\overrightarrow{AB} \cdot \overrightarrow{AC} = \left(- 2\right) \left(- 5\right) + \left(3\right) \left(- 4\right) + \left(- 1\right) \left(- 7\right)`

**[M1]**

Evaluate the three products and add them

`\overrightarrow{AB} \cdot \overrightarrow{AC} = 10 - 12 + 7 = 5`

**[A1]**

Find the magnitude of each vector

`\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\right| = \sqrt{\left(- 2\right)^{2} + 3^{2} + \left(- 1\right)^{2}} = \sqrt{14}`

`\left|\overrightarrow{AC}\right| = \sqrt{\left(- 5\right)^{2} + \left(- 4\right)^{2} + \left(- 7\right)^{2}} = \sqrt{90}`

Rearrange the second form to make $\text{cos}  θ$ the subject

`\text{cos} \; \theta = \frac{\overrightarrow{AB} \cdot \overrightarrow{AC}}{\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\right| \left|\overrightarrow{AC}\right|} = \frac{5}{\sqrt{14} \sqrt{90}}`

**[M1]**

Evaluate the quotient, keeping the unrounded value

$\text{cos}  θ = 0 . 140859 \dots$

**[A1]**

Take the inverse cosine

$θ = 81 . 9024 \dots$*°*

**Final answer:** `\angle BAC = 81.9`**° (1 d.p.)**

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Check that both vectors point away from the vertex before you use the scalar product. Here $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{AC}$ both start at $A$, so the scalar product gives the angle you want directly. If one of them had pointed towards $A$ instead, the scalar product would give the supplementary angle and you would need to subtract from $180$°.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct process to evaluate the scalar product of the two given vectors, multiplying corresponding components and summing the results.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value $5$ for the scalar product.
> 
> **M1**: Correct process for both magnitudes, together with dividing the scalar product by their product to obtain $\text{cos}  θ$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct unrounded value of $\text{cos}  θ$, or the exact form $\frac{5}{\sqrt{14}\sqrt{90}}$ or equivalent. Because the answer is given, a value for $\text{cos}  θ$ must be seen. Writing down an inverse cosine and jumping straight to $81 . 9$° does not earn this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Correct angle of $81 . 9$° obtained from fully correct working, with a more accurate value such as $81 . 90$° seen before rounding.

parts.problemMd:
With respect to the origin $O$, the points $R$ and $S$ have position vectors given by

$\overset{\rightarrow}{OR} = - i + 5 j + 14 k$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{OS} = 7 i - 2 j + 12 k$

Find

(i) the vector $\overset{\rightarrow}{RS}$,

(ii) a unit vector parallel to $\overset{\rightarrow}{RS}$.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Subtract the position vector of $R$ from the position vector of $S$

`\overrightarrow{RS} = \overrightarrow{OS} - \overrightarrow{OR} = \left(7 \mathbf{i} - 2 \mathbf{j} + 12 \mathbf{k}\right) - \left(- \mathbf{i} + 5 \mathbf{j} + 14 \mathbf{k}\right)`

$\overset{\rightarrow}{RS} = 8 i - 7 j - 2 k$

**[B1]**

(ii)

A unit vector has magnitude $1$, so first find the magnitude of $\overset{\rightarrow}{RS}$

`\left|\overrightarrow{RS}\right| = \sqrt{8^{2} + \left(- 7\right)^{2} + \left(- 2\right)^{2}} = \sqrt{64 + 49 + 4} = \sqrt{117}`

Divide the vector by its own magnitude

`\hat{\mathbf{u}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{117}} \left(8 \mathbf{i} - 7 \mathbf{j} - 2 \mathbf{k}\right)`

**[M1 A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct vector $8 i - 7 j - 2 k$, or the column vector form. The reverse vector $\overset{\rightarrow}{SR}$ does not earn this mark.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method, dividing $\overset{\rightarrow}{RS}$ by its own magnitude. Follow through on an incorrect vector from part (i).
> 
> **A1**: Correct unit vector. The form with the fraction written outside the bracket and the separated component form $\frac{8}{\sqrt{117}} i - \frac{7}{\sqrt{117}} j - \frac{2}{\sqrt{117}} k$ are equally acceptable, as is the column vector form, and the negative of this vector is also accepted.

parts.problemMd: Find the angle that $\overset{\rightarrow}{RS}$ makes with the positive $y$-axis.
parts.solutionMd:
The positive $y$-axis has direction $j$, so take the scalar product of $\overset{\rightarrow}{RS}$ with $j$. Only the $j$ component survives

`\text{cos} \; \theta = \frac{\overrightarrow{RS} \cdot \mathbf{j}}{\left|\overrightarrow{RS}\right| \left|\mathbf{j}\right|} = \frac{- 7}{\sqrt{117}} = - 0.647150 \ldots`

**[M1]**

The cosine is negative, so the angle is obtuse. Take the inverse cosine

$θ = 130 . 327 \dots$*°*

**Final answer:** $θ = 130 . 3$**° (1 d.p.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method, dividing the $j$ component of $\overset{\rightarrow}{RS}$ by the magnitude of $\overset{\rightarrow}{RS}$, or equivalently taking the scalar product with $j$ and dividing by the product of the magnitudes. A value for $\text{cos}  θ$ must be seen.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to $130 . 3$°. The acute angle $49 . 7$° does not earn this mark, since the question names the positive $y$-axis.

parts.problemMd:
The vector $\overset{\rightarrow}{TU}$ is given by $\overset{\rightarrow}{TU} = - 24 i + 21 j + 6 k$.

Explain, giving a reason for your answer, whether the vectors $\overset{\rightarrow}{RS}$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{TU}$ are parallel.
parts.solutionMd:
Two vectors are parallel when one is a scalar multiple of the other, so compare the components in turn

$\frac{-24}{8} = - 3 ,  \frac{21}{-7} = - 3 ,  \frac{6}{-2} = - 3$

**[M1]**

The same multiplier works for all three components

**Final answer:** $\overset{\rightarrow}{TU} = - 3 \overset{\rightarrow}{RS}$**, so the vectors are parallel**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct comparison of the two vectors component by component, showing the same multiplier arises each time. Dividing in the other order, giving $- \frac{1}{3}$ throughout, is equally acceptable.
> 
> **A1**: Correct conclusion that the vectors are parallel, supported by a statement that one is a scalar multiple of the other, such as $\overset{\rightarrow}{TU} = - 3 \overset{\rightarrow}{RS}$. A bare assertion that they are parallel does not earn this mark, and neither do reasons phrased as the vectors being different, the components being unequal, or the scalar product not being zero. The negative multiplier does not prevent the vectors being parallel.

parts.problemMd:
Find the equation of each of these lines in vector form.

The line joining `\left(3 , - 2\right)` to `\left(- 1 , 5\right)`.
parts.solutionMd:
A line through two points needs a direction, which is the displacement from one to the other

`\mathbf{d} = \left(- \mathbf{i} + 5 \mathbf{j}\right) - \left(3 \mathbf{i} - 2 \mathbf{j}\right)`

**[M1]**

Subtract component by component, taking care with the double negative in the $j$ direction

$d = - 4 i + 7 j$

**[A1]**

Use the vector form of a line, $r = a + t b$, taking the first point as $a$ and this displacement as $b$

`\mathbf{r} = 3 \mathbf{i} - 2 \mathbf{j} + t \left(- 4 \mathbf{i} + 7 \mathbf{j}\right)`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for a direction vector, subtracting the position vector of one point from the other.
> 
> **A1**: Correct direction $- 4 i + 7 j$, or its negative $4 i - 7 j$.
> 
> **A1**: Fully correct equation, which must include $r =$. Either point may be used as the starting point, any letter may be used for the parameter, and any non-zero multiple of the direction is accepted.

parts.problemMd: Find, in vector form, the equation of the line passing through `\left(3 , 1\right)` parallel to $4 i - 12 j$.
parts.solutionMd:
Parallel lines share a direction, so $4 i - 12 j$ can be used as it stands. Both components share a factor of 4, so divide through to keep the equation tidy

`4 \mathbf{i} - 12 \mathbf{j} = 4 \left(\mathbf{i} - 3 \mathbf{j}\right)`

**[M1]**

Take the given point as the position vector and substitute into $r = a + t b$

`\mathbf{r} = 3 \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} + t \left(\mathbf{i} - 3 \mathbf{j}\right)`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct identification of $3 i + j$ as the position vector of a point on the line, together with a direction parallel to $4 i - 12 j$. Available without $r =$ being written.
> 
> **A1**: Fully correct equation, which must include $r =$. The direction need not be simplified, so `\mathbf{r} = 3 \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} + t \left(4 \mathbf{i} - 12 \mathbf{j}\right)` is equally acceptable, as is any other non-zero multiple.

parts.problemMd:
Find the equation of each of these lines in vector form.

(i) Through `\left(2 , - 7 , 9\right)` in the same direction as $6 i + 3 j - 9 k$.

(ii) Through `\left(4 , - 3 , 1\right)` and `\left(- 8 , 3 , - 5\right)`.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The direction is given, and all three components share a factor of 3, so divide through to keep the equation tidy

`6 \mathbf{i} + 3 \mathbf{j} - 9 \mathbf{k} = 3 \left(2 \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} - 3 \mathbf{k}\right)`

**[M1]**

Take the given point as the position vector and substitute into $r = a + t b$

`\mathbf{r} = 2 \mathbf{i} - 7 \mathbf{j} + 9 \mathbf{k} + t \left(2 \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} - 3 \mathbf{k}\right)`

**[A1]**

(ii)

Two points are given this time, so start with the displacement between them

`\mathbf{d} = \left(- 8 \mathbf{i} + 3 \mathbf{j} - 5 \mathbf{k}\right) - \left(4 \mathbf{i} - 3 \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}\right) = - 12 \mathbf{i} + 6 \mathbf{j} - 6 \mathbf{k}`

**[M1]**

All three components share a factor of $- 6$, so divide through

`\mathbf{d} = - 6 \left(2 \mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}\right)`

**[A1]**

Take the first point as the position vector and the simplified displacement as the direction

`\mathbf{r} = 4 \mathbf{i} - 3 \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k} + t \left(2 \mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}\right)`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct identification in (i) of $2 i - 7 j + 9 k$ as the position vector of a point on the line, together with a direction parallel to $6 i + 3 j - 9 k$.
> 
> **A1**: Fully correct equation in (i), which must include $r =$. The direction need not be simplified.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method in (ii) for a direction vector, subtracting the position vector of one point from the other.
> 
> **A1**: Correct direction, either $- 12 i + 6 j - 6 k$ or any non-zero multiple such as $2 i - j + k$.
> 
> **A1**: Fully correct equation in (ii), which must include $r =$. Either point may be used as the starting point.

parts.problemMd: Show that the point `\left(10 , - 6 , 5\right)` does not lie on the line found in part (a)(ii).
parts.solutionMd:
If the point were on the line, one value of $t$ would reproduce all three components, so use the $i$ component to find the only candidate

$4 + 2 t = 10$

$t = 3$

**[M1]**

Test this value in the other two components

$- 3 - 3 = - 6$

$1 + 3 = 4$

*The *$j$* component matches but the *$k$* component does not*

**Final answer:** $4 \neq 5$**, so the point does not lie on the line**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method to find a value of the parameter from one component, giving $t = 3$. Follow through on an incorrect line from part (a)(ii).
> 
> **A1**: At least one remaining component shown to disagree for that value of $t$, with a conclusion that the point does not lie on the line. Because the result is given, the disagreeing values must both be evaluated and compared. Checking only the $i$ and $j$ components is not sufficient, since those two agree.

parts.problemMd:
The coordinates of three points are `A \left(2 , - 1 , 5\right)`, `B \left(4 , 1 , 1\right)` and `C \left(- 2 , - 5 , 9\right)`.

Find $\overset{\rightarrow}{BA}$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{BC}$.
parts.solutionMd:
Both vectors start at $B$, so subtract the position vector of $B$ from each of the others

`\overrightarrow{BA} = \left(2 \mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} + 5 \mathbf{k}\right) - \left(4 \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}\right)`

$\overset{\rightarrow}{BA} = - 2 i - 2 j + 4 k$

**[B1]**

Apply the same subtraction to find $\overset{\rightarrow}{BC}$

`\overrightarrow{BC} = \left(- 2 \mathbf{i} - 5 \mathbf{j} + 9 \mathbf{k}\right) - \left(4 \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}\right)`

$\overset{\rightarrow}{BC} = - 6 i - 6 j + 8 k$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct $\overset{\rightarrow}{BA} = - 2 i - 2 j + 4 k$.
> 
> **B1**: Correct $\overset{\rightarrow}{BC} = - 6 i - 6 j + 8 k$. Column vector form is equally acceptable. Both vectors reversed, giving $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{CB}$, produces the same angle in part (b) and is condoned there, but the vectors named in the question are what these marks require.

parts.problemMd: By considering the scalar product `\overrightarrow{BA} \cdot \overrightarrow{BC}`, or otherwise, calculate the angle between $\overset{\rightarrow}{BA}$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{BC}$. Give your answer in degrees, accurate to 1 decimal place.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the component form of the scalar product, `\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = a_{1} b_{1} + a_{2} b_{2} + a_{3} b_{3}`

`\overrightarrow{BA} \cdot \overrightarrow{BC} = \left(- 2\right)\left(- 6\right) + \left(- 2\right)\left(- 6\right) + \left(4\right)\left(8\right) = 56`

**[M1]**

Find the magnitude of each vector using `\left|x \mathbf{i} + y \mathbf{j} + z \mathbf{k}\right| = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}}`

`\left|\overrightarrow{BA}\right| = \sqrt{\left(- 2\right)^{2} + \left(- 2\right)^{2} + 4^{2}} = \sqrt{24}`

`\left|\overrightarrow{BC}\right| = \sqrt{\left(- 6\right)^{2} + \left(- 6\right)^{2} + 8^{2}} = \sqrt{136}`

Rearrange the definition of the scalar product, `\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = \left|\mathbf{a}\right| \left|\mathbf{b}\right| \text{cos} \; \theta`, and substitute

$\text{cos}  θ = \frac{56}{\sqrt{24}\times\sqrt{136}} = 0 . 980196 \dots$

**[M1]**

Take the inverse cosine, keeping the unrounded value for the rounding step

`\theta = \text{cos}^{-1} \left(0.980196 \ldots\right) = 11.4217 \ldots`*°*

Round to 1 decimal place, as the question requires

**Final answer:** $θ = 11 . 4$**° (1 d.p.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct process for the scalar product of the two relevant vectors, giving 56.
> 
> **M1**: Correct process for both magnitudes, with the scalar product divided by their product to give the cosine. Follow through on incorrect vectors from part (a).
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to $11 . 4$ degrees. The unrounded value is $11 . 4217 \dots$. An answer in radians does not earn this mark, since degrees are specified. The question allows an alternative method, so applying the cosine rule to the three side lengths of the triangle scores equally.

parts.problemMd:
In the triangle $A B C$, the vectors $\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{AC}$ are given by

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AB} = 7 i + j - k$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AC} = - 2 i + 5 k$

![Triangle ABC, with A at the bottom, B at the upper left and C to the right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-maths-20-pure-3/vectors/vector-equations-of-lines-and-the-scalar-product/assets/004-triangle-abc-with-a-at-the-bottom-b-at-the-upper.png)

Show that angle $B A C = 119 . 6$°, correct to 1 decimal place.

**[A1]**

> **M1**: Correct process to evaluate the scalar product of the two given vectors, multiplying corresponding components and summing the results.

> **M1**: Correct process for both magnitudes, together with dividing the scalar product by their product to obtain $\text{cos}  θ$.

parts.problemMd: Hence find the area of the triangle $A B C$, giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the formula for the area of a triangle given two sides and the angle between them, $\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} a b  \text{sin}  C$, with the two sides meeting at $A$

`\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} \left|\overrightarrow{AB}\right| \left|\overrightarrow{AC}\right| \text{sin} \; \angle BAC = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{51} \sqrt{29} \, \text{sin} \; 119.6070 \ldots`*°*

Evaluate, using the unrounded angle from part (a)

$\text{Area} = 16 . 7182 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{Area} = 16 . 7$** square units (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method, using `\frac{1}{2} \left|\overrightarrow{AB}\right| \left|\overrightarrow{AC}\right| \text{sin} \; \theta` with the two magnitudes and the angle from part (a). Follow through on an incorrect angle.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to $16 . 7$. Using the rounded angle $119 . 6$° still gives $16 . 7$, so it is not penalised here.

parts.problemMd:
The vertices of triangle $A B C$ are the points with coordinates `A \left(5 , - 3 , 0\right)`, `B \left(- 2 , 0 , - 1\right)` and `C \left(1 , 2 , 1\right)`.

(i) Calculate the scalar products `\overrightarrow{AB} \cdot \overrightarrow{AC}`, `\overrightarrow{BA} \cdot \overrightarrow{BC}` and `\overrightarrow{CA} \cdot \overrightarrow{CB}`.

(ii) What does the result of part (i) tell you about the triangle $A B C$?
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Each scalar product needs the two vectors running out of one vertex, so start with the pair at $A$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AB} = - 7 i + 3 j - k$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AC} = - 4 i + 5 j + k$

**[M1]**

Use the component form of the scalar product, `\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = a_{1} b_{1} + a_{2} b_{2} + a_{3} b_{3}`

`\overrightarrow{AB} \cdot \overrightarrow{AC} = 28 + 15 - 1 = 42`

**[A1]**

Now take the pair running out of $B$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{BA} = 7 i - 3 j + k$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{BC} = 3 i + 2 j + 2 k$

Multiply the matching components and add the results

`\overrightarrow{BA} \cdot \overrightarrow{BC} = 21 - 6 + 2 = 17`

**[A1]**

Finally take the pair running out of $C$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{CA} = 4 i - 5 j - k$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{CB} = - 3 i - 2 j - 2 k$

Multiply the matching components and add the results

`\overrightarrow{CA} \cdot \overrightarrow{CB} = - 12 + 10 + 2 = 0`

**[A1]**

(ii)

Only the third scalar product is zero, and a zero scalar product means the two vectors are perpendicular. Those two vectors both run out of the vertex $C$

**Final answer:** **Triangle **$A B C$** is right-angled at **$C$

**[B1]**
